Think of a tenant who signs a new lease every year and treats the terms as a formality that has never been enforced, and who is surprised when the landlord finally acts on a clause. Agreements had been made here and set aside repeatedly, and the question suggests that the repetition had become invisible to the people doing it. The closing clause explains why: an agreement is only as strong as the belief behind it, and where belief is thin the paper is treated as decoration. A reader can run the same test on the promises he makes in the ordinary course of his life, since the Book's interest in this passage is in what a person's repeated conduct says about the value he places on his word. The verse asks the question and leaves the reader to find his own case in it.

**THE HABIT AND WHAT IT REVEALS**

The last clause of the verse supplies the diagnosis, and it is stated as a fact about most of the community rather than as a suspicion. Unbelief is treated here as the soil in which covenant-breaking grows, and the people's own account of their hearts has already appeared earlier in the sūrah. The verdict falls on people who accepted something and then treated their acceptance as negotiable, not on those who never accepted anything at all. The Book's language about belief is consistently about what a person's conduct shows, which is why a broken agreement counts as evidence in this passage. The next verse names the specific occasion that had provoked the question, and it shows what the community did when the messenger it had been promised finally arrived. Today, repeated broken promises usually reveal not a weak memory but a weak commitment to the authority behind the promise. Because unbelief weakens the authority of the covenant at its root, repeated casting aside is presented as evidence rather than as an unrelated flaw.

---

## Verse 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know

**A BOOK CAST BEHIND THE BACK**

The verse names the specific occasion behind the question and describes how the community received what it had been waiting for: ***“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming”***, ***“their own Scriptures—some of”***, ***“the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah”*** behind their backs, and the Book adds that they did so as though they did not know. The messenger arrived confirming what they already held, and the response was to discard the confirmation as an item of rubbish. The gesture in the verse is worth pausing over, because it is the gesture of a person who wants something out of the way rather than something to be refuted. Nothing in the sentence suggests an examination of the messenger's claims; the Book records a movement, and the movement is away from the evidence. What the community did with the confirmation is stated in its own closing clause, and the clause is the Book's judgement on the whole gesture: ***“as if they did not know”***.

**THE GESTURE AND WHAT IT MEANS**

The phrase used for the discarding describes an object thrown behind the back, which is the posture of a person who intends never to look at the thing again. The Book uses the same image elsewhere for people who treat a scripture as an encumbrance, and it uses it here for the people who were its custodians. The clause about acting as if they did not know is a comment on the shape of the refusal rather than on their information, since the same community had been described in earlier verses as recognising what had arrived. The reading handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās describes a deliberate forgetfulness here, and it fits the verse's placement after the account of covenants discarded as a habit. The motion resembles a committee quietly shelving the report it had commissioned.

**THE CONFIRMING THAT MADE THE REFUSAL STRANGE**

The messenger's arrival is described as confirming the community's own scripture, which means the new revelation did not ask them to abandon anything they held. The Book has already made this point several times in the sūrah, and it returns to it here because the refusal has now become an act rather than a debate. The same charge is laid out in another passage where the covenant to make the scripture known is joined to the account of what was hidden: (3:187 — **“who were given the Scripture to make it known to”**). A reader might reasonably ask what could be objected to in a message that agreed with the books already in hand, and the answer is supplied by the whole section: the objection was to the messenger and to the community that would receive him. The confirmation made the refusal harder to justify rather than easier.

**A FIRM THAT BURIES ITS OWN REPORT**

Think of a company whose auditors report exactly what the accounts show, and whose directors respond by filing the report and never mentioning it again. The confirmation of its own scriptures was in these people's hands, and the document was treated as an inconvenience to be put out of sight. The comparison is uncomfortable because the report is the only item in the story that could have settled the argument, and the Book records what was done with it. A reader who has watched an institution receive the evidence it asked for and then stop discussing the question has seen the same movement performed on a smaller stage. The verse names the manoeuvre and leaves the reader to notice where he has seen it.

**EVIDENCE ARRIVES AND IS SET ASIDE**

The passage settles an old question about the value of proof by showing what a community does when the proof arrives, and the answer has nothing to do with the quality of the proof. The Book's account is that the evidence was recognised and discarded in nearly the same breath, which is why it appends the remark about acting as though they did not know. A reader who has spent time trying to settle a religious question with arguments should notice what the verse assumes: that the barrier in the cases described here was never the argument. The next verse turns to a different subject, the magic that this community was said to have followed, and the transition shows the Book moving from what people refuse to what they prefer. What remains from this sentence is the gesture, and the gesture is the part a reader can check in himself. Today, an institution can honour a founding document in ceremony while placing its inconvenient terms behind every practical decision.

---

## Verse 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew

**THE ART THEY TOOK UP INSTEAD**

The verse begins by naming what the community had been doing while the confirming Book lay behind its back, and the first words set the alternative in place: ***“They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon.”***. The ˹instead˺ in the translation marks a substitution, as though a choice had been made between two available things, and the choice was made in favour of an art that the devils themselves had promoted. The period the verse names is the reign of Solomon, which places the practice in a time the community remembered as its own golden age rather than in some foreign or forgotten era. A report carried from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the community's claim in this connection as one that traced the art back to that reign, and the verse corrects the attribution in the same breath that it records the practice. What the reader is being shown is a people that had something better in its hands and reached for something else.

**SOLOMON IS CLEARED BEFORE THE STORY IS TOLD**

Before anything is said about what was taught, an accusation that had attached itself to a prophet is removed, and the removal is emphatic: ***“Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved.”***. The order of the two clauses matters, since the denial is placed first and the true subject of the charge second, placing the correction before the account of the deed. The Book has already shown, earlier in this sūrah, how a people's own traditions can dishonour the prophets it claims to honour, and the pattern repeats here in a single sentence. The historical claim that this king had commanded the art is traced by Ibn ʿAbbās to a story the community itself circulated, which means the verse is correcting an inherited slander rather than answering an outside critic. What stands after the correction is the true account of the art's transmission, and the transmitters are not the king but the devils who claimed it.

**THE TRANSMISSION AND ITS RECIPIENTS**

The sentence continues with the activity of those devils and names the recipients: ***“They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon.”***. The construction is worth a second look, because the revelation to the two angels is placed in the same clause as the teaching of magic, and the Book is careful to distinguish the two in what follows. Babylon is named as the place, and the naming gives the practice a location and a history rather than leaving it as a vague menace. The setting is the same city the community remembered as the site of its own exile, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās places the two angels' descent there with a warning attached. A reader who has seen how quickly a practice acquires a respectable lineage will notice what this verse does with the lineage it is offered: it separates the divine revelation from the human art and refuses to let them share a name.

**THE WARNING THAT CAME WITH THE TEACHING**

The verse then reports the terms on which the knowledge was delivered, and the terms turn the whole episode into a test: ***“The two angels never taught anyone without saying,”*** and then the words they never omitted: ***“We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.”***. The disclaimer is spoken by the teachers themselves, which means the people who took the art up had been told plainly, at the moment of receiving it, what it was for and what it risked. There is no suggestion in the sentence that the information was unavailable or hidden, and none that the buyers were misled about the price of the transaction. The verse makes the two angels witnesses against the very use their knowledge was put to, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read the clause as a warning rather than an invitation. What the reader should see is a decision made in the open, with the outcome stated in advance by the people who knew most about it.

**A PATIENT WHO READS THE WARNING LABEL**

Picture a patient who reads the leaflet that comes with a medicine, understands the risk it sets out, and takes the dose anyway because the effect is what he wants. The next words of the verse describe exactly that decision and its result: ***“Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife;”***, and the harm named is domestic rather than spectacular. The art's first effect is to split what the Book has spent much of this sūrah binding together, and the phrase marks the damage as reaching the smallest unit of the community. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the practice in this period as one that set spouses against each other, and the verse's own report of it is that it worked in exactly that way. Anyone who has seen a household come apart over something that promised an advantage to one of its members has seen the mechanism described here, and the Book is not finished with the subject.

**THE LIMIT ON THE HARM THEY COULD DO**

The following clause places a boundary around the whole practice: ***“although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will.”***. The art that the community had taken up, then, was neither self-sufficient nor secure, since the harm it produced was always within the permission of the One who permitted no other power. The same boundary appears in another sūrah where the claim of the magicians is measured against what God does with it: (10:81 — **“Allah will surely make it useless”**). The Book never treats magic as a rival power; it treats it as a technique that works inside limits, and this clause is one of the clearest statements of that position. A reader who has feared such things more than he feared God has the verse's correction in the sentence, and the correction is not so much a warning as a description of where the power actually lies.

**THEY TRADED SOMETHING FOR NOTHING**

The verse then states the bargain from the buyers' side: ***“They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—”***, and the verdict is followed by a clause about knowledge that leaves no room for ignorance: ***“although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter.”***. The transaction described is one in which the purchaser knew the price and the loss before he paid, which places this community in the same family as the buyers of guidance named earlier in the sūrah: (2:86 — **“These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world”**). The Book's account of the episode is therefore about a settled decision rather than a seduction, and the sentence repeats the point about knowledge to keep that fact in front of the reader. What the people acquired here was a technique with no lasting use, and the clause about the Hereafter makes the accounting explicit rather than implied.

**THE SUM PAID FOR THE ART**

The verse closes with a verdict on the terms of the sale and then with an exclamation that leaves the reader holding the loss: ***“Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls,”*** and then ***“if only they knew”***. The word for the price suggests a measure that anyone could inspect, and the Book's judgement is that the sum was pitiful for what it bought. The final clause returns to knowledge, which the verse has already stated the buyers possessed, so that the exclamation reads as a lament over a knowing choice rather than a comment on information that never arrived. The passage has therefore come full circle from its opening: it began with a community following an art instead of a revelation, and it ends with the price of that decision stated in the plainest terms. The reading carried from Ibn ʿAbbās treats the closing exclamation as a lament over a knowing choice, and the verse's own words support him: the buyers had been told what the art was and what it cost. The next verse names the alternative that had been available the whole time, and the reader can compare the two outcomes for himself. Present-day fascination with hidden techniques still becomes destructive when power is sought without concern for the homes, trust and consciences it breaks.

---

## Verse 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew

**FAITH AND RESTRAINT LEFT UNCHOSEN**

The verse that closes this stretch turns from what the community did to what it might have had, and it opens with a wish: ***“If only they were faithful”***. The word for faithfulness here carries the sense of holding to something with confidence, and the Book places it first, before any mention of the reward that would have followed. The previous verse ended with the price the community paid for an art that could not profit it, and this sentence supplies the alternative it passed over. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the wish as a statement about what was available rather than a regret about what was impossible, which is the reading the grammar supports: the condition was within reach of the people being addressed. The method on display is the Book's habit of closing a section this way, describing a loss in terms of a choice that was open.

**FAITH AND MINDFULNESS NAMED TOGETHER**

The wish is completed by a second quality, and the two are joined in a single phrase: ***“and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah”***. Faithfulness and mindfulness are treated as the two halves of one posture, and the Book consistently pairs them when it describes what it means to hold a religion rather than to merely inherit one. The reward is described as better rather than large, which measures it against what the community actually received in the transaction just described. Someone who has been given a great deal and who has watched the same condition appear in the sources will recognise the comparison being drawn here. The sentence does not say the reward would have been infinite or immediate; it says it would have been better than the thing the buyers took instead, because the comparison being drawn is with the bargain the community actually struck.

**THE REWARD THAT WOULD HAVE FOLLOWED**

The phrase about the reward is placed where the reader expects a description of profit, and its wording is deliberately plain: what was on offer is named as a reward from Allah rather than as a technique, a status, or a possession. The contrast with the magic described in the preceding verse is exact, since that practice brought harm to its buyers while this reward is described from the hand of the One who gives it. The point of naming the giver rather than the gift is that the terms belong to the giver, and no resentment can alter them. Another sūrah states the rule this sentence assumes, and states it as a general law rather than a promise to one community: (16:96 — **“Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting”**). The verse's wish is therefore about a durable return rather than a temporary advantage, and that contrast is the subject of the whole passage. A reader who measures his own choices by what lasts will find the comparison here easy to apply.

**A TRADER WHO KEEPS TWO SETS OF BOOKS**

Think of a trader who keeps two sets of books: the one he shows when he wants a quick return, and the one that would have grown quietly if he had credited it and left it alone. The community addressed here had a scheme beside it that cost more than it paid, and the verse names the alternative with the simplicity of a single word. The comparison is not between two equal offers; it is between something that ends and something that is described as coming from Allah, which places the two beyond any real competition. What turns on the comparison is the whole weight of the verse's regret, since the community is not accused of choosing a worse bargain by a small margin. Anyone who has watched a business kept alive for years on an arrangement everyone recognised as ruinous has seen the pattern, and the verse's regret is aimed at the recognition rather than the loss. What the sentence offers is the plain arithmetic of the choice.

**THE KNOWING THAT CHANGES NOTHING**

The verse ends where it began, with the same clause, and the repetition turns the wish into an assessment: ***“if only they knew”***. The Book has already stated, in the previous verse, that the buyers knew what they were taking on, so the closing clause is not a comment on missing information. It describes the gap between knowing a fact and letting the fact govern a decision, which is the subject the section has been building toward throughout. The clause is read by Ibn ʿAbbās as a statement about the community's knowledge of the scripture in its hands, and the reading fits the placement of the verse after the account of a covenant discarded and a Book cast away. What the reader carries away from the sentence is a question about whether his own conduct is governed by what he knows, and the question applies to the reader before it applies to anyone else. Today, a profitable skill remains a loss when its reward depends on abandoning faith, restraint and the welfare of another person.

---

## Verse 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment

**THE CONGREGATION TAKEN TO TASK**

The verse opens with a call to the believers, and the address establishes who is being corrected before the correction is stated: ***“O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.”*** ***“[Herd us!]”***. The instruction is given to the community that has accepted the message, which means the warning is not about an outsider's mockery but about a habit inside the household of faith. The word itself is an ordinary request in one language and an insult in another, and the translation supplies both meanings in brackets so that the reader can see the double edge. The Book's concern in the sentence is with what a community's speech signals about its stance, since the same request could be made with a word that carried no insult at all. What the reader is shown is a congregation being taught to weigh its words rather than to rely on its intentions.

**A DOUBLE MEANING REMOVED FROM SPEECH**

The first word is set aside in the same sentence that names its replacement, and the reason is the way it fell on the ear of the people being addressed. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the believers had taken up a form of address they had heard from the People of the Book, and that the form carried a jeer in the other community's usage. The verse does not require the believers to have intended the insult; it requires them to stop using a word that had become a mark of mockery in the mouths of others. This is the Book's consistent treatment of speech, since it judges what a phrase does in a community rather than what a speaker privately meant by it. A reader who has adopted the idiom of a hostile group without noticing what the idiom carries will find the instruction addressed to him.

**THE REPLACEMENT AND WHY IT WAS CHOSEN**

The verse supplies the substitute immediately, and the substitute is a word that asks to be attended to: ***“But say, “Unẓurna,”*** ***“[Tend to us!]”***. The change is not a matter of taste; the second term asks for attention in a way that carries no hint of diminishment, which is what the first term had come to suggest. The Book's habit of replacing a defective practice with a sound one, rather than merely forbidding it, appears throughout this sūrah and is at work here in a single sentence. Another passage states the rule the verse applies, in the same four words it takes to give the instruction: (33:70 — **“Be mindful of Allah, and say what is right”**). A community's speech is treated as part of its obedience rather than as a private matter, and the verse's replacement shows how ordinary the corrected form was meant to be.

**A GUEST WHO COPIES THE WRONG PHRASE**

Think of a guest who copies a phrase he hears at a neighbour's table, not knowing that the phrase means something dismissive in the neighbour's own family. The community in this verse had been using the form with a decent intention, and the instruction came because the form itself had been turned against the faith. The account given in another passage describes the same practice from the other side, where the phrase is listed among the things said by a group that had made a game of the language: (4:46 — **“playing with words and discrediting the faith”**). What the verse corrects, then, is not a slip of the tongue but the acceptance of a vocabulary that had been fashioned to undermine the community that used it. A reader can carry the lesson to any idiom he has absorbed without asking what it was built to do.

**LISTENING AS PART OF SPEECH**

The instruction continues with a single imperative, and it is joined to everything that came before: ***“and listen ˹attentively˺.”***. The Book places hearing beside speaking, so that the corrected form is not enough by itself; a community that has been given a better word is also required to use its ears. The verse then names the consequence of refusing the whole matter, and the punishment is stated with the same brevity as the rest of the sentence: ***“And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment”***. The connection between mockery and disbelief is drawn by the verse rather than inferred by the reader, since the people who turned the greeting into a joke are named in the clause that follows. The duty to hear is placed on the community in another passage as well, where the listening is joined to the mercy that follows from it: (7:204 — **“listen to it attentively and be silent”**). What remains is the doubled instruction, one for the mouth and one for the ear, leaving both disciplines for the believing community to practise. The next verse explains why the hostility behind the mockery exists at all. In the present day, coded insults and double meanings still turn apparently polite speech into a weapon, making disciplined language a form of moral protection.

---

## Verse 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty

**ENVY AT THE BLESSING OF OTHERS**

The verse turns from the corrected greeting to the resentment behind the mockery, and it names the parties without softening the description: ***“The disbelievers from the People of the Book”***. The Book has been speaking to the community that received the message, and here it explains that the objection to the message was never only about the wording used in the street. The party named first is the one that possessed scriptures of its own, which makes its resentment of a new blessing a matter of a different order from the ignorance of a people who had never received anything. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the verse as coming down over the leaders of that community and their refusal to see the Messenger's people favoured at all. What the reader is being prepared for is the reason behind the mockery, and the reason is named as a posture rather than an argument.

**DISBELIEVERS AND POLYTHEISTS MADE ONE PARTY**

The sentence joins a second party to the first, and the joining is itself a statement: ***“and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord”***. The two groups had little in common in their beliefs, and the Book places them together at the point where their attitude converges, which is the refusal to see the believers favoured. The blessing in question is from the Lord of the believers, so the refusal is directed at His choice rather than at their merit, and that is the subject of the sentence. The verse does not engage the objections of either group in detail here; it states the desire that stands behind them, and the statement is short because the desire is simple. A reader who has met hostility that could not be reasoned with has met the thing this clause describes, and the Book names it without pretending it is an argument.

**THE CHOICE THAT BELONGS TO ALLAH**

The next clause supplies the answer to the resentment, and it is an answer about authority rather than about merit: ***“but Allah selects whoever He wills”***. The verse does not argue that the believers deserved what they received; it places the giving where the Book always places it, in a choice that belongs to the giver. The same sentence reappears in another sūrah in nearly the same words, which shows how central the point is to the Book's treatment of favour: (3:74 — **“He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy”**). The resentment described in the earlier clauses is therefore a quarrel with a decision that was never submitted to the objectors in the first place. What the reader takes from the sentence is the ground of his own confidence, since a gift that depends on the giver's will is not diminished by anyone's disapproval.

**A DOOR NO ONE CAN SHUT**

Think of a house whose owner opens the door to a guest that the neighbours had decided to keep out, and who does not ask the neighbours for permission before doing it. The verse describes a favour that no amount of resentment could withhold, because the giving is placed in the hands of the One who owns the favour. The Book states the same position elsewhere when it discusses the bounty that passes between communities, and the verse here is one of its plainest statements of the principle. A reader who has been made to feel that his share of guidance was a matter for other people to approve has the sentence as his answer, and the answer is not a claim about his own worth. What is being refused in the earlier clauses is not the blessing but the freedom of the giver to bestow it.

**BOUNTY DESCRIBED AS A LORDLY ATTRIBUTE**

The verse closes by describing the One who gives, and the description is a statement about abundance rather than merely about power: ***“for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”***. The word for bounty carries the sense of a giving that does not run down, which is why it is used to close a sentence about resentment over a gift. The sending of the Book is therefore presented as one instance of a generosity that has no narrow channel, and the verse intends the reader to see the objection as small beside the description that ends it. A community that reads the sūrah in order has already met this attribute in its opening verses, and the repetition at this point in the argument is deliberate. The same open-handedness is stated where the Book describes the reward of those who work: (24:38 — **“And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”**). The next verses answer a related objection, this time about what happens to earlier revelations when a new one arrives. Today, envy of another person's calling can disguise itself as criticism of the gift, even when the Giver was never bound by the critic's preference.

---

## Verse 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything

**WHAT ABROGATION MEANS IN THIS BOOK**

The verse takes up a question that had been raised against the revelation, and it answers it in the form of a law rather than a defence: ***“If We ever abrogate a verse”***. The Arabic term behind the translation carries the sense of lifting or transferring, and the Book uses it here for the withdrawal of a ruling by the One who gave it. The sentence is stated in the first person plural, which is the Book's usual manner when it describes acts it attributes to God, and the phrasing makes the whole matter an exercise of authority rather than an accident in the text. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse to a specific objection from the People of the Book, who had asked why a ruling would be replaced if the earlier one had come from God. What the reader is offered is not an argument about the mechanics of revelation but a statement about who its author is.

**THE VERSE THAT IS REMEMBERED AND THE VERSE THAT IS REPLACED**

The sentence adds a second case to the first, and the second is the more striking of the two: ***“or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better”***. The forgetting here is attributed to the same authority that sends, which places the removal of a revelation within the same will as its delivery. The Book treats both cases identically in the sentence, and the equality is part of the answer, since the objection had been to replacement as such. The two cases are placed side by side because the will behind the sending is the same will behind the removal, which is the point the objectors had missed. The objection is not that something was lost but that something was changed, and the verse meets it by naming the one who does both. A reader who has wondered why the Book would speak of a verse passing out of memory has the sentence's own account of it here, and the account is short.

**BETTER AND SIMILAR, NOT LESSER**

The replacement is described in two words that between them close off every way of complaining about the change: ***“or similar one. Do you not know”***. The substitute is either better than what it replaces or equal to it, and the Book's choice of the two words rules out the complaint that something valuable had been taken away. What turns on the pairing is that no replacement can be described as a loss, which is why the sentence moves straight from the two words to the question that follows. Another sūrah records the same exchange from the side of those who refused it, and it supplies the accusation that was made against the one who brought the change: (16:101 — **“When We replace a verse with another”**). The sentence's own words then address the reader directly with a question, which moves the matter from a dispute about texts to the plainest available fact. The one who has followed the argument this far is asked to test the objection against what he already knows about the one who gives and withdraws.

**THE JEWISH OBJECTION THE SENTENCE ANSWERS**

The objection behind the verse was not a request for explanation; it was a use of the change as evidence against the mission. The Book meets it by refusing the premise, and the refusal is made in a sentence that never mentions the objectors, because the argument rests on a fact about God rather than on anything the objectors accept. What the verse assumes is that the right to revise a ruling belongs to the one who issued it, and that assumption is what makes the question that follows so pointed. The same line of reasoning appears elsewhere in the sūrah where the community's objections are answered by an appeal to divine prerogative rather than to the objector's satisfaction. Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse with a challenge about the direction of prayer and similar changes, which puts it squarely among the objections the section has been addressing. A reader sees here how the Book handles a dispute it does not consider to be about evidence.

**CAPABILITY AS THE GROUND OF THE ANSWER**

The verse ends with a question about knowledge that is also a statement about power: ***“that Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The clause gives the ground on which the whole answer rests, since a change of ruling is only a difficulty for someone who doubts the competence of the one who makes it. Capability is named here because the entire objection presupposes that a ruling was settled beyond revision, and the question leaves that presupposition with nowhere to stand. The Book frequently closes an argument in this way, and the closing here is deliberately placed after the objector has been asked twice whether he knows. Another passage states the same authority in terms of what is written and what is erased, which places the verse's own claim in the plainest company: (13:39 — **“Allah eliminates and confirms what He wills”**). What the reader carries away is a question addressed to himself, since the verse asks whether he has understood the position of the one whose words he is reading. Present-day changes in a sound programme may likewise serve one settled purpose better at a later stage rather than prove that the earlier stage lacked wisdom. It is like a physician changing a patient's dose as healing advances: the changed instruction serves the same cure at a different stage.

---

## Verse 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah

**A SECOND APPEAL TO SETTLED KNOWLEDGE**

A second question turns from divine power toward knowledge already held by the audience: ***“Do you not know”***. The repetition of the address is deliberate, since the Book is not asking for information but for attention to something the audience already holds. The question is placed before the content it introduces, so that the reader arrives at the statement that follows with the answer already half given. In the preceding verse the same phrasing introduced the claim about capability, and here it introduces a claim about ownership, which is the foundation the rest of the sentence rests on. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two questions as one argument, the first about power over the revelation and the second about power over the order it addresses. What he is being asked to acknowledge is not a subtlety but the plainest fact the Book states about the world.

**THE KINGDOM THAT TAKES IN HEAVEN AND EARTH**

The question is followed by the statement it was preparing, and the statement moves from the heavens downward: ***“that the kingdom of the heavens”*** and then ***“and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian”***. The claim is one of ownership rather than of rule alone, and it covers both realms in a single sentence, so that nothing in the created order falls outside it. Another sūrah states the same fact in language close enough to serve as its witness, and it draws the same conclusion about protection: (9:116 — **“Indeed, to Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth”**). The Book's arguments about dependence repeatedly begin from this premise, and the verse here gives the reader the premise without ornament. A person who has accepted the opening of the sūrah has already accepted the sentence that follows from it.

**NO GUARDIAN AND NO HELPER BESIDE HIM**

The verse completes its claim with the human consequence, added to the ownership without a pause: ***“or helper besides Allah”***. The two terms name the two things a person in difficulty looks for, someone to take charge and someone to assist, and the sentence denies both outside the One who owns the kingdom. The clause is not a threat but a description, since a kingdom that is entirely owned leaves nothing and no one outside its owner's authority. The Book returns to this pair of words when it describes the condition of those who have no protector on the day the ownership becomes visible, and the vocabulary is consistent across the sūrah. A reader who has placed his confidence in a person or an institution has the sentence to reckon with, and the verse states the matter as something already known rather than as news.

**TRUST PLACED WHERE THE SENTENCE PLACES IT**

The sentence leaves the reader with a choice about where to put his reliance, and it does so by removing all the alternatives in one clause. The Book's treatment of trust follows the same pattern as its treatment of mercy in the earlier verse, where the giving is placed in the hands of the One who gives freely. The sentence never argues for reliance on God; it states the ownership, and the reliance follows from it as a conclusion. The Book's confidence in this method is visible throughout the sūrah, where statements about God's prerogative are used to settle disputes rather than to win them. A reader who has tried to hold the ownership of the heavens and the earth and the loyalty of his own heart at the same time will find the sentence's logic unavoidable. Another passage puts the conclusion in the mouth of the Prophet himself, and the words are the answer to the absence of any helper: (9:129 — **“Allah is sufficient for me”**).

**WHAT FOLLOWS FROM OWNERSHIP**

The verse closes the sequence that began with the objection to the believers' greeting, and it does so by returning the argument to its foundation. If the kingdom belongs to Allah, then the selection of whom to favour is His, the replacement of a verse is His, and the protection of a community is His. The question the verse asks is therefore a test of the reader's own position rather than a request for agreement, and the Book leaves it there. The next verses turn to what this community was told to do with the guidance it had been given, and the reader can follow the argument from ownership to obligation without a break in the reasoning. What the passage has established by this point is that the objections raised against the revelation were quarrels about a prerogative that was never delegated to the objectors at all. Today, dependence on a powerful sponsor can feel secure until the sponsor reaches the boundary beyond which neither friendship nor force can help. The claim to another protector is like carrying a paper umbrella into a flood after refusing the only high ground.

---

## Verse 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way

**THE ADDRESS TURNED ON THE BELIEVERS**

Attention shifts from outside objections to a question put to the believers themselves, and the question is about an appetite: ***“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger”***. The address is startling because the community had just been defended against those who wanted to turn it back, and now it is asked whether it shares the very habit that made the others refuse. Nothing in the sentence claims that the believers had already asked anything; what is asked about is intention, and a question about intention is a warning rather than an accusation. The verse is attached by Ibn ʿAbbās to the Muslims in Medina, after some of them had begun to press the Prophet for the kind of signs their predecessors had demanded. The point of the question is to catch the desire at its root, because a community that copies the demands of an earlier people will eventually copy their conclusion as well.

**WHAT MOSES' PEOPLE HAD ASKED BEFORE**

The question is made concrete by a comparison with an earlier community: ***“as Moses was asked before?”***. The reference is to the demands recorded of the people who followed Moses, who asked to see God and asked for revelations in writing, and the Book treats the pattern as a familiar one rather than as an isolated incident. Another sūrah records the same demand being made to the Messenger in his own time, which shows how direct the likeness was: (4:153 — **“bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven”**). The question in this verse therefore does not need to describe the earlier demands in detail, because the audience knew what had become of the community that made them. What the reader is asked to see is that the appetite for proof is not new, and that the Book's answer to it has been consistent from the beginning.

**THE INSTRUCTION ABOUT ASKING**

The comparison carries a warning that the verse states separately in another place, where the believers are told to leave certain questions alone: (5:101 — **“Do not ask about any matter which, if made clear to you, may disturb you”**). The Book's concern is not with curiosity as such but with the demand that God answer on the questioner's terms, which is what turned an earlier generation's request into a refusal. The verse assumes that a question can be an act of faith or an act of bargaining, and the difference lies in whether the questioner is prepared to accept the answer. A community that puts its confidence in the fact that the proof is available will not need to keep asking for more of it, because the point of asking has more to do with the asker than with the evidence.

**A CUSTOMER WHO KEEPS ASKING FOR SAMPLES**

Think of a buyer who asks for a sample of every item in a shop and never carries one home, and who eventually explains that he had no intention of buying. The people of Moses asked for signs and kept asking, and the Book records that the request did not improve their position; the verse asks the believers whether they intend to walk the same road. The comparison is uncomfortable because the motive in the shop is at least honest, whereas the demand for proof often dresses itself as a search for certainty. Someone who has watched a person demand more and more evidence before committing to anything has seen how the appetite works, and the verse's question is aimed at exactly that appetite. What the sentence offers as an alternative is the acceptance of a messenger, which is the thing the demands were designed to postpone.

**THE TRADE THAT ENDS IN STRAYING**

The verse closes by naming the outcome of the posture it has described, with commercial language returning once more: ***“But whoever trades belief”*** and ***“for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way”***. The metaphor of trade has run through this part of the sūrah, and the verb used here describes an exchange in which the better article is handed over for the worse. The clause about straying is the natural conclusion of the metaphor, since a person who has left the road is not one who is still examining the route. The verse therefore treats the persistent demand for proof as a transaction with a known price rather than as a neutral enquiry, and the reader is warned about the trade before he makes it. The opening question therefore leaves a sharpened test of whether further requests seek guidance or merely delay the obedience already due. In the present day, endless demands for one more demonstration often postpone commitment more effectively than an open refusal would.

---

## Verse 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE WISH HELD IN THE HEART OF THE OTHERS**

A concealed desire explains the hostility the chapter has been describing, and it names the people it belongs to: ***“Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief”***. The wish is described as directed at a whole community rather than at an individual, and it is described as a wish rather than an attempt, which shows that the thing being reported here is an inner disposition. The Book has just finished answering the objections about abrogation and the choice of messengers, and it now identifies the source of the objections it has been meeting. The same aspiration is reported in another sūrah in almost the same terms, which shows that the verse is describing a settled attitude rather than a passing mood: (3:69 — **“Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you”**). What the reader receives is a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is offered so that the community can meet the wish without being surprised by it.

**WHY THEY WANTED IT**

The motive is stated in the verse itself, and it is stated with a word that leaves no room for a generous reading: ***“because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon”***. The truth had been made clear to them, and the verse places that clause immediately before the command to pardon, so that the reader measures the offence in the light of what the offenders knew. The Book's treatment of envy here is consistent with its treatment elsewhere, where it asks the community to look at what has been given to others rather than at what it wishes for itself: (4:54 — **“Or do they envy the people for Allah’s bounties?”**). The desire to see the believers return to disbelief is not presented as a response to anything the believers had done; it is presented as resentment at a gift. A reader who has felt a similar pull when someone else received what he wanted will recognise the condition the verse is describing, and the recognition is not meant to be comfortable.

**THE COMMAND TO PARDON AND TO BEAR WITH THEM**

The next words are addressed to the community that had been wronged, and they are unexpectedly restrained: ***“and bear with them”***, followed by ***“until Allah delivers His decision.”***. The Book does not tell the community to argue down the envy or to answer it in kind; it tells the community to carry on with patience while the matter remains with God. The choice of patience rather than silence is significant, since the community is not asked to abandon its position but to hold it without retaliating. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with dating the verse before the permission to fight, which would explain the direction given here, and the reading also fits the sequence of the sūrah. What the sentence asks of the believer is endurance of a specific kind, the kind that keeps its conduct unchanged while it waits.

**A NEIGHBOUR WHO WAITS FOR A TENANCY TO FAIL**

Think of a man whose neighbours would like him evicted, not because he has damaged anything but because they dislike the fact that he was given the house. The verse describes a community living beside people who wanted to see it fail, and the instruction given to the community is to keep living as it had been living. The Book's method here is to name the wish without making it the centre of the believer's attention, since a person who is always watching his envious neighbour will eventually imitate the behaviour he is watching for. Someone who has been made the object of dislike for the good that came to him will find the verse's counsel more useful than a strategy, because it removes the need to settle the account. What is left for the believer is the ordinary work of the community, carried on in the meantime.

**THE DECISION THAT BELONGS TO ALLAH**

The verse closes with the attribute that has ended several sentences in this stretch: ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The clause gives the community the reason it can wait, since the matter of who is favoured has already been shown to lie with the One who gives. The Book's habit of closing a command with a statement about God's capacity is a way of making the obedience reasonable rather than merely obligatory. What Ibn ʿAbbās hands down describes the warning here as one later answered by the command to fight and by the judgement that came upon the community that had chosen envy over the truth in front of it. A reader who has finished the sentence knows where the account will be settled, and the knowledge is the whole of the patience the verse asks for. Today, envy can appear as helpful advice intended to pull a person back from a conviction whose truth the adviser privately recognises.

---

## Verse 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE WORK THE COMMUNITY IS TOLD TO DO**

After the envy and the command to wait, the verse gives the community something to occupy it, and the instruction is about practice rather than controversy: ***“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth”***. The order of the sentence matters, since the Book answers the wish of the envious with a command about the believers' own conduct rather than with a rebuttal of the wish. Prayer and almsgiving are named together throughout this sūrah, which presents the two as one posture: worship directed upward and expenditure directed outward. The verse's placement after the report of hostility suggests that the community's best defence was never an argument but a pattern of life that could be seen. What the reader is given here is a way to spend the interval the previous verse described. Ibn ʿAbbās read the good sent ahead as prayer, alms and every righteous deed preserved for its doer, while the closing sight includes both the act and the intention behind it.

**THE FIGURE OF SENDING GOOD AHEAD**

The phrase about sending good ahead is a figure drawn from travel, and it describes goods dispatched before the traveller arrives: ***“for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. The Book uses the figure to teach that the reward for a deed is not collected in the present but stored where the deed was sent, which is why the verse says the community will find it rather than receive it now. The plural form is used throughout the sentence, which places the responsibility on the community rather than on individuals alone, since prayer and almsgiving in the Book are gathered into the description of the believers as a body. Another sūrah joins the same practices to the same promise, which shows how stable the pairing is: (2:277 — **“Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord”**). The verse therefore turns a report about other people's envy into an occasion for the believers' own accounting.

**THE EYES THAT SEE WHAT IS SENT**

The sentence ends with an attribute that answers the unspoken concern about who keeps a reward stored beyond the sender's sight. The clause answers by naming God as All-Seeing of what the community does, which places the smallest deed inside a supervision that never lapses. The attribute also closes off the possibility that a good act might be lost through being unnoticed, since the Book treats the accounting as a matter of sight rather than of memory. The point of the clause is not that God is aware in general but that He is aware of this community's conduct in particular, and the verse places the two statements side by side without a connective. A reader who has given something quietly and wondered whether it counted has the sentence as the answer to his question, and the answer is stated before he asks it.

**A TRAVELLER WHO SENDS HIS LUGGAGE AHEAD**

Think of a traveller who sends his bags ahead to the city he is going to, so that he arrives without them and finds them waiting when he gets there. The verse uses the same logic for good deeds, and the travellers in the comparison are the believers who will one day arrive at the place where what they sent has been kept. The comparison also explains why the Book can call a deed an investment rather than a payment, since the reward is not presented as something received in exchange but as something restored to its owner. A reader who has experienced the ordinary truth that what is given away lasts longer than what is held will find the figure easy to carry, and the verse's instruction stands on that plain experience. What the sentence asks for is not a large gesture but a habit of sending, performed while the interval lasts.

**THE CLOSING ATTRIBUTE IN THIS VERSE**

The clause about sight has one more function in the passage, and it is aimed at the community's morale. The believers had been told to wait while others worked to turn them back, and a community in that position can easily conclude that its conduct is invisible and its patience unrewarded. The verse answers that conclusion by naming the One whose observation settles the account, and it places the answer at the end of a command rather than at the end of an argument. The Book's method in these verses is to move from what others wish to what the community does, and the movement is the whole of the answer. A reader who has kept to a practice he was told to keep and seen no return on it has the sentence as the statement he needs, and it is short enough to hold on to through the interval the verse has in view. Present-day charitable work done beyond public sight still enters an account that does not depend on applause, publicity or institutional memory.

---

## Verse 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**THE CLAIM THAT PARADISE BELONGS TO ONE COMMUNITY**

Two communities are reported here as holding a conviction about themselves, and the belief is stated plainly: ***“The Jews and Christians each claim that”*** ***“none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof”***. The Book joins the two communities in one sentence because the claim is formally the same on both sides, each excluding the other while using identical logic. The clause about desires comes before the invitation to bring proof, and its placement tells the reader that the Book is treating the belief as an expression of preference rather than as a conclusion drawn from evidence. The following verse supplies the answer, and this one prepares for it by asking the claimants to produce what they have. What the reader is watching is the Book's standard method with confident assertions: it asks for the document.

**A DESIRE NAMED AS A DESIRE**

The word used for the claim describes a wish rather than a judgement, and the choice of word does the work of an argument. A person who wants a conclusion to be true will often hold it with the confidence that belongs to a demonstrated fact, and the Book names the difference between the two. The claim is not answered by denying that its holders are sincere; it is answered by asking them to show that it rests on something outside their own wanting. Another sūrah states the same principle in the form of a direct correction, and its words are near enough to be the verse's own comment: (4:123 — **“neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book”**). A reader who has held a belief because it favoured his own community will find the sentence uncomfortably exact, and the exactness is the point of the verse.

**THE PROOF CALLED FOR AND WHAT IT WOULD BE**

The invitation to produce proof is phrased as a challenge rather than a request for a discussion, and its last clause qualifies the proof being asked for: ***“if what you say is true.”***. The qualification makes the demand reasonable, since a claim about the unseen can only be settled by a report from the One who knows the unseen. The Book does not ask the claimants to argue better; it asks them to demonstrate the authority behind a statement that no human being could otherwise make. The same standard is applied to the believers elsewhere in the sūrah, where their confidence is grounded in what has been sent down rather than in their own standing. The reading attached to Ibn ʿAbbās treats the proof being called for as the scripture already in the claimants' hands, which is why the correction that follows is not introduced as an argument. Anyone who has heard a person speak with certainty about who is saved and who is not will find the challenge useful, because it returns the matter to the only place where it can be settled.

**TWO FAMILIES DISPUTING AN INHERITANCE**

Think of two families who each insist that the estate belongs to them alone, neither of them able to produce the document that settles it. The two communities in this verse made the same claim about the inheritance of the world to come, and the Book asks both of them for the paper. The comparison is sharp because the claimants in it are not dishonest people; they are confident people, and confidence is easy to mistake for evidence. Someone who has seen a dispute run for years on nothing but the certainty of the parties can see how the Book wastes no time in choosing between them: it asks for the proof, and the absence of proof is the answer. What the verse leaves with the reader is a standard he can apply to his own convictions about who will be saved.

**WHAT REMAINS UNSETTLED HERE**

The verse does not name the answer to the claim, and that is deliberate, because the next verse supplies it in the Book's own words. What this sentence establishes is the common ground between the two claimants: both had a desire, both expressed it as doctrine, and neither could produce the authority they were asked for. The Book's order in the passage is worth noticing, since it lets the claimants state their case fully before it gives the correction that follows. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sequence as a single argument in which the demand for proof and the answer that follows are two halves of one reply. Anyone who has followed the sūrah this far is now in a position to hear the correction as something more than a denial of two communities' hopes. Today, exclusive claims about salvation require revealed proof rather than confidence produced by repeating the claim inside one community.

---

## Verse 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE CORRECTION THAT OPENS WITH A REFUSAL**

The claim of the previous sentence is met here, and the reply refuses the whole framing rather than adjusting it: ***“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah”***. The refusal is aimed at the idea that salvation belongs to a community by name, and the sentence replaces the criterion with a description of a person. Submission and good conduct are named as the two marks of the one who has a reward with his Lord, and neither of them is an inherited identity. The Book's method here is to widen the door at the same moment that it removes the labels from it, which leaves the reader with a test he can apply to himself. What the previous verse asked the claimants to prove, this one answers by stating the condition on which the reward actually rests. Ibn ʿAbbās understood surrender of the face as making religion and works sincere to God, and doing good as joining right speech to right action.

**SUBMISSION AND GOOD CONDUCT NAMED TOGETHER**

The two qualities are placed together because the Book does not recognise a submission that leaves conduct untouched, and the pairing is what turns a slogan about belonging into a description of a life. The word for submission carries the sense of handing over the whole self, and the good conduct that follows is the visible form of that handing over rather than a separate achievement. Another sūrah describes the same pair as a firm hold that a person can grasp, using language that fits this verse closely: (31:22 — **“Whoever fully submits themselves to Allah and is a good-doer”**). The sentence therefore states a condition that any person can meet, whatever community he was born into, which is why the refusal at its opening is followed by an invitation rather than by an exclusion. A reader who has been told that his standing depends on the group he belongs to will find the sentence's terms refreshingly ordinary.

**SECURITY FOLLOWING SINCERE SURRENDER**

The next clause places the reward with the Lord rather than with the community: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”***. The Book consistently describes the reward as held by God rather than distributed by institutions, and the phrasing here removes every claim of ownership a community might assert over it. The same promise is made in the account of the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians earlier in the sūrah, and the repetition of the terms there and here shows that the standard is not new: (2:62 — **“will have their reward with their Lord”**). What this sentence has accomplished, in two clauses, is to strip the claim of its exclusivity and to restate the condition in a form that applies to every human being. A reader who wants to know where he stands has the sentence's own criterion in front of him.

**AN ENTRANCE WITH NO GUEST LIST**

Think of a hall where the organisers had been arguing over whose names were on the list, and where the announcement comes instead that the door is open to anyone who meets the stated condition. The verse functions as that announcement, and it does so without naming the communities whose claims it has just refused. The comparison makes plain why the Book's answer is not a compromise between the two claimants, since neither is given what it wanted and both are offered the same terms. Anyone who has seen an argument about belonging collapse when the actual requirement is read out loud has seen the movement of this verse, and the movement is the Book's way of settling a dispute about privilege. What remains after the sentence is the condition itself, which each reader may test in his own life.

**THE FEAR AND THE GRIEF THAT ARE REMOVED**

The verse closes with a promise that appears in the Book when the reward has just been named, and it is stated twice in one sentence: ***“And there will be no fear”*** and then ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. The two clauses remove the anxiety that belongs to the future and the sorrow that belongs to the past, which together cover the whole span of a person's worry. The Book uses the pair together here because the promise is being given to people who had been made anxious about their standing by the claims of others. The Book's habit of using these two words together makes the sentence a recognisable signature, and its appearance here ties the promise to the condition stated in the earlier clauses. The result is a verse that answers the claim of the previous sentence completely: it denies the exclusive reading, states the real condition, names where the reward is kept, and then takes away the two fears that motivated the dispute in the first place. A reader who has finished the sentence knows what is being asked of him and what he is being spared. In the present day, surrender becomes visible when worship, work and treatment of others point in one direction rather than merely sharing a label. This is why the answer begins with surrender before it names reward: outward good receives its direction from the allegiance that animates it.

---

## Verse 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute

**TWO CLAIMS MADE IN THE SAME BREATH**

A dispute between two communities that each held a scripture is reported here, with both positions set out side by side: ***“The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on”*** and ***“and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,”***. The symmetry is the point of the construction, since the Book puts the accusation and its mirror image side by side and lets the reader hear how they cancel each other. Neither claim is answered here with an argument about who is right, because the sentence is doing something else: it is showing that the two parties had made the same move against one another. The dispute had reached the believers as an invitation to take sides, and the Book's first response is to display the dispute for what it is. Anyone who has been drawn into a quarrel between two confident parties will recognise the pattern on display here. Ibn ʿAbbās located the dispute among the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran, each denying the other's religion despite reading a revealed Scripture.

**EACH SIDE ACCUSED OF HAVING NO GROUND**

The phrase translated as having nothing to stand on describes a position without a foundation, and each community applied it to the other while claiming the ground for itself. The Book has already described this community's habit of treating its own inheritance as the measure of everyone else, and the verse shows the same measure being used in the opposite direction. Another sūrah names the same dispute and gives its cause as envy rather than conviction: (3:19 — **“Those who were given the Scripture did not dispute ˹among themselves˺ out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them”**). The accusation in this verse is therefore not presented as the fruit of study, since each side was reading the same claim in the other's mouth. What the reader learns from the symmetry is that a quarrel conducted in these terms cannot produce a winner.

**SCRIBES WHO READ THE SAME BOOKS**

The verse then states the fact that makes the quarrel remarkable, and it states it briefly: ***“although both recite the Scriptures.”***. Both communities possessed and recited texts that they took to be from God, and the verse's clause places that shared practice beside the mutual accusation without comment. The contradiction is left to speak for itself here, since a person who recites a scripture and denies another community any ground occupies a position that the recitation will not support. The sentence does not say that the two scriptures were identical; it says that both parties were reciting, which is enough to show that the argument was not about information. A reader who has watched two people argue from the same document while each denies the other's reading of it has seen the condition the verse describes.

**THE PAGANS WHO REPEATED THE FORMULA**

The sentence widens to take in a third party, and the widening is a judgement on the first two: ***“And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺.”***. The people who had no scripture at all used the same formula as the communities who did, which means the formula belonged to a habit of mind rather than to a tradition. The Book's comparison is severe because it places the learned and the ignorant side by side on the strength of a shared sentence. What the verse establishes is that the denial of another person's ground is not produced by study, since the same denial appears where no study exists. Anyone who has heard a slogan repeated across very different groups will find the observation familiar.

**THE DAY THE DISPUTE IS SETTLED**

The verse closes by moving the dispute out of the community's hands and into a court that no party controls: ***“Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute”***. The same sentence is used elsewhere for the whole range of communities that disagreed about religion, and it is deliberately general: (22:17 — **“Allah will judge between them ˹all˺ on Judgment Day”**). The Book's answer to the quarrel is therefore not an adjudication in the present but a postponement to the day when the judgement is made by the One who knows what each community was given. The final picture holds two claims ringing against one another beside a single sentence about the day of settlement, a refusal to take the quarrel up on its own terms. What the passage requires of the believer is patience rather than a verdict, since the verdict has been reserved. Today, rival communities may each dismiss the other with absolute slogans while reading sources that should have taught greater care. The exchange is like two students holding copies of the same syllabus while each insists the other was assigned no course at all.

---

## Verse 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**THE WORST WRONGDOING NAMED IN A QUESTION**

A question now measures one deed against every other deed, and it asks it in a form that expects no answer: ***“Who does more wrong than those”***. The Book uses this opening when it wants to place a piece of conduct beyond comparison, and the conduct here is not disbelief in the abstract but an act committed against a place and a name. The question is framed as a comparison, which means he is being asked to look for a worse offence and to find none. The verse's placement continues the sūrah's account of the communities that received scriptures, and it turns from their disputes to the harm some of them inflicted. What the reader is given first is a scale, and the deed is placed on it before it is described.

**THE NAME PREVENTED FROM BEING MENTIONED**

The deed is then spelled out, and its first part concerns speech: ***“who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship”***. The offence is not the neglect of worship by those who were charged with it; it is the active prevention of others from mentioning God where He is worshipped. The Book's attention to the divine name runs through the sūrah, and this verse treats access to it as a matter of right rather than of favour. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse to the destruction of the sanctuary by a foreign power and to the obstruction the believers faced at the Sacred Mosque, which shows how the two halves of the deed belong together. The offence named first is an offence against speech, since the places are built for the mentioning of the name.

**STRIVING TO PULL THE PLACES DOWN**

The question adds a second charge to the first, and it escalates from obstruction to demolition: ***“and strive to destroy them?”***. The word for striving describes an effort that does not stop at a single act, which is why the verse attaches it to a campaign rather than an incident. The Book elsewhere describes the protection of houses of worship as a reason for the defence of a whole community, and it names the same kind of aggression in that connection: (22:40 — **“those who have been expelled from their homes for no reason”**). What the verse shows is that hostility to a place of worship is treated as hostility to what is mentioned in it, and the second charge therefore explains the first. Someone who has seen a community lose its place of gathering knows what the sentence is describing.

**ENTERING IN FEAR, OR NOT ENTERING**

The next clause states the consequence for the offenders, and it is phrased as a right that has been forfeited: ***“Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.”***. The sentence does not describe a penalty imposed from outside; it describes the condition the offenders have brought on themselves, since a place they have attacked can no longer be a place of confidence for them. Another passage describes who is fit to maintain such places, and its answer turns on belief and conduct rather than on possession: (9:18 — **“The mosques of Allah should only be maintained by those who believe”**). The Book's logic here is that the guardianship of a sanctuary is a moral qualification rather than a legal title, and the verse's sentence removes both from those who fight it. A reader can see how the two communities that disputed in the previous verse are answered here by a standard about deeds.

**DISGRACE NOW AND PUNISHMENT LATER**

The verse closes by naming the two parts of the offender's lot, and it separates them by time and by severity: ***“For them is disgrace in this world”*** and ***“and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”***. The pairing of an immediate shame with a deferred penalty is the Book's customary treatment of those who damage what belongs to God, and the same combination of the two outcomes appears in another passage about those who attack the community: (5:33 — **“This ˹penalty˺ is a disgrace for them in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”**). The verse therefore does not leave the matter to the day the previous verse named; it states that the loss begins in the present, in the standing of those who act this way. The sentence shows the seriousness with which the Book treats the protection of worship, since it matches the offence with a loss in both worlds. The next verse turns from the attackers to the breadth of the One they were attacking, and it answers the restriction of worship to particular places. Present-day attacks on places of worship begin long before demolition whenever access, remembrance and repair are deliberately obstructed. It is like locking a public well and then breaking its walls, combining the denial of access with destruction of the place itself.

---

## Verse 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

**BOTH DIRECTIONS BELONG TO HIM**

The dispute about places and directions is settled here by removing the ownership of them from human hands, and the answer comes in the opening words: ***“To Allah belong the east”*** and ***“and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing”***. The two directions are named as a pair because they cover the whole compass between them, and the Book's point is that the owner of one half is the owner of the other. The previous verse had described people who tried to control where God's name is mentioned, and this one states who owns the space in question. The verse therefore answers the whole dispute about sanctuaries and orientations without mentioning either party to it. What the reader is offered is a fact about ownership rather than a ruling about a building.

**WHEREVER A PERSON TURNS**

The sentence draws a conclusion from the ownership, and the conclusion is stated without conditions: wherever the turning happens, the One being faced is Allah. The Book's phrasing is generous in its breadth, and the clause has been read by the early authorities in more than one setting: some reports tie it to a change of prayer direction, others to a prayer offered in the wrong direction by mistake. Ibn ʿAbbās is said to have connected the verse with a question the community raised about the earlier direction, and the answer given is about the One faced rather than about the wall faced. The sentence's purpose in the sūrah is to prevent a place from becoming a rival to the One who is worshipped in it, since a direction belongs to its owner as surely as the place does. A reader who has made a sacred thing out of a location will find the verse's correction in the clause about turning.

**DIRECTION LOST DURING THE JOURNEY**

The verse sits in a passage where the community's change of orientation had been raised by its critics, and the sentence supplies the ground on which such a change is no difficulty. Another sūrah records the same principle in a positive command, and its wording fits the situation this verse addresses: (2:148 — **“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good”**). The Book's interest is in the competition of deeds rather than in the geography of prayer, and the sentence here states the reason that competition is possible: no direction is distant from its owner. The argument establishes that the dispute about orientation was never a dispute about access, since access has never depended on a wall.

**A MERCHANT WHO FINDS THE SAME OWNER EVERYWHERE**

Think of a traveller who looks for a particular merchant and discovers that every shop he enters belongs to the same man, so that no mistake about the address can keep them apart. The verse's claim about east and west works the same way, and it explains why the Book can treat a change of orientation as a small matter. The comparison also answers the resentment of the people described in the previous verse, since a person who owns the whole of a street cannot be shut out of part of it by anyone. Anyone who has feared that he was praying in the wrong place will find the sentence reassuring for the plainest reason, which is that the One addressed is not confined to the place. What the verse leaves the reader with is the freedom of the person who knows whose the ground is.

**ENCOMPASSING AND KNOWING**

The verse closes with two names that answer two different fears: the first answers the worry about being out of reach, and the second answers the worry about being unnoticed. The name translated as All-Encompassing describes a presence that no boundary can exclude, and the name that follows describes a knowledge that no hidden act escapes.
