Another passage addresses the community of believers in the same terms and with the same conclusion, which shows that the counsel to the family became the counsel of the Book itself: (3:102 — **“and do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission ˹to Him˺”**). The choice that God made is therefore presented as a gift whose value depends on how a person ends.

**AN INHERITANCE THAT HAS TO BE KEPT**

The verse treats the faith as an estate that is passed on and that can also be lost, and the warning about how a person dies is a warning about the whole interval between receiving it and leaving it. The account of the Children of Israel in this sūrah has been a study of exactly that risk, since a community can carry the name of a tradition and end somewhere else. The same message is given in another passage where the community is told to follow the way of the ancestor rather than the customs that grew up around his name: (16:123 — **“Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.”**). Someone who has watched a family keep its name and lose its practice has the warning in view without needing a commentary, and the sentence is written for him as much as for the children addressed.

**A FATHER LEAVING INSTRUCTIONS WITH AN ESTATE**

Think of a man who gathers his sons before he dies and tells them that the land matters less than what they do with the name attached to it. The counsel in this verse is given exactly at that point in the family's history, and the phrase about the manner of dying shows where the father's concern was fixed. The comparison explains why the advice is recorded rather than the bequest, since the inheritance that survives a death is the one that has been spoken into the next generation. Anyone who has been entrusted with something by a parent and has had to decide what to do with it will find the sentence more than a piece of ancient history. The responsibility that comes with receiving a tradition is what the sentence puts on him.

**A COUNSEL CARRIED ACROSS TWO LIFETIMES**

The verse names Abraham and Jacob together, and the pairing is important because the counsel was not a single man's preference but a practice that the family carried forward. Jacob had his own history in the Book, and he appears here as the one who repeated the instruction to his own children, so that the sentence spans two lifetimes of transmission. The pattern is the same in this sūrah's account of the covenant, whose terms were given once and then repeated. The picture is of a religion moving through a household, and that movement is the part of the story the arguing communities had left out. The next verses turn to the question of who the ancestors actually were, which the Book answers from the record rather than from the claims. In the present day, the most valuable inheritance a parent leaves is not a religious label but a lived charge to remain surrendered until death.

---

## Verse 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**A DEATHBED QUESTION PUT TO THE FAMILY**

An appeal to the reader's own knowledge stands at the head of this verse, and it takes the form of a question: ***“Or did you witness”*** and ***“when death came to Jacob?”***. The communities that argued about the ancestors had not been present at any of these scenes, and the Book's question quietly removes them from the position of witnesses. The scene itself then begins with the dying man, and his first concern is not his property but the worship of the household he is leaving. Another passage records the same man as one of the patriarchs to whom the way was given, which places this conversation inside the line the sūrah has been tracing: (2:132 — **“This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children”**). The question at the start of the verse is therefore aimed at everyone who claims to know this family from the outside. Ibn ʿAbbās read the question as a challenge to those claiming Jacob had bequeathed Judaism, while his sons' answer names the one God of Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac.

**THE FATHER'S OWN WORDS**

The dying man's question is recorded in his own words, and it asks about the future rather than the present: ***“He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?”***. The question is about loyalty after the asker is gone, which makes it a test of what the household carried in itself rather than of what it owed to a living father. The patriarchs come back to this point again and again in the Book, since the danger for a family of prophets is that the inheritance becomes a name rather than a worship. Anyone watching a family's practice weaken within a generation of the founder's death will understand why the question was asked in that form. What the verse shows is a man checking the foundation at the last possible moment.

**THE SONS NAME THEIR INHERITANCE**

The children's reply follows at once, and it names the object of worship with precision: ***“They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers”*** and ***“Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac”*** and ***“the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”***. The answer moves from a personal God to a family tradition and then to the unity of that God, the sequence this chapter has been building from its opening verses. The reply also ends with submission in the first person plural, exactly the posture the founder had asked for in prayer and performed when he was commanded. The same list of names appears in another passage as the company whose revelation the believers are told to accept, which shows how the family and its descendants belong together: (42:13 — **“what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus”**). What the reader hears in the answer is a household that knew what it was handing on.

**SONS GATHERED AT THE BEDSIDE**

Think of a man who calls his sons to his bed and asks them not whether they will keep the business but whether they will keep what the business was for. The scene in the verse is that kind of exchange, and the Book preserves it because the answer given there is the answer the sūrah has been asking its own readers to give. The brevity of the reply suggests a household in which the question had been settled long before it was asked, which is the opposite of the hesitations the sūrah has reported elsewhere. Anyone who has been present at such a conversation will know how much it reveals about a family, and what the patriarchs left behind is disclosed in this exchange. What the verse offers is a picture of a tradition being confirmed at the point where it could most easily have been lost.

**UNITY AND SUBMISSION IN THE LAST WORDS**

The last words of the reply are the most important in the verse, since they name the unity of God and the family's own submission in a single sentence. The phrase about the One God answers every later attempt to divide the family's religion among communities, and the clause about submission describes the response that the whole account has been illustrating. Several accounts of the prophets in the Book close with the same two elements, and here they come from children standing beside a dying father. What the reader should carry from the scene is that the answer given at that bedside is the answer the sūrah has been inviting him to give, and the invitation has been in front of him since the chapter's opening. The next verse tells him what that inheritance means for his own account. Today, end-of-life conversations often reveal what a household truly considers worth carrying into the next generation.

---

## Verse 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**A COMMUNITY THAT HAS GONE BEFORE**

The verse is a short reckoning with the generations this passage has been describing, and it opens by naming them in the past tense: ***“That was a community”*** and ***“that had already gone before.”***. The sentence places the whole history it has narrated at a distance from the reader who is hearing it, and it does so without diminishing the importance of what was described. The communities that argued about the patriarchs had made their ancestry into a claim, and the Book's reply is that the ancestors are finished with their own account. Another passage carries the same words about the same history, so that the sentence is repeated where the sūrah closes this discussion: (2:141 — **“That was a community that had already gone before”**). Lineage is thus treated as a record rather than a possession. Ibn ʿAbbās treated the earlier people as a closed account whose good belongs to them, while later people answer for what they themselves earn rather than for ancestral speech.

**WHAT EACH GENERATION EARNS**

The verse then states the terms of the accounting in two parallel clauses: ***“For them is what they earned”***, ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. The two halves are identical in form and separated only by the people they refer to, and the construction states a general law in a single sentence. The word for earning places every generation under the same measure, so that the merits of the ancestors neither add to the descendants' credit nor carry their burdens. Another passage states the same law about individuals in a form that leaves no room for misunderstanding: (53:38 — **“no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”**). Anyone tempted to rest on ancestral standing finds the answer in this sentence.

**A CLOSED ACCOUNT AND AN OPEN ONE**

The two clauses describe one account that has been closed and another that is still being written, and the sūrah has just shown what the ancestors did with theirs. The Book's interest in Abraham and Jacob lies not in their standing as a credit balance for their descendants but in the pattern of submission they handed on to a living community. The same law is applied in another passage where the descendants of the righteous are raised to the rank of their parents, and the reward there is a mercy rather than a transfer: (52:21 — **“We will elevate their descendants to their rank”**). The reader should see that the Book's handling of inheritance is generous where God wills it and never automatic, which is precisely the distinction the arguing communities had missed in their treatment of the patriarchs.

**AN ESTATE SETTLED LONG BEFORE THE HEIRS ARRIVE**

Think of heirs who arrive at a property that was settled long ago and quarrel over a document their ancestors signed, without asking what the document asked of them. The verse turns the whole argument about ancestry into a statement about finished accounts, and it leaves the reader with the one that is still open. The comparison explains why the Book keeps returning to the deeds of the ancestors rather than to their titles, since a title settles nothing about the person holding it. Anyone who has watched an inheritance argued over while the work of the family goes undone can see the point being made, since the document being waved about settles nothing for the people waving it. The past is evidence rather than currency, which is what the sentence assumes.

**THE ACCOUNTABILITY THAT STOPS AT THE GRAVE**

The verse closes with the third clause, and it removes the last remaining ground for resting on another person's record: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** and ***“for what they have done”***. The same words stand in another passage where the Book applies the law to individuals rather than to peoples, and the repetition shows how firmly the principle is fixed: (6:164 — **“No one will reap except what they sow. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.”**). The sentence is symmetrical with the two before it, and the three together answer the claims of descent that have run through the sūrah. What stands in front of the reader is a community that has been judged, a community that is being judged, and a boundary between them that no claim of kinship can cross. The Book states this boundary without severity and without argument, which suggests that the fact was obvious to its first audience even as they disputed over ancestry. The plain question left is what his own page will say. Present-day pride in ancestors becomes an excuse when their achievements are treated as credit against duties that remain unpaid now. Therefore the repeated division of earnings is not a dismissal of history but the reason history can instruct without becoming inherited credit.

---

## Verse 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**AN INVITATION TO JOIN A COMMUNITY**

An invitation from the two communities is quoted in their own terms: ***“The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No!”***. The offer is put in the language of guidance, as though the only way to be rightly guided were to join one of the two communities, and the argument so far has shown how often that offer had been made. The reply begins with the shortest refusal in the passage, and the Book gives the Messenger a single word to open his answer. The reader should notice what the invitation takes for granted, since it assumes that guidance is held by a community rather than given by God. What the verse does is to decline the terms and, in the same sentence, to name the way the Messenger already follows.

**THE REFUSAL AND THE REASON FOR IT**

The answer names the faith of Abraham rather than a new religion, which places the reply inside the tradition the communities themselves claimed: ***“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright”***. The Book's argument here is not that the two communities had nothing, but that the tradition they were offering was not theirs to dispense and was already being followed. The word for uprightness describes a person who has turned away from everything else, and the description is applied to a man who lived before either community existed. Another passage makes the same point by naming what Abraham was not: (3:67 — **“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness”**). A reader who has been told that his standing depends on joining a particular group will find the sentence's answer refreshingly direct.

**A DESCRIPTION THAT ALSO FORECLOSES A CLAIM**

The verse's last clause adds a detail that the two communities would have found difficult: ***“who was not a polytheist.”***. The description excludes both the charge of idolatry that the communities traded about each other and the assumption that one of them had inherited the man's religion by right. The Book uses the phrase consistently when it discusses this prophet, and its appearance here gives the lie to the idea that his way was the property of a group. The report that carries Ibn ʿAbbās's name notes that the phrase was used to correct a claim the two communities had each made about the patriarch, and the correction sits inside the reply itself. The tradition on display is defined by what its founder was rather than by who claims him.

**LATER LABELS MEASURED AGAINST ABRAHAM**

Think of a family that is invited to join an exclusive association on the condition that it accepts the association's version of its own history. The verse declines the invitation on the ground that the family's way is older than the club, and the reply names the ancestor rather than arguing with the membership terms. The comparison explains why the Book does not engage the offer's details, since accepting the premise would already have conceded the point at issue. Anyone who has been invited to secure his position by adopting someone else's label can see the shape of the answer given here, and the answer is a statement rather than a debate. What the verse leaves with its reader is the confidence of a person who knows what he follows and who it belonged to.

**THE WAY THAT WAS THERE FIRST**

Read with the verses around it, the sentence explains why the sūrah has spent so much space on Abraham, Jacob and their family. The Book has been establishing the age and the content of the way it names, so that when the invitation comes the reply can point to a tradition older than the invitations. The same priority appears in another passage where the believers are told to follow the way of the man the whole argument has been about, which places the final instruction on the same foundation: (16:123 — **“Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.”**). What the reader should carry away is that the answer to a claim about belonging is a question about conduct, and the sūrah has been preparing him for that question since its opening verses. The next verse states the content of the belief the believers are to declare. Today, competing invitations to join a group must be measured against the older upright way, not against the confidence of the recruiter. What turns on the reply is the source of guidance: communal membership is rejected as the measure because Abraham's upright submission came before both later labels.

---

## Verse 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**THE CREED THE BELIEVERS ARE TOLD TO DECLARE**

The verse gives the community the words it is to use, and the words begin with the articles of belief: ***“Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah”*** and ***“and what has been revealed to us”***. The sentence is addressed to the believers rather than to their opponents, which makes it a statement of identity before it becomes an answer to anyone. The Book places the revelation given to this community first, and then extends the same belief backward through the prophets, so that the creed is presented as one continuous giving. The reader should notice the order, since the sentence begins with God and then moves through history without a break. The faith described in the sentence is not a new departure but the acknowledgement of a single source. Ibn ʿAbbās read the confession as faith in every prophet and Scripture without denying any messenger sent to teach divine oneness, ending in acknowledged submission to God.

**THE PROPHETS NAMED IN A SINGLE BREATH**

The list then reaches back to the family at the centre of the sūrah's argument and continues through the lawgivers: ***“and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”***, ***“and his descendants”***, ***“and what was given to Moses, Jesus”*** and ***“and other prophets from their Lord.”***. The names are given without rank and without a distinction drawn between the earlier and the later, which is the point the following clause states directly. Another passage repeats the same creed in almost the same words, so that the reader meets it as a formula the community was taught rather than a sentence composed for one occasion: (3:84 — **“We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”**). What the list does is to prevent any part of the prophetic history from becoming a separate religion.

**NO DISTINCTION DRAWN BETWEEN THEM**

The sentence then states the position the community is to take toward the whole company, and it states it as a refusal: ***“We make no distinction between any of them.”***. The refusal is aimed at the practice of accepting some messengers and rejecting others, which the Book treats as a rejection of the sending itself. Another passage describes that practice as a desire to split the matter in half, and it names the wish in the same words used here: (4:150 — **“wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers”**). The verse's creed therefore does not merely add prophets to a list; it makes the acceptance of all of them the test of accepting any. A reader who has been taught to honour one messenger while dismissing another will find the clause addressed to him.

**A SUBMISSION NAMED AT THE END**

The declaration closes with the word that has run through this stretch since the account of Abraham: ***“And to Allah we all submit.”***. The sentence therefore moves from belief to submission in one breath, which keeps the creed tied to the posture the Book has been demanding all along. The word used here has appeared in the command given to Abraham, in the answer he gave, and in the advice he left his children, and it appears now in the mouth of the whole community. The Book's practice is to close a statement of doctrine with a statement of the response it requires, and the verse follows that practice exactly. What the reader is left with is a creed whose last word is a handover rather than an assertion.

**A LETTER OF RECOMMENDATION READ ALOUD**

Think of a family that is asked to declare its loyalties and that answers by listing every ancestor it honours, including the ones the questioners had claimed for themselves. The believers are given a declaration of that kind here, and its form is brief enough to be repeated in a single sitting. The comparison explains why the list of names matters as much as the statement about God, since the argument of the sūrah is about who owns the prophetic inheritance. Anyone who has heard a community claim an ancestor while rejecting the message that ancestor followed can see what the creed is doing here. What remains after the sentence is the unity of the giving and the unity of the response, and the community's identity rests on both. In the present day, selective reverence for agreeable prophets fractures the single source and purpose the confession is designed to preserve.

---

## Verse 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**GUIDANCE THROUGH AN UNDIVIDED CREED**

The verse follows the creed with a statement about who is guided, and the statement is put as a condition: ***“So if they believe in what you believe”*** and ***“then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided.”***. The guidance is attached to agreement with a community already described, which makes the believers the measure of the thing being offered. The Book's wording is deliberately simple, and it does not require adherence to a nation or a lineage before it requires agreement with the truth. The verse therefore answers the invitation reported in an earlier sentence, where the two communities had offered their own religions as the road to guidance, and it answers by naming the content of belief rather than the label attached to it. A reader who has been taught that guidance is a possession to be handed over will find the sentence's terms plainer than that.

**BELIEVING BY THE SAME MEASURE**

The phrase about believing as the believers believe has been read in more than one way, and the readings converge on the same requirement. The objection that the verse makes God the object of a comparison is answered by the usage of the language, where the word for likeness in such a sentence marks a similarity of the two acts of belief rather than of their object. Ibn ʿAbbās read the clause as a description of faith in all the prophets and their scriptures, which is the creed the previous verse had just spelled out. The Book's standard here is not a new doctrine invented for the occasion but the faith the community itself had received, and the sentence measures everyone else by it. What the reader is being told is that the door is open to anyone who will believe what the believers believe.

**TURNING AWAY AND WHAT IT IS CALLED**

The verse then names the alternative, and the word it uses is stronger than disagreement: ***“But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺.”***. The term describes a split or a breach, and the Book uses it for the condition of being on one side while the truth is on the other. The account of the earlier communities in this sūrah has prepared the reader for the word, since the pattern of knowing the truth and standing against it has been the chapter's recurring subject. The clause is therefore not a description of people who have not heard but of people who have heard and turned. Someone who has refused a conclusion after understanding it has known the state the word describes.

**REFUSING THE LIGHT ONCE REQUESTED**

Think of a household that requests a lamp for a dark room and then shuts the door when the lamp arrives. The verse's two clauses describe the same two outcomes for the people who had been asking, and the second clause names the state of those who sent the light away. The comparison makes clear why the Book uses a word about fracture rather than a word about ignorance, since the parties in view had the means of knowledge in front of them. A person who has chosen a position against his own information has lived the condition described here, and the description is short because the condition is familiar. The difference between not knowing and turning away is what the verse asks him to hold on to.

**SUFFICIENCY AND THE TWO ATTRIBUTES**

The verse closes by naming what the community is promised instead of the agreement it had sought, and the promise is stated as sufficiency: ***“But Allah will spare you their evil.”*** and ***“For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. The sentence does not promise that the opposition will cease; it promises that the community will be defended from what the opposition intends. The two names that follow explain the basis of the promise, since a God who hears what is said and knows what is planned is not caught unaware by either. Another passage places the same sufficiency in the mouth of the Prophet as a statement of trust, which shows how the community was taught to use it: (9:129 — **“Allah is sufficient for me”**). He is left with the arrangement the verse describes, where the argument is allowed to run its course and the community is told where its protection lies. Today, hostility and organised opposition may feel overwhelming, but the verse measures safety by divine sufficiency rather than by the opponent's numbers.

---

## Verse 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him

**A RELIGION LIKE A DYE**

The religion the community has been discussing is named here with an image from the dyeing trade: ***“This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah.”***. The translation offers two renderings of the term, and both are worth holding together, since one describes the religion as a way laid down and the other describes it as a colour that has soaked into the material. The term carries the sense of a mark that cannot be washed out because it has entered the cloth, and the claim here is that the religion in question is that kind of mark. The previous verses had described the creed of the believers and the guidance that follows from it, and this sentence names the whole matter in a single word. The religion, then, is not an ornament worn over the surface but a change in the fabric.

**THE DYE THAT TAKES AND THE DYE THAT SITS ON TOP**

The verse's second clause presses the image with a question: ***“And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?”***. The question compares the colouring God provides with every other colouring a person might acquire, and it leaves the answer to the reader because there is no doubt about it anywhere. The comparison also rules out the notion that a person may keep several colourings at once, which is the assumption behind so much of the inherited religion the passage has been examining. The earlier communities in this sūrah have been a study in the difference between the two, since a people can carry the mark of a tradition while the tradition itself has not entered them. The word used here describes the standing colour of a thing rather than a coat applied for an occasion, which explains the severity of the Book's criticism of inherited religion. Anyone who has watched cloth dyed and then left in the rain can see what the sentence guards against.

**THE NATURAL WAY AND WHERE IT IS TRACED**

Another passage names the same reality and traces it to the constitution God gave human beings at their making, which is the sense the term's translation as natural Way is reaching for: (30:30 — **“the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people”**). This verse says the same thing by calling the religion a colouring that belongs to its owner rather than to its wearer's choice. The two together explain why the guidance of the earlier prophets is treated in the Book as one religion rather than as a series of separate dispensations, since a constitution given at a people's making is not replaced by a later fashion. The phrase is read by Ibn ʿAbbās as the religion of God without any addition, and that reading suits a sentence that closes an argument about inherited claims of every kind. The reader should see that the image is a correction of the assumption that religion is a garment a community may tailor.

**A DYER WHO OWNS THE VAT**

Think of a workshop where the colour in the vat is mixed by the owner and where the customer is invited to bring his cloth rather than his own dye. The verse's question works the same way, and it excludes every attempt to add a private colouring to the one provided. The comparison explains why the sentence is phrased as a comparison rather than a command, since the Book is asking the reader to look at the alternatives and find none. Anyone who has blended a private practice into a religion and then wondered why it feels provisional will recognise the situation, since a colour mixed by the wearer never holds as well as the one the dyer put there. The religion has one owner, and his colouring is the standard by which every other is measured.

**WORSHIP AS THE WHOLE RESPONSE**

The verse closes with the response the community makes to the colouring it has received, and that response is given as a statement about their practice: ***“And we worship ˹none but˺ Him”***. The Book's habit of ending a statement about God with a statement about the worshippers places the two halves of religion in one sentence, and it does so here to show what a dyed life looks like from the outside. The declaration is in the first person plural, which makes it the community's answer to the question embedded in the sentence, and the answer is a claim about conduct rather than about ancestry. Another passage makes the same claim in fuller form, where the speaker devotes his whole life and death to the Lord of all worlds: (6:162 — **“my prayer, my worship, my life, and my death are all for Allah—Lord of all worlds”**). What the reader carries from the verse is an image of a community marked by a colouring it did not choose and did not dilute. Present-day identity is often coloured by nation, market and fashion; worship asks which influence has penetrated deepest.

---

## Verse 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺

**A DISPUTE THE MESSENGER IS TOLD TO ANSWER**

A question placed in the Messenger's mouth turns the argument back on those who raised it: ***“Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah”***. The dispute in view was about the choice of a messenger, and the reply begins by asking on what ground the objection could stand. The account that carries Ibn ʿAbbās's name traces the objection to the two communities and to those who thought a prophet should not be raised from among the Arabs, which is the ground the question removes. The sūrah has been answering claims made by the two communities about their own standing, and this sentence changes the subject from inheritance to the relation between God and both parties. The question is asked for the reader's benefit as much as for the disputants', since the reader is invited to see how little there is to argue about once the relation is stated. A reader who has been drawn into a quarrel about who is favoured will find the sentence moving the ground under the quarrel.

**THE LORD WHO BELONGS TO BOTH PARTIES**

The question then supplies the ground of its own answer: ***“while He is our Lord”*** and ***“and your Lord?”***. The clause places the two disputing sides under a single lordship, which removes the premise that one of them could own the deity or the messenger. The Book's argument here is not that the believers have a better claim to God but that the claim to exclusive possession is incoherent, since a lord who is the lord of both sides cannot be a party's private patron. The two names are placed in the same sentence without a rank between them, and the even-handedness is the whole point of the clause. Nothing in the sentence claims a superior position for the believers, which is what makes the reply to the dispute so difficult to answer. What the reader should notice is that the argument is settled before the next clause arrives.

**DEEDS THAT BELONG TO THEIR OWNERS**

The sentence continues with a statement about accountability, and it distributes the responsibility in two halves: ***“We are accountable for our deeds”*** and ***“and you for yours.”***. Throughout this sūrah a claim about standing is answered with a statement about deeds, and the sentence here does it in six words. The measure is applied to both sides equally, which is what makes it an answer rather than an assertion of superiority. Another passage records the same reply being given to the Prophet as an instruction for disputes he could not settle, and its wording keeps the two parties separate in the same way: (10:41 — **“My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours”**). Anyone who has tried to settle a religious argument by appealing to his own history has the correction in the sentence.

**TWO LEDGERS AND ONE LANDLORD**

Think of two tenants who argue about which of them the landlord prefers, and who are told that he owns the whole building and keeps a separate account for each. The verse's reply has that shape, and it leaves the tenants with nothing to argue about except their own records. The comparison clarifies why the Book calls the parties back to their deeds, since a claim about favour is a claim about another person's business. A dispute about standing that runs for years while both parties ignore their own ledgers is the situation addressed here. The reply does not settle which party the landlord prefers, and the silence is the answer. What he is left holding is a dispute dissolved rather than decided.

**DEVOTION AS THE ONLY DIFFERENCE ASKED FOR**

The verse closes with the one point on which the two sides could actually differ, and it states it as a fact about the believers: ***“And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺”***. The word describes a sincerity that keeps nothing back, and the Book uses it to describe a loyalty that is undivided rather than one that is merely professed. The distinction is the one the whole passage has been drawing, since the communities in view had a profession without the devotion that goes with it. The claim is made in another passage where the community is told to state it in the face of argument, and it is placed beside submission to God rather than beside victory in debate: (3:20 — **“I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers”**). The sentence therefore ends without a verdict on the opponents, which is deliberate, since the verse's purpose is to define the community's own position rather than to pass sentence on anyone else's. The plainness of the difference that actually matters is what the verse leaves. Today, argument about who owns God collapses when every party is returned to its own work and the sincerity with which it was done.

---

## Verse 2:140

> Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**AN IDENTITY PROJECTED BACKWARD**

The verse states the last of the community's claims and puts it as a question addressed to them: ***“Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”***, ***“and his descendants were all Jews”*** or ***“or Christians?”***. The claim is about retroactive identity, and the Book asks the claimants to notice what they are saying when they say it. Everyone named in the question lived long before the two communities existed, as the section on the covenant and the sanctuary had already shown. Another passage puts the same point in the form of a question about chronology and leaves the claimants to answer it: (3:65 — **“Why do you argue about Abraham, while the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until long after him?”**). What is on display is a claim that cannot survive its own timeline. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the hidden testimony as knowledge in the Torah concerning the Prophet, and the question about the patriarchs as a contrast between human claims and divine knowledge.

**WHO KNOWS BETTER, ASKED ONCE**

The verse then supplies the question the Messenger is to ask, and the question is about the relative value of two kinds of knowledge: ***“Say, “Who is more knowledgeable”*** and ***“you or Allah?”***. The comparison is one-sided by design, and the argument needs no further step because the answer sits inside the question. Another passage puts the same comparison and measures the claim against what God has said about the patriarch, and there the verdict is stated directly: (3:67 — **“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness”**). What the sentence does is to move the dispute from the plane of inherited authority to the plane of information, where the claimants have nothing of their own to offer. Anyone who has seen a tradition shaped to suit its inheritors will recognise the movement.

**THE TESTIMONY PUT AWAY**

The offence underneath the claim is then named, in a question of its own: ***“Who does more wrong than those”*** and ***“who hide the testimony they received from Allah?”***. The charge is not that the communities invented a claim but that they concealed something they knew, which belongs to the same family as the obligation to make the scripture known that this passage has already set out. The account behind the accusation is that the earlier books contained descriptions of the coming prophet, and that the testimony had been withheld from those who were entitled to hear it. The word used for the hiding describes an act rather than an omission, since a document that has been put away has been put away by someone. Anyone who has seen evidence buried by the institution it told against will recognise the offence named here.

**A WITNESS KEPT OFF THE STAND**

Think of a court in which the decisive witness has been locked in a room by the party that was supposed to produce him. The verse names that conduct as the greatest wrong available in the situation, and the sentence places it beside the question about knowledge so that the two are read together. The comparison shows why the Book treats concealment as worse than ignorance, since a person who hides a testimony has decided that his own position matters more than the truth in his keeping. Anyone who has seen a community's scholars withhold what they knew will find the verse's question less rhetorical than it sounds. What the reader is left with is the search for what was put away.

**THE ATTRIBUTE THAT CLOSES THE MATTER**

The verse ends by naming what the concealers seem to have forgotten: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. The clause is placed after the accusation rather than after the question, which turns the sentence into a statement about the record rather than a threat to the offenders. A reminder of God's knowledge closes an account of hidden conduct throughout this sūrah, and the formula is consistent because the temptation it addresses is consistent. Another passage repeats the same closing words in a sentence about the direction of prayer and the truth of what was sent down, so the reader meets the formula here as a pattern rather than an isolated remark: (2:149 — **“And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do”**). The fact that nothing here has been lost, whether the community admitted it or not, is what remains. In the present day, archival knowledge can be hidden by experts whose silence protects inherited claims from inconvenient evidence.

---

## Verse 2:141

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**THE SENTENCE THAT CLOSES THE DEBATE**

Almost the same words closed an earlier stretch of this argument, and the echo marks the end of a section: ***“That was a community”*** and ***“that had already gone before.”***. The Book's decision to state the same principle twice is not redundancy but punctuation, since the second occurrence falls where the argument has been carried to its furthest point. The intervening verses have taken the reader through the claim about the patriarchs, the witness that was withheld, and the question about who knows better, and this sentence closes the file. The principle stated here had already been stated once, and it is repeated now that the argument has run its course, which shows that the matter was settled on the same ground from the start and is settled there again. Ibn ʿAbbās read the two earnings as goodness credited to each generation separately and the final clause as freedom from answering on the Last Day for another people's conduct.

**THE ACCOUNT THAT CLOSES WITH THE DEAD**

The first clause puts the ancestors in the past tense, so that their page is shown to have been closed. The reason the wording matters is that those who argued about them had been treating them as living assets, and the wording leaves them where they are. Nothing here diminishes them; what is refused is a later generation's attempt to collect on their behalf. Another passage states the same principle in a sentence about the day of reckoning, and the unit of account there is the individual rather than the family: (6:164 — **“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”**). What the clause draws is a line where the arguing parties had been trying to cross it.

**TWO ACCOUNTS KEPT SEPARATE**

The middle of the sentence sets out the terms of the accounting in two identical halves, and the echo between the phrases is the argument: ***“For them is what they earned”*** and ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. The Book sets the two records side by side and refuses to let either be transferred, which answers the whole claim about inherited standing. The word used for earning covers everything a person does, so that the clause leaves room neither for an assumed credit nor for an assumed debt. The point of saying it twice is that the two sides of the sentence are being measured on one scale, which is why no one may borrow against another's record. Another passage carries almost the same words about the same history, and there the repetition closes the discussion at its end: (2:134 — **“That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned”**). Anyone who has counted on the standing of others has the correction in the sentence.

**AN LEDGER THAT CANNOT BE INHERITED**

Think of a man who inherits a warehouse and believes the reputation attached to it will be entered into his own accounts at the day of settlement. The verse separates the two records and leaves each party with what he has done, and the identical phrasing is what makes the separation visible. The comparison explains the Book's repeated returns to the deeds of the ancestors, whose record is a warning and an example rather than a balance a descendant may draw on. Anyone who has seen a family live off a name it no longer deserves can see the situation the sentence describes. The plain arithmetic of a personal account is what the verse sets before him, and the warehouse is a reminder that a reputation is not a balance.

**THE INHERITANCE THAT DOES PASS ON**

The last clause of the formula removes the remainder of the descendants' expectations: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** and ***“for what they have done”***. The two records are left separated, the ancestors already judged and the living still writing, and the long argument about Abraham and his family is settled on that basis. What has been on offer all along is the tradition that can be inherited rather than the standing that cannot, and the account of the man's prayer and his answer has shown what that tradition consists of. Another passage names the inheritance that does transfer, and it describes a community raised up for the benefit of others through the same mercy that answered Abraham's prayer: (52:21 — **“We will elevate their descendants to their rank”**). The choice left is between resting on a closed account and attending to an open one. Today, family honour may open social doors, but it cannot transfer a completed moral record from an ancestor to a descendant.

---

## Verse 2:142

> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

**SHALLOW CRITICISM AFTER THE TURN**

The verse turns to a question that the sūrah knew was coming, and it reports it as a prediction about the shallowest element in the community: ***“The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?””***. The objectors are named before they speak, so that the question's weight is settled in advance. The change of direction had been a public act, and the sentence shows that the Book expected it to be discussed by people whose interest was in the appearance rather than in the obedience. The account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the questioners as those in Medina who used the change as a handle against the community, and the answer is addressed to everyone who might follow them. The objection was anticipated, which is itself part of the answer.

**A TURNING MADE AN ISSUE**

The words put in the objectors' mouths concern a turning rather than a teaching, and the sentence treats a matter of orientation as though it had to do with the ownership of God. The previous stretch of the sūrah had just finished answering claims about ancestors and inheritance, and the passage now takes up a question about ritual that had been raised against the community. The Book's practice in these disputes is to answer the premise rather than the complaint, and the answer that follows does exactly that. Anyone who has seen a change in practice become the centre of an argument can see what the question is designed to do. The objection, then, is not about the direction at all.

**OWNERSHIP STATED BEFORE GUIDANCE**

The reply opens with a statement of ownership and closes with a statement of guidance: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east”***, ***“and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.””***. The two directions were named together in an earlier verse of the sūrah, and the repetition keeps the answer on the same foundation: the ground belongs to its owner. Another passage names the same principle when it tells the believers that every community has its own direction and that the competition is in good deeds: (2:148 — **“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good”**). The closing clause then places the guidance where the Book always places it, with the One who gives it rather than with the people who argue about the form it takes. He is left with a reply that would end the dispute if the disputants were interested in the answer.

**ARGUING OVER WHICH WALL FACES THE ROAD**

Think of a family that receives instructions to move the table to the other wall and that spends the evening arguing about which of the two walls the owner of the house prefers. The sentence in the verse answers the argument by naming the owner, and it does so before anyone has a chance to settle the matter the way the objectors wanted. The comparison clarifies why the Book refuses to discuss the change on the terms offered, since the terms assume that a party other than the owner has standing in the question. Anyone who has watched a household spend its energy on the placement of furniture while the owner's instructions go elsewhere can see the situation described. The plainness of the answer and the folly of the question are what the verse leaves behind.

**WHAT IS SETTLED BY THE REPLY**

The verse settles two things in three sentences: the ground belongs to God, and the guidance of the community is His gift rather than a consequence of the direction it faces. The sūrah will go on to explain the purpose of the change in the verses that follow, but the answer given here does not wait for that explanation. The Book's manner in this passage is to place the principle before the history, so that the reader understands the reason before he hears the account. Anyone who has followed this sūrah from its opening verses will recognise the method, since the same order has been used in nearly every dispute the chapter has recorded. The difference between the objection anticipated and the answer provided is what the sentence leaves. Present-day changes in communal practice can provoke the same shallow charge of inconsistency when observers ignore the authority that issued both directions.

---

## Verse 2:143

> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity

**JUSTICE AT THE CENTRE OF WITNESS**

The community's purpose is stated at the head of this verse, which opens with a comparison to what came before: ***“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community”*** and ***“so that you may be witnesses over humanity”***. The word translated as upright carries the sense of the middle and the best at once, and the verse's claim is that the position of the community is both. Nothing in the sentence calls the community the largest or the oldest; it is described as placed in the middle, which in the usage of the language means the just. The sentence's purpose is then stated, and the purpose is a function exercised toward others rather than a privilege enjoyed for its own sake. What has been constituted here is a community made for the sake of a testimony. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the middle community as upright witnesses, the former direction as a nineteen-month test, and the preserved faith as prayers offered before the ruling changed.

**THE MIDDLE POSITION AND WHAT IT MEANS**

The term that describes the community is placed in a sentence that also names the Kaʿbah as the centre of the earth in some of the reports, and the two centres are joined by the comparison that opens the sentence. Justice is therefore the quality of the middle, not a weak compromise between truth and error. Another sūrah names the community with the same vocabulary and adds what it was raised for, which shows how fixed the description is in the Book: (3:110 — **“You are the best community ever raised for humanity”**). The middle, then, is not a compromise between two extremes but the point from which witness can be given to both sides. Someone taught to think of moderation as a lack of conviction will find the verse's sense of the word different from that.

**THE WITNESS THE COMMUNITY BEARS**

The sentence names the role the community will play on the day the accounting is made: ***“and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.”***. The two witnesses are named in one sentence, and they run in a sequence, with the community testifying about humanity and the Messenger testifying about the community. Another passage describes the same scene with the same two levels of testimony, which places the sentence among the Book's standard accounts of the reckoning: (4:41 — **“We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours”**). The Book's arrangement is hierarchical without being arbitrary, since each witness answers for what he was given. The community set before him will be asked about others, and its own messenger will be asked about it.

**AN INSPECTOR WHOSE OWN WORK WAS CHECKED**

Think of an inspector from a firm who is sent to examine other offices and who knows that his own work was examined before he was sent. The community in this verse has been placed in that position, and the Messenger's testimony about it is the inspection that comes before its own. The comparison explains why the sentence says the community was made for this role rather than that it achieved it, since the appointment is a commission rather than a promotion. Anyone who has been given authority over other people's work will recognise the weight in the sentence, and the weight falls on the one who holds it rather than on those he inspects. What remains is the responsibility of being placed in the middle.

**A DIRECTION THAT SIFTED THEM**

The next sentence explains why the community had been made to face a direction that was later changed, and it states the purpose plainly: ***“We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those”***, ***“who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those”*** and ***“who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except”***. The change was not a correction of a mistake; it was a test that separated the people whose allegiance was to the command from those whose allegiance was to the custom. The account given earlier in this sūrah of those communities has shown the same pattern in the demand for signs and in the calf. One early authority places the test in the interval when the community faced Jerusalem, and that reading fits the words of the sentence exactly. Anyone who has watched a community divide over a change in practice has seen the instrument the verse describes.

**THE FAITH THAT WILL NOT BE DISCOUNTED**

The verse closes with the assurance that answers the anxiety the test would have created, and the words are generous: ***“for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah.”***, ***“And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious”*** and ***“and Most Merciful to humanity”***. The sentence guarantees that the prayers offered in the earlier direction were not wasted, which is the practical worry the change would have raised among the believers. The two names at the close explain the guarantee, since the One who gives the guidance is the One who keeps the record. The assurance is stated in another passage for a community that feared its earlier worship had been wasted, and the words there match the promise here: (3:195 — **“So their Lord responded to them: “I will never deny any of you—male or female—the reward”**). The Book's manner here is to state the purpose of a difficult command and then to remove the fear that the command had produced, and the order is worth noting. The picture left is of a community tested, distinguished, and then reassured about what it had already done. Today, a balanced community proves its fitness to testify through justice, while changes in familiar practice expose whether loyalty belongs to revelation or habit.

---

## Verse 2:144

> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do

**A FACE TURNED TOWARD HEAVEN**

The verse begins with what God saw in His Prophet, and the sight is described in words the Prophet himself would have recognised: ***“Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺”*** and ***“that will please you.”***. The longing is named before it is answered, so that the desire is dignified before it is granted. Nothing in the sentence says that the Messenger had complained or asked; what it says is that God saw him turning, and the answer came to the turning rather than to a request. The reading credited to Ibn ʿAbbās describes the turning as a waiting for Gabriel to arrive with the command about the House, and the description fits the reply that follows. What stands in the scene is a petition heard before it was spoken.

**THE SANCTUARY LONGED FOR**

The direction that would please the Messenger was the one belonging to Abraham's sanctuary, which the sūrah has just spent a long passage describing as the first house of worship. The communities of Medina had their own orientations, and the announcement that the believers would face the ancient House settled a matter that had been unsettled since the migration. The earlier account of the patriarchs in this sūrah has shown that the House was built as a refuge for all who came to pray, which makes the change of orientation a return rather than an innovation. Someone who has followed the chapter from the account of Abraham's prayer will see why the answer to the longing was also a claim on a heritage. The change was a restoration in the eyes of the community that had been waiting for it, which is what the sentence settles.

**TURNING TOWARD THE HOUSE**

The command that follows is doubled, since it is given to the Messenger and then to everyone with him: ***“So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺”***, ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those”*** and ***“who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord.”***. The change is absolute, and the clause about the believers' location removes any exception for distance, land, or sea. Another passage states the same command in nearly the same form and adds the reason it was given, which shows how central the sentence is to this part of the sūrah: (2:150 — **“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque”**). The sentence's final clause then lays a claim about the people of the earlier scriptures, which the following verses will take up: they knew what the command confirmed, and the verse says so before they are accused of hiding it.

**A DEED ARRIVING AFTER LONG WAITING**

Think of tenants who have lived in a rented house for years and who one day receive the deed to the house they had always regarded as theirs. The verse's change of direction has that quality for the community, which had been facing the sanctuary of another people while the House of its own ancestor stood in the south. The comparison also explains the clause about the People of the Scripture, since a deed transferred is best understood by those who knew its history. A long anticipation ending in a plain command is the shape of the sentence, and the command is plain because the matter had been settled long before. The moment of arrival is what the passage holds out.

**KNOWLEDGE HELD BY THE OTHERS**

The verse closes by naming God's awareness of what the others do, and the clause is placed after the statement about their knowledge rather than before it: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what they do”***. The pairing is deliberate, since the sentence has just said that the communities knew the truth of the change, and the closing words state that their conduct with that knowledge is being recorded. The combination repeats where the Book addresses what the People of the Scripture knew and what they concealed: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children”**). A sentence is given that grants the knowledge, names the command, and leaves the accounting to God. The next verses draw out the consequences of that knowledge for the people who held it. In the present day, repeated longing may be answered by a duty whose fulfilment requires the whole community to turn together.

---

## Verse 2:145

> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers

**NO PROOF THAT WILL MOVE THEM**

The verse states what no amount of evidence could accomplish with the communities that had received scriptures, and it states it with an opening that concedes the maximum: ***“Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺”***. The proof is granted in full and refused in the same sentence, which removes the possibility that the matter was a question of evidence. The sūrah has come back to this point again and again in its account of these communities, and the verse states it without qualification. Someone who has tried to settle a dispute by producing the strongest argument available will find the sentence describing the limit of that method. The refusal, then, belongs to the will rather than to the understanding. Ibn ʿAbbās read every sign as unable to move those determined not to follow the new direction, while the warning protects revealed knowledge from surrender to competing desires.

**A REFUSAL THAT RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS**

The verse then adds two more refusals, and they are symmetrical with the first: ***“nor would you accept theirs”*** and ***“nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another.”***. The sentence leaves no party holding a position the others will adopt, which means the disagreement is settled by the Book rather than by agreement among the parties. The same outlook is stated in another passage where the Messenger is told that the two communities will never be satisfied with him short of conversion: (2:120 — **“Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you”**). The symmetry in the sentence is a kind of mercy, since it lifts a burden that argument could never have carried away. What the reader is released from is the hope that the right evidence would finally produce agreement.

**A CONDITION AIMED AT THE BELIEVERS**

The matter is then turned toward the community itself, in a warning about following what the others desire: ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”***, ***“that has come to you”*** and ***“then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers”***. The condition is hypothetical, and the Book uses the form to name a danger without predicting that it will happen, which is how it addressed the same community in an earlier verse about the desire for the neighbours' approval. The warning is placed after the knowledge has been named, so that the fault described would be a decision against information rather than a failure of information. Another passage states that following the majority of people on earth leads away from the path, which places this sentence in a pattern the sūrah has already established: (6:116 — **“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way”**). Where the severity is directed is worth noticing, since the warning falls on the believers rather than on the others.

**TWO SHOPS THAT WILL NOT TRADE**

Think of two shops on the same street, each of which refuses to stock what the other sells, and neither of which will be persuaded by the other's catalogue. The verse describes that standoff in the matter of the direction of prayer, and it ends the discussion by naming the one thing that would make the believer a wrongdoer. The standoff explains why no further argument is invited here, since the parties are not in a state of enquiry that more information could advance. Watching a community argue itself into the position of its opponents by small accommodations shows what the warning is for. The boundary drawn around the community's own position is what the verse leaves in place. A boundary crossed in small steps is still crossed, and the warning is aimed at the steps rather than at the final position.

**THE GROUND UNDER THE WARNING**

The final clause's force depends on the phrase before it, since the knowledge said to have come to the community is the measure of what following the others' desires would cost. The Book's use of this phrase in this sūrah is consistent: the knowledge is what the community received, and it is also what makes its conduct accountable. Another passage states the same truth in a form addressed to the Prophet's own heart, where doubt is forbidden on the ground of what has already arrived: (3:60 — **“This is the truth from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt”**). The warning's weight comes entirely from what the community already knows, and not from any fresh evidence that could be brought forward, which is why the matter can be stated as settled rather than as a question still open to debate. The next verse turns to that knowledge again and to what a group among the others does with it. Today, unlimited evidence does not persuade a person whose real condition is that truth must first conform to existing desire.

---

## Verse 2:146

> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly

**A RECOGNITION AS CLEAR AS FAMILY**

What the people who had received scriptures knew about the Messenger is stated here, with a comparison drawn from ordinary life: ***“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺”*** and ***“as they recognize their own children.”***. The comparison is drawn from the most familiar recognition a person has, which makes the knowledge asserted here the opposite of a vague impression. This stretch does not charge the others with missing information; it charges a group among them with choosing concealment after recognition. Another passage makes the same claim in a sentence about the scripture they had been given, which is a pattern the Book uses in more than one place: (6:114 — **“Those who were given the Scripture know that it has been revealed”**). What the sentence establishes is the level of certainty the communities possessed. Ibn ʿAbbās applied the recognition to people who knew the Prophet's description as distinctly as a child among other children, yet noted that a party knowingly concealed it.

**THE OBJECT OF THAT RECOGNITION**

The recognition had a content, and part of it has already been described in the account of the covenant that bound them to publish the scripture. The descriptions of the coming prophet in the earlier books are what the sentence refers to, and the Book treats the match between those descriptions and the Messenger as a matter of settled knowledge rather than of interpretation. The comparison with a father's recognition of his own children implies the kind of certainty that does not need to be argued into a person, which is why the following clause is about conduct rather than about doubt. The terms are exact for the act they name: a claim acknowledged and then buried. What the verse leaves no room for is the plea that the communities did not know.

**THE GROUP THAT HIDES WHAT IT KNOWS**

The conduct is then named in a single clause: ***“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”***. The word for the concealment covers an act of putting something out of sight, and the clause adds the adverb that removes every excuse, since the hiding is done with knowledge. The Book has already described the same offence in its account of the covenant sworn to make the scripture known, and this sentence shows the offence continuing into the community's dealings with the Prophet himself. The qualification about the group is important, since the sūrah has also described people among the same communities who were upright and followed what they had. Anyone who has seen a document quietly withdrawn from circulation will recognise the act the sentence names.

**RECOGNITION FOLLOWED BY SILENCE**

Think of a family that meets a young man in the street, knows him to be the son who was given away years before, and walks past him in silence. The verse describes a recognition of exactly that kind and an act of concealment that follows it, and the two clauses stand together so that neither can be read alone. The comparison explains the severity of the charge against these communities, since the failure named is not ignorance but the burial of knowledge. Anyone who has watched a man withhold the identity of someone he recognised can see how the situation is constructed. What the verse offers the reader is the difference between knowing and acknowledging. The difference between knowing and acknowledging is the lesson on offer.

**A TESTIMONY PUT AWAY**

The truth is the object of the concealment, which means what was hidden was not an opinion but the thing itself. The same word is used for the revelation throughout the sūrah, and the sentence places it in opposition to a group's conduct rather than to their understanding. Another passage describes the same concealment as the reason for a curse pronounced by the tongues of the prophets, which shows how seriously the Book treats the handling of knowledge: (3:187 — **“when Allah took the covenant of those”**). A sentence is left that grants the communities everything except honesty. The verses that follow turn to the question of what the community itself is to do with the truth it has received. Present-day recognition can coexist with concealment when professional or communal cost makes an acknowledged truth inconvenient to state.

---

## Verse 2:147

> ˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt

**FROM YOUR LORD, PLAINLY SAID**

The status of what has come down to the Messenger is stated here in the plainest words available: ***“˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord”***. The sentence follows an account of communities that knew the truth and concealed it, and it places the Prophet's own footing on the same fact they had buried. The practice in these verses is to name the source of the revelation for the benefit of the one receiving it, and the naming here answers the doubt that other people's concealment might have produced. Nothing in the sentence depends on the communities' acknowledgement, which is what makes it a statement about the revelation rather than about its reception. Anyone who has seen a truth buried by its custodians will find the sentence a relief. Ibn ʿAbbās read the truth as confirmation of the Prophet's mission and the closing prohibition as refusal to let another party's concealment produce doubt.

**SPOKEN TO ONE MAN**

The instruction that follows is given in the second person singular, and it addresses the one who had received the revelation rather than the crowd around him: ***“so do not ever be one of those who doubt”***. Prophets are warned about doubt in other places as well, and the warnings are always attached to the knowledge that has already arrived rather than to an absence of it. Another passage uses nearly the same words in a similar setting, which shows the phrase to be a recognised way of steadying the recipient of revelation: (3:60 — **“This is the truth from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt”**). The sentence therefore treats doubt as something other than an intellectual position, since it is forbidden in the presence of the truth rather than after a proof of it. The certainty being asked for rests on the source of the message and not on the strength of the recipient's own conviction.

**REACHING THE BELIEVERS THROUGH HIM**

The command reaches the community through its messenger, and the Book makes the same demand of the believers elsewhere when it tells them to ask those who had read the earlier scriptures rather than to waver. Another passage addresses the Prophet in the same terms and adds the instruction to seek out the people who had been reading the scriptures before him, which shows how the Book handles doubt when it arises: (10:94 — **“The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord”**). The sentence's brevity is part of its method, since the matter is settled by naming the source rather than by rehearsing the evidence. Anyone who has followed the long account of signs and covenants in this sūrah will recognise the point to which every argument in it returns. The sentence leaves a plain choice between what has arrived and what the doubters prefer.

**CERTAINTY THAT DOES NOT BORROW ITS SEAL**

Think of a man who receives a letter from someone he knows and who hears his neighbours say the letter is a forgery. The verse's sentence gives the recipient what he needs for that situation, and it does not consist of an argument about handwriting but of the identity of the sender. The comparison explains why the warning is addressed to the one who received the message, since the doubt that matters is the doubt that could enter the household that received it. Anyone who has had to hold to what he knew against a chorus of denial will understand the sentence's purpose. What the verse offers is not a defence of the message but a reminder of where it came from.

**CLOSING THE ARGUMENT**

Read with what follows, the sentence closes the passage on the qiblah and the communities that refused it, and it leaves the community with an identity rather than a quarrel. The sūrah is about to turn to a different subject, so this verse functions as the last word on the argument: the truth has come, the doubters are named, and the believers are told where to stand. The Book's manner of closing a discussion in this way appears at several points in the sūrah, and it always leaves the reader with the revelation rather than with the objections to it. He who has traced the argument from the change of direction to the concealment of the testimony now sees the whole matter gathered into one sentence. He is left with the instruction that the truth is not improved by doubting it. Today, doubt should not be manufactured merely because confident opponents conceal evidence they already understand.

---

## Verse 2:148

> Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**A COMPASS FOR EVERY HOUSEHOLD**

The sentence opens by granting each community a direction of its own: ***“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺”***. What follows can be read in two ways: a people turns itself towards what it faces, or a people is turned towards it. The second reading gives the sentence more weight, since the direction then belongs to an appointment rather than to a preference. Ibn ʿAbbās extended the phrase to the communities around the first believers, and the wording can encompass every adherent of a religion. The sentence answers a quarrel, since neither side was following the other's direction and each side already had what it faced. The breadth of that reading matters because the command redirects attention from inherited difference to accountable action before the final gathering.

**A RACE WITH THE FINISH IN VIEW**

From the difference in directions the verse moves at once to the thing that counts, and what it commands is a competition in good: ***“So compete with one another in doing good”***. Striving in acts of obedience and in the acceptance of them is the sense the command bears, so that the rivalry is not over the direction but over the response. Ibn ʿAbbās gave the command the sense of an address to the community to hasten towards good works beyond every other nation. The Book uses the same words where the differences between communities are mentioned and then set aside for the same purpose: (5:48 — **“So compete with one another in doing good. To Allah you will all return,”**). The verse is not indifferent to the direction; it refuses to let the direction become the whole religion.

**GATHERED FROM LAND AND SEA**

The promise that follows turns the matter toward the end of the road: ***“Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺”***. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase with land and sea, since distance is no obstacle to the One who gathers, and the sentence names the assembly at which the competition and the quarrels are finally weighed. The command to compete adds promptness and completeness to the mere doing of good, so the community is asked for its best effort rather than for the minimum that satisfies the letter. Competition changes adequate action into an eager pursuit without changing the field from goodness to rivalry in status. The verse closes on the ground of that confidence: ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The power that will gather the scattered is the same power that will settle what the competitors disputed.

**TWO RUNNERS IN LANES THEY ARGUE ABOUT**

Think of two runners on separate lanes of the same track who spend the morning disputing which lane the organizer intended, while the organizer stands at the finish line and waits. The dispute is not settled by one of them proving the other's lane wrong; it is settled when the race is run and the times are read. The community is given the same instruction here: leave the quarrel about lanes to the One who set the course, and put the whole of one's strength into running well. Every community that argues about its own correctness while neglecting what it was told to do has repeated the first half of the scene and missed the second. The image also shows why the sentence leaves the others' directions alone: the question has been moved to another field.

**THE DISPUTE LEFT WHERE IT IS**

The verse neither abolishes the differences nor pretends they do not matter, and the way it handles them is instructive. The community is not asked to prove that its direction is right before it begins to act; it is asked to act, and the proof is left to the day when all are gathered. The Book makes the same point elsewhere when it denies that righteousness lies in the direction a face is turned: (2:177 — **“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west.”**). What follows that sentence is a list of deeds, which is exactly the order this verse establishes.
