## Verse 2:212

> The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit

**THE ATTRACTION OF THE WORLD**

***“The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they”*** establishes the attraction of the world. The verse explains why people may exchange guidance for worldly gain. The life of this world is made attractive to those who disbelieve. Wealth, status, pleasure, comfort, and immediate success can appear so complete that a person forgets death and judgement. The Qur’an does not say that worldly beauty is unreal or that believers may not enjoy lawful blessings. It warns against allowing temporary attraction to define the whole meaning of life. The verb made appealing—zuyyina—can describe both a test in Allah’s creation and the work of Satan and desire. The world becomes dangerous when its decoration hides consequences. A person sees the profit but not the injustice that produced it, the pleasure but not the addiction that follows, or the applause but not the emptiness of living for approval. When believers refuse a profitable sin or challenge a dominant culture, they may be mocked as naïve, backward, weak, or impractical. The verse acknowledges this social pressure. The disbelievers’ ridicule is not proof that the believers are inferior. It often reveals the discomfort of people who do not want their priorities questioned. Believers must not respond with arrogance or mockery of their own. The Qur’an forbids one people ridiculing another and teaches dignified speech. Firmness means maintaining faith and justice without becoming intoxicated by a sense of superiority. The worldly hierarchy will be reversed on the Day of Resurrection. (49:11 — **“O believers! Do not let some ˹men˺ ridicule others, they may be better than them,”**) Because the attraction of the world frames ridiculing the believers, ridiculing the believers returns attention to the attraction of the world. An account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās names Bilāl, Salmān, and Ṣuhayb among the poor believers who were mocked, making social contempt part of the verse’s historical setting.

**RIDICULING THE BELIEVERS**

***“mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them”*** deepens ridiculing the believers. People who appeared powerful may be exposed as spiritually bankrupt, while servants who were mocked for faith are honoured by Allah. Being above them refers to rank, security, and reward in the Hereafter, not a command for believers to seek domination over people in this life. The promise is not for every person who uses a religious identity. It is for those who are muttaqūn, mindful of Allah in belief and conduct. A believer who claims Islam while oppressing others cannot rely on the verse as a guarantee. Taqwā is proven through truth, patience, and justice. Allah gives provision—rizq—without measure. This can mean abundant worldly provision, unexpected spiritual gifts, or reward beyond calculation in the Hereafter. The phrase also comforts the believer who loses worldly status for refusing falsehood. Allah’s storehouses are not limited by the approval of a market, ruler, or audience. Provision is not always a sign of divine favour. The disbelievers may receive great wealth as a test, while a believer may be poor yet rich in faith and dignity. The Qur’an asks people to distinguish temporary distribution from final honour. Allah gives according to wisdom and will, and no lawful sacrifice is lost. Islam does not teach hatred of the created world. The earth, family, food, work, and beauty are signs and gifts. The problem is dunyā when it becomes the ultimate object of love and fear. (2:211 — **“Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them.”**) Since the last reversal of social rank follows the attraction of the world, ridiculing the believers links purpose to the last reversal of social rank.

**THE LAST REVERSAL OF SOCIAL RANK**

***“on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”*** clarifies the last reversal of social rank. A believer uses the world as a means to the Hereafter, earning lawfully, supporting family, helping the poor, and cultivating knowledge. The Prophet ﷺ lived simply but accepted lawful gifts, married, traded, governed, and cared for society. He taught that wealth in itself is not blameworthy; what matters is how it is acquired, what it does to the heart, and how it is spent. A believer responds to mockery with patience, clarity, and good character. He does not abandon a command to gain acceptance, but he does not turn every disagreement into a fight. If ridicule becomes harassment or violence, he may seek protection and justice. Patience never requires accepting abuse without lawful remedy. Communities should support those who face pressure. Children, converts, minorities, and people leaving harmful environments may need companionship and practical help. The promise of Allah’s provision is lived partly through believers who become means of support for one another. Think of the attraction of the world through a man who laughs at a labourer for carrying water while he sits beside a well he has paid to dig. When the well dries up in the summer, the labourer's route to the spring is the only one left, and the man with the empty well is the one who asks for a cup. The attraction of the world reaches a reader today who measures his neighbours by the cars in their driveways and his own worth by the same count. (3:14 — **“The enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children, treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle,”**) Provision without measure matters, which means the last reversal of social rank returns provision without measure to the attraction of the world.

**PROVISION WITHOUT MEASURE**

The verse gives him a ranking that is announced on another day and a provision that is given without limit, and it asks him which scale he uses when he looks at a poor man who prays. Because the comparison is placed on the day of judgement rather than in the market, the attraction of the world shows that the account is not settled by the ledger of this world. Since the mockery is named as the fruit of the adornment, the attraction of the world shows that a wrong measure of wealth turns into a wrong measure of people. The ranking is named as the reward of a quality and not of a fortune, and the last reversal of social rank leaves each person to ask which ladder he is climbing. The Book states the same reversal in the passage of the tables of the earlier community, so that the attraction of the world reveals the wealth of a denier and the punishment of a denier in one frame. A further verse keeps the guidance in the hand of God alone, and the attraction of the world shows that the two gifts of this verse and the next belong to one Giver. Ridiculing the believers makes the attraction of the world practical; the last reversal of social rank therefore matters.

## Verse 2:213

> Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path

**HUMANITY’S ORIGINAL UNITY**

***“Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and”*** establishes humanity’s original unity. The statement that humanity was one community—kāna al-nāsu ummatan wāḥidah—can carry related senses. It may refer to their original unity upon a simple recognition of Allah before disputes multiplied, or to their being one undivided human community before revelation and social differences required detailed guidance. The broader lesson is clear: division is not humanity’s highest destiny, and revelation came to restore truth amid competing claims. Unity in the Qur’an does not mean that all people must share one culture or that every disagreement is blameworthy. It means unity upon truth, justice, and the recognition of Allah. Human diversity in language, nation, and custom can be a sign of Allah. What destroys community is arrogant rivalry, oppression, and the refusal to accept correction. Allah sent prophets as bashīrīn and mundhirīn: bearers of good news and warners. Good news encourages faith, repentance, mercy, Paradise, and the honour of obedience. Warning protects people from disbelief, injustice, and the consequences of refusing truth. A message with only warning may produce despair; one with only promise may produce complacency. Prophetic teaching balances hope and fear. The prophets share one essential call—to worship Allah alone—while the details of law can differ according to time and community. Muslims believe in all of them and do not insult one messenger to honour another. The Prophet ﷺ described the prophets as brothers with the same father but different mothers, meaning one faith with different legal forms, as both al-Bukhārī and Muslim report. (30:22 — **“And one of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth,”**) Because humanity’s original unity frames prophets bring good news and warning, prophets bring good news and warning returns attention to humanity’s original unity.

**PROPHETS BRING GOOD NEWS AND WARNING**

***“as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed”*** deepens prophets bring good news and warning. Allah sent the Book in truth so that it might judge between people in their disagreements. Revelation is not merely a collection of private spiritual inspirations. It establishes a criterion for belief, worship, ethics, contracts, family rights, and public justice. When people disagree, they return to Allah’s Book and the prophetic explanation rather than allowing power or popularity to decide. The Book does not erase the need for human judgement. Scholars interpret language and apply principles to changing circumstances. Courts examine evidence and protect procedure. But all these efforts remain accountable to revelation. A judge who accepts a bribe or a leader who uses scripture to protect himself has betrayed the Book’s purpose. The verse says that some people differed only after clear proofs came to them. This is not a condemnation of every difference in interpretation. Honest scholars may disagree over evidence that is probabilistic, language that admits more than one reading, or new circumstances. The blameworthy dispute is the one that arises after clarity and is driven by baghy, jealous hostility and transgression. Such rivalry may be caused by envy of another community’s status, fear of losing authority, desire for wealth, or refusal to accept that a truth has come through a person outside one’s group. The result is not merely a theoretical disagreement. People conceal proofs, distort texts, and mobilize followers against one another. Allah guides believers to the truth in what people differ over, by His permission. This guidance is a gift, but believers seek it through sincerity, knowledge, consultation, prayer, and willingness to be corrected. (10:19 — **“Humanity was once nothing but a single community ˹of believers˺, but then they differed.”**) Since revelation as judge of disputes follows humanity’s original unity, prophets bring good news and warning links purpose to revelation as judge of disputes.

**REVELATION AS JUDGE OF DISPUTES**

***“the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by”*** clarifies revelation as judge of disputes. A person who begins a discussion determined to defeat an opponent may possess information yet miss guidance. The verse does not promise that believers will agree on every secondary matter. It promises that Allah can guide them to the truth and to proper conduct in disagreement. They may say, Allah knows best, respect legitimate scholarship, and preserve brotherhood while remaining firm on clear principles. The Qur’an identifies both ignorance and hostility as causes of division. Ignorance is addressed through teaching; hostility requires purification of the heart. A community can possess libraries and institutions while still fighting because envy has made knowledge a weapon. The remedy includes sincere intention, justice toward opponents, and recognition that Allah’s guidance is not a personal possession. The Prophet ﷺ warned that disputation can lead people astray when it is not based on sincere learning. He taught mercy, consultation, and returning matters to the Qur’an and Sunnah. A community should create spaces where questions are safe, evidence is examined, and disagreement does not become a reason for humiliation. The straight path does not erase legitimate diversity. It directs diversity toward worship, justice, and mutual recognition. Muslims can differ in language, legal school, architecture, food, and social custom while sharing the testimony, prayer, Qur’an, and prophetic model. They must distinguish these permissible differences from rivalry that fragments the faith. Allah guides whom He wills, and His will is joined to wisdom and justice. The servant does not claim that his group owns guidance. (16:36 — **“We surely sent a messenger to every community, saying, “Worship Allah and shun false gods.”**) Difference after clear proofs matters, which means revelation as judge of disputes returns difference after clear proofs to humanity’s original unity.

**DIFFERENCE AFTER CLEAR PROOFS**

***“His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path”*** closes with difference after clear proofs. He asks Allah to guide him and acts upon the truth he knows. Think of humanity’s original unity through an inheritance divided among brothers who each hire a lawyer to read the same will. The will is read aloud in the court, the estate is spent on the reading, and the only one who leaves with his share is the brother who never hired anyone. Humanity’s original unity confronts anyone treating prophets bring good news and warning as remote; under humanity’s original unity, such a person has watched a community divide over a fine point and has decided to keep out of every question. The verse gives him a history in which the dispute is named as jealousy and the guidance as grace, and humanity’s original unity asks which of the two he is carrying into his own argument. Because the guidance is promised to those who believe, humanity’s original unity shows that neutrality is not the same thing as faith. The Book gives the same account of the sending in the chapter of the family of ʿImrān, and names the path again in the verse of the prayer of the community, so that humanity’s original unity lets a person hear the last words of this verse as an echo of the daily prayer. (42:13 — **“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah,”**) Prophets bring good news and warning makes humanity’s original unity practical; revelation as judge of disputes therefore matters. Today, communities facing religious disagreement need revealed judgement, honest study, and freedom from rivalry disguised as principle.

## Verse 2:214

> Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near

**PARADISE IS NOT REACHED WITHOUT TESTING**

***“Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested”*** establishes paradise is not reached without testing. The verse corrects an expectation that faith should remove every hardship. Believers may hope for Allah’s protection, but they should not assume that Paradise is earned without trial. The path of the prophets included persecution, poverty, exile, illness, grief, and opposition. Testing reveals sincerity, purifies the heart, strengthens reliance, and distinguishes a living commitment from a claim made only when life is comfortable. The question Do you think. is an invitation to examine assumptions. A person may say he is ready to sacrifice, but hardship reveals what he truly values. The Qur’an does not promise that every believer will face the same trial or that suffering itself guarantees Paradise. It teaches that tests are part of the path and must be met with faith, patience, and lawful action. The previous generations were touched by baʾsāʾ and ḍarrāʾ. The first includes poverty, deprivation, and external hardship; the second includes illness, injury, and painful affliction. These words cover both social conditions and personal suffering. The believer is permitted to seek food, medical care, shelter, employment, and protection. Patience does not require refusing help or romanticizing poverty. The community also bears responsibility. When people are tested by hunger or displacement, other believers must provide material aid rather than simply telling them to be patient. Zakah, charity, fair policy, and protection of the oppressed are practical expressions of faith. They were shaken—zulzilū—describes intense fear and pressure. (2:153 — **“O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient”**) Because paradise is not reached without testing frames poverty and hardship, poverty and hardship returns attention to paradise is not reached without testing.

**POVERTY AND HARDSHIP**

***“like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were”*** deepens poverty and hardship. The trial disturbed their outward security and tested their inward certainty. The verse does not condemn them for feeling fear. Even prophets experienced anxiety in dangerous circumstances. What matters is that they remained turned toward Allah and waited for His help rather than abandoning faith or becoming unjust. The statement When will Allah’s help come. is not necessarily a complaint against Allah. It can be the cry of people who long for relief while still trusting the promise. Yaʿqūb grieved and complained to Allah; Ayyūb called upon Allah in illness; the Prophet ﷺ sought help in battle. Honest lament before Allah is different from accusing Him of injustice. Allah’s answer is immediate: His help is near—alā inna naṣr Allāhi qarīb. Nearness does not always mean that relief arrives according to the servant’s timetable. Help may come through victory, a change in circumstances, protection from sin, unity of the believers, forgiveness, or reward in the Hereafter. Allah may delay the visible outcome while strengthening the people who will carry it. The promise gives hope without prescribing a date. Impatience can lead people to unlawful shortcuts, betrayal, or despair. Taqwā means taking means, persevering, and trusting that no trial is outside Allah’s knowledge. A believer facing illness, unemployment, persecution, or grief may wonder whether Allah has rejected him. The verse shows that the best servants were tested. (3:142 — **“Do you think you will enter Paradise without Allah proving which of you ˹truly˺ struggled ˹for His”**) Since they were shaken follows paradise is not reached without testing, poverty and hardship links purpose to they were shaken.

**THEY WERE SHAKEN**

***“so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried”*** clarifies they were shaken. Hardship is not automatically punishment, and comfort is not automatically approval. The meaning depends upon the person’s response and Allah’s wisdom. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the people most severely tested are the prophets, then those nearest to them in righteousness, according to Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī. This does not make people seek pain. It teaches that difficulty can accompany honour and spiritual growth. The verse uses the messenger and believers together. Trials are faced collectively through leadership, mutual support, consultation, and prayer. A righteous leader does not hide hardship from the people or demand sacrifices he will not share. Believers encourage one another, distribute resources, protect the vulnerable, and avoid rumours that deepen fear. The Prophet ﷺ built resilience through prayer, brotherhood, lawful planning, and trust. The community’s spiritual language was matched by action: sheltering migrants, feeding the poor, defending the oppressed, and fulfilling covenants. When an individual is shaken, he can divide the crisis into duties: maintain the obligatory prayer as able, seek expert and medical help, speak honestly, protect dependants, avoid unlawful relief, and ask Allah for patience. He should not compare his trial with another person’s or assume that weakness makes him a hypocrite. Healing can be gradual. A person may say, When will Allah’s help come. while continuing to seek it through lawful means. The promise of nearness gives him permission to hope again each day. (29:2 — **“Do people think once they say, “We believe,”**) Help is near matters, which means they were shaken returns help is near to paradise is not reached without testing.

**HELP IS NEAR**

***“out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near”*** closes with help is near. Think of paradise is not reached without testing through a father who takes his son up a mountain by a path he has used for years. The boy asks three times how much further, and the father answers each time for the same reason: the top is not far, and the boy has never been there before. Paradise is not reached without testing confronts anyone treating poverty and hardship as remote; under paradise is not reached without testing, such a person has served a good cause for years and has begun to ask when the effort will be answered. The verse gives him a cry from the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and a promise that the help is near, and paradise is not reached without testing asks what he expected the road to be like. Because the question of the sufferers is written in the Book without blame, paradise is not reached without testing shows that the tired person’s complaint differs from an enemy’s denial. The testing described under paradise is not reached without testing reappears in the words of the verse of trial, so that paradise is not reached without testing reveals the promise of testing given before the events. A further verse keeps the duty of the fight with the same comfort, and the two passages together show that the servant is not told the schedule. (47:31 — **“We will certainly test you ˹believers˺ until We prove those of you who ˹truly˺ struggle ˹in Allah’s”**) Poverty and hardship makes paradise is not reached without testing practical; they were shaken therefore matters. Today, prolonged care, reform, or public service may shake faithful people without making their weariness a denial of Allah’s help.

## Verse 2:215

> They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”

**ASKING ABOUT THE RIGHT USE OF WEALTH**

***“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say,”*** establishes asking about the right use of wealth. The question concerns what should be spent—mādhā yunfiqūn—and the answer directs attention not only to the amount but to the people who have claims. Charitable spending is not merely an expression of generosity; it is a social responsibility. Allah names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travellers because wealth should reach those whose protection, provision, or temporary circumstances make them vulnerable. The verse does not mean that every voluntary donation must always be distributed in precisely this order regardless of circumstance. It establishes priorities and reminds believers to notice needs close to them rather than pursuing distant public praise while neglecting dependent parents or struggling relatives. Parents often deserve support because of their lifelong care and because old age, illness, or poverty can make them dependent. Relatives combine the right of need with the bond of kinship. Supporting them can be both charity and maintaining ṣilat al-raḥim, the connection of family ties. Yet family connection must not become nepotism or a reason to deny assistance to non-relatives who are in greater danger. The Prophet ﷺ taught that charity to a relative can carry the reward of charity and maintaining kinship. The giver should still avoid reminding the recipient of the favour or using money to control family members. (4:2 — **“Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺,”**) Because asking about the right use of wealth frames parents and relatives, parents and relatives returns attention to asking about the right use of wealth. In Ibn ʿAbbās’s reading, the verse orders the named recipients as parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the stranded guest, giving generosity a circle of concrete claims.

**PARENTS AND RELATIVES**

***““Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and”*** deepens parents and relatives. Support should preserve dignity and encourage wellbeing. Orphans—yatāmā—need care because they have lost a parent or guardian and may lack someone to defend their rights. The Qur’an strongly warns against consuming their property or treating them harshly. Giving to an orphan includes food, education, shelter, emotional support, and careful guardianship of any inheritance. The needy—masākīn—may have some resources but not enough for basic life. Their poverty can be hidden, and they may avoid asking. A compassionate community learns to identify needs without humiliating people. The traveller—ibn al-sabīl—may be wealthy at home but stranded without access to his property. Help is based on present need, not on stereotypes about the person’s overall status. Whatever good you spend includes lawful money, time, food, clothing, expertise, and effort. A person may provide transport, teach a skill, pay a medical bill, or protect someone from abuse. The word khayr reminds us that spending should produce real benefit and not support harm, vanity, or corruption. The source of the wealth matters. Charity from theft does not purify the thief, and a donation that buys political silence may be a form of bribery. Allah accepts what is good and given with sincere intention. (93:9 — **“So do not oppress the orphan”**) Since orphans, the needy, and travellers follows asking about the right use of wealth, parents and relatives links purpose to orphans, the needy, and travellers.

**ORPHANS, THE NEEDY, AND TRAVELLERS**

***“˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.””*** clarifies orphans, the needy, and travellers. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the upper hand is better than the lower hand, while also encouraging moderation and responsibility toward dependants. Islam does not teach a person to give away what his family needs and then call the resulting hardship piety. The Prophet ﷺ advised beginning with those for whom one is responsible and leaving dependants secure. Obligatory support, debt repayment, and the rights of workers come before optional public generosity. After fulfilling immediate duties, believers look outward. A relative may need help, but so may a refugee, disaster victim, student, or neighbour of another faith. Allah’s categories establish compassion, not a narrow circle of tribal preference. The best spending reaches people with justice and wisdom. The final statement assures the giver that no act is lost. People may not know about a quiet payment, a meal delivered at night, or time spent caring for an orphan. Allah knows the amount, intention, sacrifice, and benefit. This protects charity from dependence upon human applause. It also warns the giver not to corrupt the act after giving through reminders, insults, or public humiliation. The Qur’an says that charity is cancelled when accompanied by injury and boasts. The gift belongs to Allah’s knowledge even when the recipient cannot repay it. Think of asking about the right use of wealth through a man who sends a parcel to a village he has never seen and forgets that his brother lives in the next street with an empty fridge. (2:264 — **“O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words,”**) What is good spending. matters, which means orphans, the needy, and travellers returns what is good spending. to asking about the right use of wealth.

**WHAT IS GOOD SPENDING.**

The parcel arrives, the photograph of the delivery is framed, and the brother eats at a neighbour's table. Asking about the right use of wealth reaches a reader today who gives generously to a distant cause and lets his own relatives ask a stranger for help. The verse gives him a list that begins with the two people who carried him and asks where his money goes first. Because the closing sentence names the knowledge of God rather than the thanks of the poor, the reader is taught to give for the record that matters. The Book describes the righteous in the same terms in the verse of the qualities, so that asking about the right use of wealth reveals the list of this verse used as a portrait of a life. A further passage keeps the same concern for the poor in the chapter of the cave, and the reader is shown how often the Book returns to the purse of the believer. Parents and relatives makes asking about the right use of wealth practical; orphans, the needy, and travellers therefore matters.

## Verse 2:216

> Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**A DIFFICULT DUTY**

***“Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it.”*** establishes a difficult duty. This verse acknowledges the human dislike of fighting. Violence brings fear, injury, bereavement, displacement, and moral danger. The Qur’an does not romanticize war or pretend that a believer naturally enjoys it. Fighting may become necessary to defend a community from aggression and persecution, but it remains a severe and regulated duty rather than a source of entertainment or pride. The wording has been prescribed must be read with the limits in the surrounding verses: fighting those who fight, no transgression, acceptance of cessation, and proportional response. It does not command individuals to attack people because of their faith. It establishes a community’s responsibility to defend life and religious freedom when lawful conditions are met. People often judge good and bad by immediate emotion. They dislike discipline, truthful correction, sacrifice, or a difficult responsibility, yet it may protect them. They love comfort, fame, revenge, or easy profit, yet it may corrupt them. Allah sees consequences beyond the present moment, while human knowledge is partial. The verse is not asking believers to call every painful event good without reflection. It teaches humility before Allah’s knowledge. A person seeks the best course through revelation, consultation, expertise, and prayer, then accepts that the outcome may differ from his preference. What is good in one circumstance may be harmful in another; the judgement requires wisdom. When fighting is genuinely prescribed, believers must maintain moral limits. (2:190 — **“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you,”**) Because a difficult duty frames dislike does not decide what is good, dislike does not decide what is good returns attention to a difficult duty. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the disliked duty against the possibility of martyrdom and communal protection, while refusal could forfeit a good hidden from immediate preference.

**DISLIKE DOES NOT DECIDE WHAT IS GOOD**

***“Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something”*** deepens dislike does not decide what is good. They protect non-combatants, honour covenants, avoid torture and mutilation, and stop when aggression ends. The dislike of war can help preserve these limits by preventing the heart from becoming addicted to violence. Courage is needed, but hatred is not the measure of courage. A leader may have to make a painful decision to defend people, yet he remains responsible for alternatives, proportionality, and the welfare of civilians. A soldier may be brave while still grieving and hoping for peace. Islam does not require emotional celebration of bloodshed. The final statement—Allah knows, and you do not know—is a foundation of tawakkul. Human beings know what they can observe, but not every consequence of an action. A person may be prevented from a desired outcome because Allah knows it would harm his faith or family. Another may be required to endure a burden because it will protect many people or cultivate a virtue. This does not cancel reason or consultation. The Qur’an praises deliberation and commands believers to prepare strength, and the Prophet ﷺ consulted his Companions and used practical strategy. Reliance on Allah means acting with knowledge available to us while submitting the unseen result to Him. The verse should not be used by rulers or commanders to suppress criticism. A claim that Allah knows cannot make an unjust war righteous. The cause must still be examined through Qur’anic limits, evidence, lawful authority, and the rights of people. (4:71 — **“O believers! Take your precautions and go forth either in groups or together”**) Since the ethics of necessary fighting follows a difficult duty, dislike does not decide what is good links purpose to the ethics of necessary fighting.

**THE ETHICS OF NECESSARY FIGHTING**

***“which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know”*** clarifies the ethics of necessary fighting. Human beings may be wrong about what they call necessary. Likewise, an individual cannot use the verse to follow a charismatic leader into violence without proof. The command is addressed within a revealed legal framework, not as a blank cheque for anyone who claims divine backing. The verse applies beyond armed conflict. A person may dislike prayer at its time, honest financial accounting, apologizing, caring for a sick relative, or ending a harmful habit. He may love praise, debt-funded luxury, or an unhealthy relationship. Allah’s guidance may require what the ego dislikes and forbid what it wants. The believer asks for wisdom rather than assuming that every desire is a reliable guide. He distinguishes a lawful preference from a command and does not blame himself for natural dislike of hardship. Obedience is shown by what he chooses after recognizing the truth. The verse prepares the community for the difficult commands in the following passage about fighting in the sacred month. Believers may fear social consequences, death, or uncertainty, but they are reminded that Allah’s knowledge is complete. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is disciplined action under Allah’s command, without abandoning mercy and justice. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, while there is good in both, and he encouraged seeking what benefits, asking Allah for help, and not surrendering to helpless regret. (8:60 — **“Prepare against them what you ˹believers˺ can of ˹military˺ power and cavalry to deter Allah’s enemies and”**) No excuse for blind obedience matters, which means the ethics of necessary fighting returns no excuse for blind obedience to a difficult duty.

**NO EXCUSE FOR BLIND OBEDIENCE**

Strength in Islam includes moral and spiritual strength, not merely physical force. Think of a difficult duty through a patient who argues with his doctor about the operation he dreads and wins the argument. The pain is dulled for a season, the illness is not, and he returns to the same room with the same question and less time. A difficult duty reaches a reader today who refuses a hard duty because the people around him have decided that the times do not require it. A difficult duty gives that person a command written down before his feelings were consulted and a knowledge that is held by another, and it asks him on what basis he has made his own assessment. Because the dislike of the community is recorded in the verse and not condemned in it, a difficult duty shows that a heavy heart is permitted while the duty is performed. Because the sentence is stated as a possibility and not as a rule about war, the reader is shown its reach into every part of a life. The appointment he dreads and the comfort he prefers may hold the two ends of the same story, while the verse leaves the outcome unnamed. Dislike does not decide what is good makes a difficult duty practical; the ethics of necessary fighting therefore matters.

## Verse 2:217

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**THE QUESTION ABOUT A SACRED MONTH**

***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah,”*** establishes the question about a sacred month. The verse responds to a question about an incident in which fighting occurred during a sacred month. The sacred months carry a restriction on warfare, and the believers did not dismiss that sanctity. Allah says clearly that fighting in the month is a grave matter. The answer then places the incident within the larger history of persecution: preventing people from Allah’s way, rejecting Him, blocking access to the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its inhabitants were graver offences. The Qur’an is not making the sacred month meaningless. It is exposing selective outrage. The opponents focused on one violation while ignoring the persecution, expulsion, and religious obstruction they had practised. Justice requires considering the entire pattern of aggression rather than using one rule as a shield for a greater campaign of harm. The four sacred months are protected times, and Muslims must not initiate wrongdoing in them. If an enemy uses that protection to attack or to continue expelling people, the community may defend itself within the limits of 2:190 and 2:194. The response remains proportionate and directed toward ending aggression. The principle is relevant beyond the calendar. A treaty, sanctuary, humanitarian pause, hospital, or protected status cannot be abused as a platform for attacking others. If protection is violated, the answer is lawful defence and restoration of safety, not abandonment of every rule. The verse lists offences worse than the fighting being questioned: blocking guidance, disbelief, preventing access to the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people. These acts attack faith, liberty, home, and the right to worship. Fitnah here again refers to persecution and coercion that makes people suffer for their religion and drives them from their homes. The phrase does not mean that every non-Muslim person is guilty of these acts. (2:190 — **“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you,”**) Because the question about a sacred month frames sacred time and proportional justice, sacred time and proportional justice returns attention to the question about a sacred month.

**SACRED TIME AND PROPORTIONAL JUSTICE**

***“rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they”*** deepens sacred time and proportional justice. The context concerns a hostile group and its conduct. The Qur’an separately commands justice and kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims. A believer must identify the actual aggressor rather than generalize guilt to an entire religion, ethnicity, or population. They will continue fighting you until they turn you away from your religion, if they are able. This describes the active hostility of those who sought to force Muslims away from Islam. It does not command Muslims to assume that every neighbour secretly wants to convert them or to treat ordinary disagreement as war. The conditional if they are able portrays a determined persecuting force, not a universal psychological claim about all outsiders. The believer protects his faith through knowledge and worship, but he also honours the freedom of others. Coercion cannot create īmān, and the Qur’an prohibits forcing religion. Defence against coercion is not the same as imposing belief. The final section describes apostasy joined to dying in disbelief. His deeds have become worthless refers to the final state of a person who abandons faith and never returns before death. It does not mean that every sin erases all good deeds or that a person who struggles, doubts, or commits a grave act is automatically outside Islam. The Qur’an distinguishes final rejection from repentance and return. The verse’s warning is serious because faith is the foundation that gives deeds their direction. A person should protect it through knowledge, prayer, good companionship, and asking Allah for firmness. The Prophet ﷺ taught that hearts change and frequently made supplication for steadfastness. The phrase in this world and the Hereafter has been interpreted to include the loss of honour, protection, and the legal consequences associated with leaving the Muslim community in the historical setting, as well as the loss of reward in the Hereafter if death occurs upon disbelief. (2:194 — **“˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month,”**) Since the graver offences follows the question about a sacred month, sacred time and proportional justice links purpose to the graver offences.

**THE GRAVER OFFENCES**

***“will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever,”*** clarifies the graver offences. Application of worldly legal rulings requires due process, knowledge, legitimate authority, and distinction between public treason, private doubt, coercion, and sincere questioning. Ordinary Muslims must not investigate hearts or take punishment into their own hands. The verse warns the living and directs them toward faith, while Allah judges each person’s final state with perfect knowledge. Even in this severe warning, the door of repentance remains open while life remains. The next verse praises those who believe, emigrate, and strive. The Qur’an repeatedly invites the person who has turned away to return. A believer who fears for his faith should not despair; he should seek knowledge, renew the testimony, leave harmful influence, and ask Allah for mercy. Think of the question about a sacred month through a man whose neighbour has blocked the only road to his shop for a year, and who breaks a fence in a month when building is forbidden. The fence is the offence and the road is the harm, and the court that hears the case orders the road opened before it fines either man. The question about a sacred month reaches a reader today who weighs his own small fault against a large wrong done to him and finds his own case lighter in both scales. The verse gives him a rule in which the offence he committed is named and the offence against him is measured beside it. Because the answer begins with his own fault, the question about a sacred month shows that the passage was written for the community rather than for its enemies. The Book states the same rule about persecution in the verse of the return, so that the question about a sacred month reveals the sentence used twice in the same chapter as a standard rather than a phrase. (60:8 — **“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor”**) Persisting in the attempt to turn believers back matters, which means the graver offences returns persisting in the attempt to turn believers back to the question about a sacred month.

**PERSISTING IN THE ATTEMPT TO TURN BELIEVERS BACK**

***“their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.””*** closes with persisting in the attempt to turn believers back. A further passage counts the months of the year and names the four that are sacred, and the reader of the two together is shown that the calendar of the fight is held by God. The verse opens with a question that had become an accusation: They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. The occasion concerns a small party sent out under the command of one of the men of the community, and in the course of it a man of the enemy was killed. Because the quarrel turned on the date of the killing rather than on the killing itself, the reader is shown how a community can be trapped by a calendar. The community counted the day as the last of one of the permitted months, and the enemy counted it as a day of the sacred month of Rajab. The killing became the talk of the city. The closing condition states that the enemy would do it if the power were in their hands. Because the verse describes an intention rather than an event, the reader is shown why the community was told to prepare. The quarrel was not about a single caravan; it was about the survival of the faith of the travellers. (9:36 — **“Indeed, the number of months ordained by Allah is twelve—in Allah’s Record since the day He created”**) Sacred time and proportional justice makes the question about a sacred month practical; the graver offences therefore matters.

## Verse 2:218

> Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THREE QUALITIES OF HOPE**

***“Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled”*** establishes three qualities of hope. After warning about turning away from faith, the Qur’an describes those who may hope in Allah’s mercy: they believe, emigrate, and strive in His cause. The verse joins inner conviction to costly action. Hope is not a vague optimism; it is grounded in faith and expressed through sacrifice and effort. Īmān is trust in Allah and acceptance of His revelation. Hijrah is leaving a place, condition, or influence that prevents obedience when a lawful path of departure exists. Jihād means striving and exerting effort for Allah’s sake, including striving against one’s own desires, seeking knowledge, serving the vulnerable, and, under lawful authority and strict limits, defending a community from aggression. It cannot be reduced to violence or used to sanctify terrorism. The first Muslims emigrated from Makkah to Madīnah because persecution obstructed worship and threatened their lives. They left homes, property, family networks, and familiar status for Allah. The Qur’an honours the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār for this sacrifice and for the brotherhood that followed. Hijrah has a continuing spiritual meaning. A believer may need to leave a sinful environment, an abusive situation, dishonest employment, or a social circle that repeatedly destroys faith. Physical relocation is not always possible or required. The principle is to move toward obedience while taking wise steps and protecting dependants. A person should not abandon responsibilities impulsively or create harm while claiming hijrah. (2:190 — **“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you,”**) Because three qualities of hope frames emigration for faith, emigration for faith returns attention to three qualities of hope.

**EMIGRATION FOR FAITH**

***“in the Way of Allah—they can hope for”*** deepens emigration for faith. The Prophet ﷺ taught that deeds are judged by intentions, and the jurists consider ability, safety, contracts, family rights, and the nature of the danger. Allah’s mercy is sought through wise obedience, not dramatic gestures. Striving in Allah’s way requires sustained effort and exertion. The broadest daily struggle is to obey Allah, resist sin, speak truth, acquire beneficial knowledge, and serve people. A parent who patiently raises children, a student who pursues knowledge, a reformer who resists corruption, and a person who fights addiction can all be striving for Allah when the intention and means are sound. Armed fighting is a restricted category, not the definition of every use of the word. It requires a just cause, legitimate authority, ability, and observance of the prohibitions in 2:190–194. The Prophet ﷺ forbade killing non-combatants, treachery, and transgression. No individual or group may use this āyah to declare private war. The believers hope—yarjūna—for Allah’s mercy. Hope is not a guarantee based on self-satisfaction. The servants believe, sacrifice, and still recognize their need for forgiveness. They do not say, Our deeds have purchased Paradise. They ask Allah to accept the little they offer and to cover their mistakes. The Prophet ﷺ taught that no one enters Paradise solely through his deeds but through Allah’s mercy. This teaching protects the striving person from pride and the sinner from despair. Work is required, but acceptance remains a gift. (4:100 — **“Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the”**) Since striving in allah’s cause follows three qualities of hope, emigration for faith links purpose to striving in allah’s cause.

**STRIVING IN ALLAH’S CAUSE**

***“Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*** clarifies striving in allah’s cause. Emigration can involve loneliness, financial difficulty, discrimination, or the grief of leaving loved ones. Allah’s mercy includes companionship, provision, new opportunities, forgiveness, and reward beyond what was lost. The Qur’an promises that those who emigrate for Allah will find many places of refuge and abundance. Communities receiving migrants have a duty to welcome and support them. The Anṣār were praised for loving those who emigrated to them and preferring them over themselves. A community that celebrates hijrah but exploits migrants has missed the verse’s ethics. Think of three qualities of hope through a family that sells a house in the capital to open a clinic in a village where there was none. For two years nobody thanks them and the ledger shows a loss, and the first child who is carried through the door alive settles the question they had stopped asking. Three qualities of hope confronts anyone treating emigration for faith as remote; under three qualities of hope, such a person has given something up for the sake of his religion and has begun to ask whether it was worth the price. The verse gives him a sentence with the three works in it and a hope that is named by God. Because the promise is attached to works he can still perform, three qualities of hope shows that the road is open to the one who has not yet left anything. Because the three are named as one description of one people, three qualities of hope shows that the works of the religion belong together. (59:9 — **“As for those who had settled in the city and ˹embraced˺ the faith before ˹the arrival of˺”**) Hope rather than presumption matters, which means striving in allah’s cause returns hope rather than presumption to three qualities of hope.

**HOPE RATHER THAN PRESUMPTION**

The man who believes without leaving his ease, and the man who leaves without the struggle of the self, are both told what the caravan of this verse was made of. Because the hope is named rather than the certainty, the reader is shown the rank of the travellers. Since the three works are named as one description, emigration for faith makes three qualities of hope show that the promise is not earned by a single act. Since the hope is attached to three works rather than to a feeling, emigration for faith makes three qualities of hope show that the promise belongs to the road and not to the mood. They had left their homes for a land they did not know, and the Book promised them a mercy they would ask for each day rather than a wage that would be counted in their hands. Because the names are attached to the description of the travellers rather than to their question, the reader is shown what kind of people the promise is addressed to. The verse was revealed over a doubt of men who had left their homes, and it closes on the two names that answer a doubt. Emigration for faith makes three qualities of hope practical; striving in allah’s cause therefore matters. Today, migration, demanding work, and resistance to private sin require lawful means, sound intention, and hope rather than pride.

## Verse 2:219

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect

**ACKNOWLEDGING BENEFIT WITHOUT APPROVING HARM**

***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in”*** establishes acknowledging benefit without approving harm. The verse addresses khamr, intoxicants that cloud the mind, and maysir, gambling and games of chance in which wealth is gained through speculation and another person’s loss. It acknowledges that people may perceive benefits in them: pleasure, temporary escape, social excitement, commercial income, or a chance of profit. Acknowledging an apparent benefit does not make the practice lawful. Allah states that the sin and harm are greater. This was part of the Qur’an’s gradual education concerning intoxicants. The final prohibition in 5:90–91 makes the ruling explicit and commands believers to avoid them. The progression taught the community to understand the moral and social consequences before the final boundary was established. Intoxication clouds ʿaql, the faculty by which a person understands, restrains desire, and fulfils responsibility. It can lead to violence, neglect of prayer, family breakdown, accidents, health damage, debt, exploitation, and addiction. The temporary pleasure does not cancel these harms. A person who says that he can control an intoxicant should consider the wider effect on people around him and on those who become dependent. The prohibition extends to producing, selling, transporting, serving, and promoting intoxicants when these activities support their consumption. The Prophet ﷺ cursed multiple parties connected to wine in the hadith recorded by Sunan Abī Dāwūd and Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī. The principle is to close the commercial path to a known harm. (5:90 — **“O believers! Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork.”**) Because acknowledging benefit without approving harm frames the harm of intoxicants, the harm of intoxicants returns attention to acknowledging benefit without approving harm.

**THE HARM OF INTOXICANTS**

***“both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺”*** deepens the harm of intoxicants. Maysir transfers wealth through chance, rivalry, and the hope of gaining without productive work. It can include betting, lotteries, casinos, wagering on games, and modern forms of speculative play that exploit addiction. Even when a winner receives money, the system depends upon others losing and encourages a cycle of hope, debt, and resentment. The Qur’an later says that gambling creates enmity, hatred, and distraction from remembrance and prayer. Games can be harmless when no unlawful stake or deception is involved. The problem is making chance a mechanism for consuming wealth and cultivating greed. People often reason that if a forbidden thing has any benefit, it must be permissible. The verse teaches the opposite method: moral judgement considers the whole balance of benefit and harm, not the existence of a single advantage. Medicine may contain a substance with a harmful side effect and be governed by necessity and expert judgement, but recreational intoxication is not justified by the claim that it helps a person relax. The final ruling on khamr and maysir protects individuals and society from industries that profit from weakness. It also prevents the wealthy from shifting the harm onto families, workers, and communities while keeping the visible profit. The second question concerns charitable spending: What should we spend. The answer, al-ʿafw, has been explained as what is beyond one’s needs, what can be given with ease, or what remains after fulfilling legitimate obligations. (5:91 — **“Satan’s plan is to stir up hostility and hatred between you with intoxicants and gambling and to”**) Since the harm of gambling follows acknowledging benefit without approving harm, the harm of intoxicants links purpose to the harm of gambling.

**THE HARM OF GAMBLING**

***“ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This”*** clarifies the harm of gambling. This does not command a person to neglect dependants, debts, health, or necessary provision. It teaches generosity without irresponsibility. A person begins with obligatory support and rights, then gives from what Allah has enabled. The best charity may be regular and modest rather than dramatic and financially destructive. Regarding charity, the Prophet ﷺ taught that giving begins with those for whom a person is responsible and remains best when made despite felt need. The two questions are placed together because both concern how people treat resources and judgement. Intoxicants and gambling consume wealth without producing wholesome benefit, while charity directs wealth toward people and purposes that preserve life. One feeds addiction and rivalry; the other cultivates mercy and social stability. A believer examines not only what he spends but what his spending strengthens. Supporting a harmful industry, paying a bribe, or wasting food can contradict gratitude even when the amount is small. Allah asks for responsible stewardship. Allah makes the revelations clear so that people may reflect—yatafakkarūn. The Qur’an educates the heart through explanation, gradual legislation, consequences, and reminders. Reflection should lead to action: abandoning intoxicants, refusing gambling, seeking treatment for addiction, supporting affected families, and giving wealth with wisdom. A person who is already dependent should seek medical, psychological, spiritual, and community support. Repentance includes stopping the harm, repairing rights, and removing access where possible. (4:43 — **“O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say,”**) The benefit is not a licence matters, which means the harm of gambling returns the benefit is not a licence to acknowledging benefit without approving harm.

**THE BENEFIT IS NOT A LICENCE**

***“is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect”*** closes with the benefit is not a licence. Shaming an addict can deepen the problem; mercy includes firm help toward recovery. Think of acknowledging benefit without approving harm through a fisherman who counts the fish he catches with a net that also brings up the young of the year. He knows the price of the catch and the cost of the empty season to come, and the choice he makes in the boat decides whether there is a catch next year. Acknowledging benefit without approving harm reaches a reader today who can name the harm of a habit and keeps it because he can also name its pleasure. The verse gives him a scale with the harm written on the heavier side and leaves the weighing to him. Because the sentence closes on reflection, acknowledging benefit without approving harm teaches that a scale in the hand is worth more than a ruling he has not yet applied. Because the closing word is reflection rather than obedience, the reader is shown what kind of community the passage is building. The answer about wine had left a scale in their hands, and the Book expected them to weigh with it before the next ruling came. (7:31 — **“O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat and drink,”**) The harm of intoxicants makes acknowledging benefit without approving harm practical; the harm of gambling therefore matters.

## Verse 2:220

> upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE LARGER HORIZON OF SPENDING**

***“upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans. Say,”*** establishes the larger horizon of spending. The opening words connect this verse to the balanced supplication for goodness in present life and at the final return and to the question of charitable spending. Muslims are not asked to abandon the world; they are asked to order it toward the Hereafter. Wealth, family, work, and care for vulnerable people become part of worship when guided by Allah’s commands. The verse then focuses on orphans, whose vulnerability makes the ethics of wealth especially important. An orphan—yatīm—has lost a father or responsible protector while still young. Such a child may possess property inherited from parents, making him vulnerable to guardians who control the wealth before the child can defend himself. Improving their condition—iṣlāḥ lahum khayr—includes protecting the orphan’s property, educating and nurturing the child, providing food and shelter, treating him with affection, and preparing him for responsible adulthood. It is better than treating the child as a burden or isolating him from ordinary family life out of excessive fear of financial contact. The Qur’an elsewhere commands guardians to test orphans until they reach marriageable age and sound judgement, then hand over their property. This shows that care includes physical maturity and financial competence. A guardian should not retain control merely because the orphan has reached an age at which he can manage his own affairs. If you mix your affairs with theirs, then they are your brothers. Some guardians separated their food and property so strictly that ordinary care became difficult, fearing that any shared expense would be sinful. (4:6 — **“Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans until they reach a marriageable age.”**) Because the larger horizon of spending frames reform is the best response, reform is the best response returns attention to the larger horizon of spending.

**REFORM IS THE BEST RESPONSE**

***““Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with”*** deepens reform is the best response. Allah clarifies that separate accounting is not always required if mixing is genuinely for the orphan’s welfare. The orphan is a brother or sister in humanity and faith, not an object of suspicion or an opportunity for profit. Mixing is lawful only with integrity. A guardian may combine food, household expenses, or business arrangements when he can distinguish the orphan’s rights and prevent exploitation. Clear records, fair valuation, independent oversight, and transparent accounts protect both the child and the guardian. If mixing creates confusion or temptation, separation is safer. Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. Human beings may not know whether a guardian’s complicated arrangement is honest or fraudulent. Allah knows the intention, the details, the benefit to the child, and the hidden enrichment of the adult. This is a warning against disguising consumption as care, but also a comfort to the sincere guardian who acts responsibly despite suspicion. The statement does not make intention alone enough. A person who says he wants to help while repeatedly losing the orphan’s money through negligence is not a reformer merely because he feels affectionate. Good intention must be joined to sound administration and measurable protection. The Qur’an gives severe warnings against consuming orphan property unjustly. A guardian with sufficient means should not take compensation from the orphan’s wealth; a poor guardian may take what is reasonable for necessary service, according to the legal conditions. He must not borrow without record, mix assets to conceal losses, or delay returning property when the child becomes capable. (4:2 — **“Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺,”**) Since mixing affairs with integrity follows the larger horizon of spending, reform is the best response links purpose to mixing affairs with integrity.

**MIXING AFFAIRS WITH INTEGRITY**

***“you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had”*** clarifies mixing affairs with integrity. Modern guardianship may involve bank accounts, investments, school fees, medical costs, and legal documents. The principles remain: preserve the principal, seek safe and lawful growth, document every transaction, and place the child’s welfare above the guardian’s convenience. The word brothers—ikhwānukum—gives an ethic of dignity. Orphans need more than property management. They need stable affection, education, protection from abuse, and a sense of belonging. The Prophet ﷺ warned that the person who does not show mercy to children lacks the mercy he needs, and he praised care for an orphan, as Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī records. Care should not erase the child’s history or force gratitude. The orphan has rights to identity, safety, and truthful information appropriate to his age. Guardians and institutions must listen to children and create safe ways to report mistreatment. Had Allah willed, He could have made things difficult for you. The verse shows that Islamic law is not designed to make honest guardians impossible. Allah knows that families share meals, homes, labour, and resources. He permits reasonable mixing when the purpose is reform, while maintaining the prohibition of exploitation. Ease is not negligence. The concession is a mercy for people sincerely trying to care for orphans, not a loophole for those who use the child’s wealth. The guardian combines ease with taqwā, documentation, and accountability. Orphan care is not left to private goodwill alone. The community should support guardians, supervise charitable institutions, protect children from trafficking and abuse, and establish transparent systems for inheritance and foster care. (4:10 — **“Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies.”**) Intention and outcome under divine knowledge matters, which means mixing affairs with integrity returns intention and outcome under divine knowledge to the larger horizon of spending.

**INTENTION AND OUTCOME UNDER DIVINE KNOWLEDGE**

***“Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.””*** closes with intention and outcome under divine knowledge. Zakah and voluntary charity can fund education, health, housing, and legal protection. A society that praises orphan sponsorship but allows corruption in orphanages has not fulfilled iṣlāḥ. Reform is measured by the child’s safety and flourishing, not by the institution’s public image. The case is like two men who buy a boat together and keep a ledger of every litre of fuel. The ledger says one owes the other a small sum, and the catch they would not have made alone settles the debt in a single morning on the water. The larger horizon of spending reaches a reader today who shares his table with a child of another father and finds himself counting the mouthfuls. The verse gives him a partner in the household and a ruling that weighs the intention rather than the plate. Because the orphans are named as partners in the faith, the larger horizon of spending shows that the account is kept in a register that is unrelated to the estate’s size. (2:215 — **“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say,”**) Reform is the best response makes the larger horizon of spending practical; mixing affairs with integrity therefore matters.

## Verse 2:221

> Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful

**FAITH AS THE FOUNDATION OF MARRIAGE**

***“Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may”*** establishes faith as the foundation of marriage. This verse addresses marriage to those who worship other than Allah. It places īmān before attraction, social status, wealth, and lineage. Marriage is not only companionship; it is a covenant that shapes worship, family identity, children, household decisions, and moral priorities. If the spouses disagree about the Lord to whom they owe ultimate obedience, the conflict can reach the foundation of the home. The prohibition concerns polytheists—mushrikūn—and should not be carelessly applied to every non-Muslim category without studying the Qur’an’s distinctions. Sūrah al-Māʾidah gives chaste women within the People of the Book a specific ruling, while this āyah addresses those who associate partners with Allah. Juristic conditions and contemporary circumstances require qualified guidance. The verse says that a believing bondwoman is better than a polytheistic free woman, and a believing bondman better than a polytheist. In the social world in which slavery existed, this was a radical reordering of value. Social freedom, beauty, wealth, and lineage do not make a person spiritually superior to a believer who has been oppressed and possesses none of those advantages. The verse does not praise slavery or encourage Muslims to enslave people. The Qur’an repeatedly opens the path to emancipation, commands freeing slaves as expiation, and praises the freeing of a neck. The comparison exposes the error of judging marriage by social prestige while ignoring faith. A person’s human dignity remains real, and Islam’s ethical trajectory is toward liberation and justice. Even if she impresses you and even if he impresses you acknowledge that attraction is powerful. Islam does not deny beauty, personality, or compatibility. (5:5 — **“Today all good, pure foods have been made lawful for you. Similarly,”**) Because faith as the foundation of marriage frames dignity is not measured by status, dignity is not measured by status returns attention to faith as the foundation of marriage.

**DIGNITY IS NOT MEASURED BY STATUS**

***“look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better”*** deepens dignity is not measured by status. It asks whether attraction will lead a person to compromise the foundation of his faith. A charming partner may be good in worldly manners yet invite the believer toward practices and values that conflict with tawḥīd. Marriage should therefore be evaluated through faith, character, responsibility, safety, and compatibility, not only appearance or social excitement. The Prophet ﷺ advised considering religion and character when choosing a spouse. This does not justify judging people harshly or treating a convert as morally superior in every matter; it identifies the foundation that must guide the covenant. A spouse who worships other than Allah can, without malicious intention, invite the family toward a worldview that leads away from the Hereafter. Children may be confused about worship, festivals, prayer, diet, identity, and moral authority. The phrase is about the direction of a life, not an instruction to insult or dehumanize a person of another faith. The believer continues to treat non-Muslim relatives and neighbours with justice and kindness. The marital prohibition protects the religious covenant; it does not erase the rights of people. Qur’an 60:8 commands kindness and justice toward those who do not fight Muslims because of religion. Allah’s invitation to Paradise and forgiveness is an invitation through revelation, repentance, worship, and righteous action. Marriage should help the spouses answer that invitation, not make obedience increasingly difficult. A believing spouse can remind, support, and comfort, though no spouse controls another’s final faith. The phrase by His permission teaches humility. Guidance is a gift from Allah, not a possession produced by personal superiority. A Muslim asks Allah to guide himself, his spouse, children, and all people, while respecting the limits Allah has set. (90:13 — **“It is to free a slave”**) Since attraction and long-term direction follows faith as the foundation of marriage, dignity is not measured by status links purpose to attraction and long-term direction.

**ATTRACTION AND LONG-TERM DIRECTION**

***“than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites”*** clarifies attraction and long-term direction. The verse prohibits the Muslim from entering a particular marriage; it does not license forced marriage. Consent is required, and the Prophet ﷺ rejected marriages imposed upon women. Families may advise, but they may not imprison, threaten, or marry someone without genuine agreement. Faith cannot be produced by coercion, and a marriage entered through coercion is a violation of Islamic ethics. The ruling also does not make the believer a judge of every interfaith friendship. Social kindness, neighbourly cooperation, and respectful conversation are distinct from a marriage covenant that creates intimate and generational obligations. Think of faith as the foundation of marriage through a family that buys a plot because the road to it looks wide and new, and never asks where the road leads when it leaves the town. The house is built, the traffic arrives, and the family spends its evenings listening to the lorries of a route they never chose. Faith as the foundation of marriage confronts anyone treating dignity is not measured by status as remote; under faith as the foundation of marriage, such a person has been told to consider a proposal by a family and is being asked to weigh the income, the house and the looks. The verse gives him a ledger with one line at the top and asks him what the house will be like when the income has changed. Because the invitation of each side is stated plainly, dignity is not measured by status makes faith as the foundation of marriage show that the decision of a marriage is a decision about a road. Because the attraction is named rather than denied, faith as the foundation of marriage shows that the Book speaks to the person who is looking and answers him in his own language. Since the measure set is the faith of a person, the reader is taught where the scale of a household is held. (4:92 — **“It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake.”**) They invite to the fire matters, which means attraction and long-term direction returns they invite to the fire to faith as the foundation of marriage.

**THEY INVITE TO THE FIRE**

***“˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful”*** closes with they invite to the fire. The measure it leaves him is the faith of the person beside him and nothing else in the ledger. Elsewhere, the permission concerning chaste women of the people of the Book shows that the wall of this verse is drawn around the association of partners rather than around every stranger. A further passage keeps the promise to the one who keeps the command for the sake of God, and the reader is shown what the restraint of this verse is worth. The verse lays down a wall around the household: Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe The same rule is stated later for the other side of the marriage, and the reports place the revelation in the houses of the community rather than among its enemies. The verse supports the rule with a scale: for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. Faith is weighed here against rank and beauty, and the same scale is used in the next sentence for the other side of the house: And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. (5:89 — **“Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths,”**) Dignity is not measured by status makes faith as the foundation of marriage practical; attraction and long-term direction therefore matters.
