## Verse 2:232

> When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**PROTECTING A WOMAN’S CHOICE AFTER DIVORCE**

***“When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting”*** establishes protecting a woman’s choice after divorce. This verse addresses families and guardians who might obstruct a divorced woman from remarrying her former husband after the waiting period, even when both parties agree to return in a lawful and honourable manner. The prohibition of obstruction protects her agency. Divorce does not make her permanently controlled by relatives, nor does anger give a guardian the right to decide her future for selfish reasons. The verse does not command a woman to return to her former husband. It protects the possibility when she and the man freely agree and when the marriage can be safe and sound. If she does not want to return, no family member may force her. Consent and the ability to assess harm remain central to marriage. The Companions reported an incident involving Maʿqil ibn Yasār, whose sister had been divorced and later wished to return to her former husband. Maʿqil resisted out of anger, and this verse was revealed; he then accepted Allah’s instruction. The report, recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, shows that even a protective brother could allow personal hurt to become an unjust barrier. The lesson is not that every former marriage should be restored. It is that guardians must distinguish genuine concern from revenge, status anxiety, tribal pride, or the desire to punish the former husband. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”**) Because protecting a woman’s choice after divorce frames the occasion of revelation, the occasion of revelation returns attention to protecting a woman’s choice after divorce.

**THE OCCASION OF REVELATION**

***“period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands if they come to an honourable”*** deepens the occasion of revelation. They should advise honestly and then respect a lawful decision made by the adults concerned. The phrase tarāḍaw baynahum bi-l-maʿrūf requires mutual agreement and a lawful, recognized process. Both former spouses must consent without coercion. They should discuss the causes of the earlier divorce, expectations about finances and relatives, safety, and the welfare of children. Returning without addressing the prior harm can repeat the same cycle. According to what is acceptable excludes secret arrangements that violate legal rights, deception, or the use of marriage to regain control. It includes a valid contract, proper witnesses and guardianship according to the applicable legal school, and protection of the woman’s financial and personal rights. A walī has a protective and supportive role, not a licence for arbitrary obstruction. If a guardian prevents a suitable marriage out of spite, the matter can be taken to a qualified authority, who may transfer the guardianship according to the rules of Islamic law. The Prophet ﷺ said that when someone whose religion and character are acceptable seeks marriage, people should help it rather than create corruption and fitnah, as Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī records. At the same time, guardians may raise genuine concerns about abuse, addiction, dishonesty, or inability to maintain obligations. (2:224 — **“Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good,”**) Since agreement in a honourable manner follows protecting a woman’s choice after divorce, the occasion of revelation links purpose to agreement in a honourable manner.

**AGREEMENT IN A HONOURABLE MANNER**

***“agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This”*** clarifies agreement in a honourable manner. Advice must be based on evidence, not rumour or class prejudice. The goal is the woman’s welfare, not family control. Allah calls non-obstruction purer and more virtuous. Removing resentment, allowing forgiveness, and respecting lawful choice purifies the community from prolonged feud. Sometimes a former couple can rebuild the marriage with maturity; sometimes the discussion itself closes old hostility. In both cases, justice is better than family revenge. The language does not romanticize reconciliation. A return is good only if the couple can keep Allah’s limits. Where there was serious abuse, stalking, or danger, preventing renewed contact may be protection rather than obstruction. Expert counselling and legal safeguards can help distinguish the cases. The admonition is directed to those who believe in Allah and the Last Day. Faith should change how family members exercise power. A person who remembers the Hereafter does not treat a daughter, sister, or divorced woman as an instrument for honour. He knows that he will answer for every barrier he placed before a lawful choice. The verse also warns the woman and former husband not to use the permission as a way to deceive relatives or evade responsibilities. All parties remain under Allah’s knowledge. Think of protecting a woman’s choice after divorce through a household that locks the gate of the courtyard at sunset to keep the family safe, and then finds that the children have learned to climb the wall. (4:35 — **“If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers.”**) The role of guardians matters, which means agreement in a honourable manner returns the role of guardians to protecting a woman’s choice after divorce.

**THE ROLE OF GUARDIANS**

***“is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know”*** closes with the role of guardians. The gate is as strong as it ever was, and the wall is the place where the family now meets. Protecting a woman’s choice after divorce reaches a reader today who refuses a marriage for his sister because the man is poor and the family has a name to keep. Protecting a woman’s choice after divorce gives that person a command, a condition and a sentence about knowledge, and it asks him whose name was being kept in the first place. Because the close speaks of the knowledge of God, the occasion of revelation makes protecting a woman’s choice after divorce show that the man who blocks what he cannot see is working against the only eye that can. The roads of the release are set out in the sentence before this one. And the rights of the woman are guarded in the chapter of the women. (24:32 — **“Marry off the ˹free˺ singles among you, as well as the righteous of your bondmen and bondwomen.”**) The occasion of revelation makes protecting a woman’s choice after divorce practical; agreement in a honourable manner therefore matters.

## Verse 2:233

> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**NURSING AS A SHARED RESPONSIBILITY**

***“˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing”*** establishes nursing as a shared responsibility. This āyah gives detailed guidance about breastfeeding, parental maintenance, and the welfare of a young child. It recognizes breastfeeding for two complete years as the period for whoever wishes to complete nursing. The wording allows parents to make informed decisions according to the child’s health, the mother’s condition, and professional advice. It does not make every family identical or turn a compassionate recommendation into a reason for shame. The child’s welfare is central. Breastfeeding can provide nourishment and closeness, but the mother’s health, consent, ability, and circumstances also matter. A woman must not be insulted if she cannot breastfeed, and a child must not be deprived of proper nourishment because adults are fighting. Qualified medical guidance helps apply the general command safely. The father is responsible for the mother’s provision and clothing according to what is reasonable—rizquhunna wa kiswatuhunna bi-l-maʿrūf. In context, this concerns the nursing mother and child, including the expenses required for care. The father’s responsibility does not end because the parents are divorced. He must provide food, clothing, housing, medical needs, and other reasonable necessities according to his means and the child’s needs. Maʿrūf means fairness recognized by sound custom and revelation. A wealthy father cannot provide the minimum while spending extravagantly on himself, and a struggling father is not required to give what he genuinely cannot afford. He should be transparent about income, avoid hiding assets, and seek fair legal arrangements when parents separate. No mother should be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child is a comprehensive rule. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”**) Because nursing as a shared responsibility frames the father’s financial responsibility, the father’s financial responsibility returns attention to nursing as a shared responsibility. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the father’s duty as maintenance without excess or stinginess and according to the wealth Allah has given him.

**THE FATHER’S FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY**

***“for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The”*** deepens the father’s financial responsibility. A husband must not prevent a mother from nursing in order to punish her, and a mother must not use the child to extort, threaten, or cut off the father’s lawful relationship. Neither parent may manipulate custody, visitation, maintenance, or breastfeeding as a weapon. The child must not be made a messenger in adult disputes. Parents should not interrogate the child about the other parent, make promises they cannot keep, or expose him to violence and humiliation. Where there is abuse, the priority is safety and lawful protection; shared parenting cannot be used to return a child to danger. If the father dies, the heir has a similar responsibility. The child’s maintenance does not disappear with the father. The surviving family or lawful estate bears responsibility according to the rules of inheritance and support. Early legal readings relate this either to the heir’s maintenance duty, to protection of the mother from harm, or to both. In every reading, a vulnerable child must not be abandoned because the original provider has died. The estate must first settle debts and valid obligations, then distribute inheritance according to Allah’s law. Relatives who receive wealth should remember that inheritance creates responsibilities as well as benefits. Modern guardianship and state support can assist, but relatives must not assume that an orphan is someone else’s problem. If both parents decide to wean before two years, there is no blame when they do so by mutual consent and consultation—tarāḍin minhumā wa tashāwur. The two conditions protect the child and prevent one parent from making a unilateral decision out of anger. (65:6 — **“Let them live where you live ˹during their waiting period˺, according to your means.”**) Since no parent is harmed through the child follows nursing as a shared responsibility, the father’s financial responsibility links purpose to no parent is harmed through the child.

**NO PARENT IS HARMED THROUGH THE CHILD**

***“˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to”*** clarifies no parent is harmed through the child. They discuss health, nourishment, emotional readiness, and practical circumstances. Consultation is a Qur’anic family principle. Parents can seek a paediatrician, lactation specialist, counsellor, or trusted scholar. The decision should not be dictated by relatives who ignore the mother’s health or the child’s needs. Consent must be real and free from threat. The verse permits arranging for another woman to nurse the child, provided the payment is made fairly and according to agreement. The wet nurse’s labour is valuable and must not be taken for granted. The agreement should clarify payment, duration, care, and any relevant health information. Breastfeeding also creates a relationship of riḍāʿah in Islamic law, with consequences for marriage eligibility and family ties. Parents must record the identity of the nursing woman and the child’s nursing relationship so that future generations do not unknowingly enter a prohibited marriage. The legal details of the amount and conditions of nursing require qualified guidance. The āyah repeatedly invokes fairness, capacity, mutual consent, and consultation. This protects the family from rigid formulas that ignore real life. A mother may need paid work, medical treatment, rest, or support. A father may face unemployment or illness. The answer is cooperation and honest assessment, not accusation. For household duties, the Prophet ﷺ counted family maintenance among the best spending and warned against neglecting dependants, as Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records. Supporting a child is worship when done for Allah and with kindness, not merely a financial burden imposed by court. The verse closes with taqwā and the reminder that Allah sees. (4:6 — **“Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans until they reach a marriageable age.”**) The heir’s responsibility matters, which means no parent is harmed through the child returns the heir’s responsibility to nursing as a shared responsibility.

**THE HEIR’S RESPONSIBILITY**

***“have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”*** closes with the heir’s responsibility. Parents may deceive courts, hide income, or manipulate a child while appearing respectable to relatives. Allah sees the private arrangement, the missed payment, the exhausted mother, and the frightened child. Taqwā makes parents choose justice even when no one can enforce it. The case is like two people carrying a heavy table down a narrow staircase and arguing about who is holding it wrong. The table is the same table, the staircase is the same staircase, and the dent in the wall belongs to both of them. Nursing as a shared responsibility reaches a reader today who uses his child as a message to his former wife, and who counts the missed visits as points won in an argument. The verse gives him a nursing mother with her food and her dress, a father with his capacity, and a command that neither be made to suffer, and nursing as a shared responsibility uses the father’s financial responsibility to ask which choice he has been reading. Because the closing name is the All-Seeing, the father’s financial responsibility makes nursing as a shared responsibility show that the small cruelties of a broken house are the ones most carefully written. The burden that no soul carries beyond its strength is stated in the closing of the chapter. And the duty of children towards their parents is set out in another chapter. (4:11 — **“Allah commands you regarding your children:”**) The father’s financial responsibility makes nursing as a shared responsibility practical; no parent is harmed through the child therefore matters.

## Verse 2:234

> As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**THE WIDOW’S WAITING PERIOD**

***“As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe”*** establishes the widow’s waiting period. This verse establishes the ʿiddah of a widow as four months and ten days. It is a period of mourning, legal clarity, and transition after the death of a husband. It differs from the waiting period of a divorced woman and from the waiting period of a pregnant woman, whose term ends at childbirth according to 65:4. The period is not a punishment or a statement that a widow loses her independence. It gives time for grief, protects lineage, allows immediate legal matters to be organized, and acknowledges the seriousness of a marriage covenant. The widow remains a person with rights, property, work, education, and lawful social contact. The women wait on their own behalf and observe the prescribed period. It does not mean that relatives may imprison them or make every decision for them. A widow may seek help, leave the home for genuine needs, receive visitors, and manage her affairs within the rules of modesty and safety. The Sunnah clarifies that a widow may go out for necessary work or matters and return to her home, as reported in the account of a woman whose husband died. The pre-Islamic practice of isolating a widow for a full year and subjecting her to degrading treatment was replaced with a defined, dignified period. (65:4 — **“As for your women past the age of menstruation, in case you do not know,”**) Because the widow’s waiting period frames by themselves, by themselves returns attention to the widow’s waiting period.

**BY THEMSELVES**

***“a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the”*** deepens by themselves. The waiting period includes iḥdād, mourning restrictions concerning adornment and perfume for the prescribed time. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a woman should not mourn a person beyond three days, except for a husband, for whom the period is four months and ten days, in the collections of Muslim and al-Bukhārī. This is a defined act of mourning, not a command to erase grief on the forty-first day. A widow may continue prayer, remembrance, learning, conversation, and necessary work. She should be treated with compassion rather than suspicion. Families should provide food, childcare, financial support, and emotional presence, while respecting her decisions. When they have completed their waiting period, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in a reasonable manner. After the period, a widow is free to remarry, work, travel, manage property, and make lawful decisions. The phrase fī anfusihinna bi-l-maʿrūf emphasizes her agency and the requirement that her choices remain within what is lawful and socially dignified. Relatives may advise but may not force her into a marriage, prevent a suitable proposal for inheritance reasons, or seize her property. The Qur’an forbids inheriting women against their will and commands kind treatment. (2:226 — **“Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months.”**) Since mourning with dignity follows the widow’s waiting period, by themselves links purpose to mourning with dignity.

**MOURNING WITH DIGNITY**

***“end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide”*** clarifies mourning with dignity. A widow’s grief does not make her a possession of the husband’s family. If the widow is pregnant, her waiting period is until she gives birth, as established by Qur’an 65:4 and the report of Subayʿah al-Aslamiyyah in the paired collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim. The four months and ten days apply to the non-pregnant widow. Cases of miscarriage, uncertain pregnancy, irregular bleeding, or simultaneous divorce and death require qualified legal advice. The husband’s estate must also address her inheritance, deferred dowry, debts, housing, and maintenance according to the law. The waiting period does not cancel her financial rights. Allah knows how the widow is treated by relatives, the contents of proposals, hidden pressure, and the true condition of the mourning heart. Human beings may see a family observing outward custom while privately forcing or abusing a widow. The closing reminder protects her from invisible injustice and warns guardians against exploiting grief. It also comforts the widow who feels unseen. Allah knows the loss, the patience, the private tears, and the choices made under pressure. No act of dignified endurance is lost. Think of the widow’s waiting period through a family that plants a tree in the yard when a father dies and then argues about who may cut it. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”**) After the waiting period matters, which means mourning with dignity returns after the waiting period to the widow’s waiting period.

**AFTER THE WAITING PERIOD**

***“for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do”*** closes with after the waiting period. The tree grows while they argue, and the shade it gives in the summer is shared by all the voices in the courtyard. The widow’s waiting period reaches a reader today who speaks about the widow of a neighbour with the ease of a man discussing a business. The verse gives him a term, a rule about what she may decide and a name that watches the street, and it asks him how he would speak if the room were his own. Because All-Aware closes the verse, by themselves makes the widow’s waiting period show that the dignity of a widow is a duty that has no receipt to show. The waiting of the divorced woman is set out earlier in the chapter. And the provision of a year is stated in the verse that follows, so the reader sees the two kinds of waiting side by side. (4:7 — **“For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave,”**) By themselves makes the widow’s waiting period practical; mourning with dignity therefore matters.

## Verse 2:235

> There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing

**PROPOSALS DURING A WAITING PERIOD**

***“There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in”*** establishes proposals during a waiting period. This verse addresses approaching a widow or divorced woman during her waiting period. It permits an indirect hint—taʿrīḍ—or keeping the intention private, especially because a direct proposal or contract may violate her right to complete the ʿiddah. A respectful hint might be a general statement about wishing for marriage or praising a person’s character without demanding a commitment. The permission recognizes human emotion. A person may think about marriage with a widow, and the widow may consider her future, without being blamed for the mere intention. Allah does not punish involuntary thoughts. He regulates what people say and do so that a vulnerable woman is not pressured or publicly claimed before her waiting period ends. Do not make a secret promise with them, except that you speak in an honourable manner. This allows appropriate, dignified speech while prohibiting a hidden engagement that treats the waiting period as though it has already ended. A secret promise can create jealousy, pressure, false hope, and conflict with the deceased husband’s family or a former spouse. Honourable speech—qawl maʿrūf—is clear enough to avoid deception and restrained enough to avoid emotional manipulation. A person should not exploit grief by promising wealth, protection, or rescue. (2:234 — **“As for those of you who die and leave widows behind,”**) Because proposals during a waiting period frames honourable speech, honourable speech returns attention to proposals during a waiting period. The explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās permits an indirect expression of interest during the waiting period while excluding a secret binding promise before the lawful time.

**HONOURABLE SPEECH**

***“your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can”*** deepens honourable speech. He should not ask for secrecy that isolates the woman from trusted family or legal support. A marriage contract may not be concluded until the ʿiddah is complete. The waiting period belongs to the woman and protects her legal status. A contract made before it ends is invalid or unlawful according to the details of the case and legal school. If a person is unsure whether a period has ended, he should wait and seek qualified advice. This rule also prevents confusion about lineage and preserves the seriousness of marriage. A new marriage should begin after the previous relationship’s legal consequences have been completed, not in the middle of grief, pregnancy uncertainty, or revocable divorce. The verse does not make the woman passive. She may consider a proposal, refuse it, seek advice, and plan her future. The restriction is on the manner and timing of approach, not on her ability to think. Relatives must not use the waiting period to claim her inheritance, promise her to a cousin, or prevent a lawful future marriage. The same principle applies to a divorced woman whose waiting period remains. If the divorce is revocable, the former husband’s rights and the possibility of return must be respected, while other men must not compete through secret promises. (65:1 — **“O Prophet! ˹Instruct the believers:˺ When you ˹intend to˺ divorce women,”**) Since no marriage contract before the period ends follows proposals during a waiting period, honourable speech links purpose to no marriage contract before the period ends.

**NO MARRIAGE CONTRACT BEFORE THE PERIOD ENDS**

***“only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that”*** clarifies no marriage contract before the period ends. If the divorce is final, indirect discussion may still be governed by the rules of the specific waiting period. Allah knows what people conceal within themselves. This is a comfort because sincere intentions are visible to Him, and a warning because hidden manipulation is also visible. A person may speak in carefully chosen words while planning to exploit a woman’s grief or property. Allah knows the difference between compassion and predation. The verse does not treat every private thought as a sin. The warning concerns the transition from thought to secret promises, pressure, and premature contract. Faith teaches people to manage desire with honesty rather than pretending that human emotions do not exist. Allah is Ghafūr and Ḥalīm. He forgives mistakes and is forbearing with servants who are learning how to navigate grief, divorce, and desire. A person who crossed a boundary should stop, clarify matters, and seek forgiveness. Forbearance gives time to correct before harm becomes permanent. Mercy is shown through clear rules. A woman is protected from being claimed while vulnerable, a man is protected from an unlawful contract, and families are protected from disputes about timing and lineage. Imagine a patient suitor as a man waiting outside a shop while it is being rebuilt and tells the craftsmen what he intends to buy the day it opens. (2:227 — **“But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing”**) Respect for the widow’s agency matters, which means no marriage contract before the period ends returns respect for the widow’s agency to proposals during a waiting period.

**RESPECT FOR THE WIDOW’S AGENCY**

***“Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing”*** closes with respect for the widow’s agency. The shop opens on its own day, the man is at the door with his money, and the only thing the waiting cost him was the price he did not pay for a broken window. Proposals during a waiting period reaches a reader today who sends a friend to sound out a widow's family while the months still run, and who thinks that a message carried by another mouth is no message. The verse gives him a hint, an appointment and a term, and proposals during a waiting period uses honourable speech to ask which choice he is spending. Because the close names the Forgiving and the Forbearing, honourable speech makes proposals during a waiting period show that the waiting he thinks is waste is the season in which his own intention is grown. The waiting of the widow is fixed in the preceding verse. And the terms of the settlement are guarded earlier in the chapter. (2:232 — **“When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period,”**) Honourable speech makes proposals during a waiting period practical; no marriage contract before the period ends therefore matters.

## Verse 2:236

> There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers

**A MARRIAGE MAY END BEFORE CONSUMMATION**

***“There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage”*** establishes a marriage may end before consummation. This verse addresses a marriage that ends before sexual consummation and before a specific mahr, or bridal gift, has been fixed. It acknowledges that a marriage contract can fail early and removes the assumption that divorce itself is always a sin. At the same time, it commands the husband to provide a suitable gift—mutʿah—so that the woman is not left humiliated or unsupported after the relationship ends. The verse’s compassion matters because an early divorce can still cause emotional pain, social embarrassment, and financial loss. A woman should not be treated as though nothing happened merely because the marriage was not consummated. The husband owes honourable conduct even when a specific dowry is not legally due in the same way as after consummation. Mutʿah here means a compensatory provision appropriate to the husband’s means and the recognized standard of fairness. It can include money, clothing, household items, or another useful gift. The amount should not be insulting or so extravagant that it creates a new injustice. The wealthy give according to their abundance, while the poor give according to what they can genuinely afford. The verse rejects a single fixed amount that ignores circumstances. Wealth, local custom, the length of the engagement or marriage, the woman’s needs, and the reason for separation may all be relevant. The gift is not a purchase of the woman’s silence or a payment that permits cruelty. (2:237 — **“And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry,”**) Because a marriage may end before consummation frames the mutʿah gift, the mutʿah gift returns attention to a marriage may end before consummation. Ibn ʿAbbās treats the parting gift as a real provision scaled to means when neither consummation nor a fixed dowry preceded divorce.

**THE MUTʿAH GIFT**

***“is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a”*** deepens the mutʿah gift. It is an expression of responsibility and good treatment. There is no blame upon you removes blame for the divorce under the specified conditions, not for lying, insult, coercion, or broken promises. The couple must still preserve privacy, return property, and avoid spreading accusations. A person cannot say that no dowry was fixed and therefore nothing at all is owed in kindness. Likewise, the wife should not be treated as morally defective because the marriage ended early. Families and communities must resist gossip and protect her dignity. A broken marriage is not proof that one person carries every fault. The Qur’an uses before you have touched them—mā lam tamassūhunna—as a modest expression for consummation. If a marriage ends before consummation and no dowry was fixed, the mutʿah is required or strongly emphasized according to the legal details, while the moral command of kindness is clear. If a specified dowry was fixed, 2:237 gives the rule of half the dowry, subject to waiver and the circumstances described there. The waiting period also differs. A woman divorced before consummation does not observe the ordinary waiting period, as stated in 33:49, though legal advice is needed when pregnancy or other complications are possible. The difference between the wealthy and poor gives a general principle of family law: obligations are measured by ability and fairness. (33:49 — **“O believers! If you marry believing women and then divorce them before you touch them,”**) Since no blame does not mean no ethics follows a marriage may end before consummation, the mutʿah gift links purpose to no blame does not mean no ethics.

**NO BLAME DOES NOT MEAN NO ETHICS**

***“˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according”*** clarifies no blame does not mean no ethics. Islam does not demand that a poor man give what would destroy his ability to eat or support dependants, but it does not permit the wealthy to hide behind a token gift while spending freely elsewhere. The command also encourages documentation. A couple should clarify the dowry and financial terms at the beginning of marriage, while understanding that unclear or missing documentation does not erase Allah’s rights. Transparent agreements prevent disputes and protect both parties. The final phrase calls the provision a duty upon the muḥsinīn, those who do good. Even where the minimum legal obligation is debated, iḥsān calls for generosity, apology, and a dignified conclusion. A husband may provide more than the minimum because he wants to close the relationship without bitterness. The Prophet ﷺ taught that no believer should despise a believing woman because of one disliked quality, and he encouraged kindness in family relationships. When divorce is necessary, the departing spouses should remember the good that existed and avoid rewriting the entire marriage as evil. The verse teaches that ending a contract does not erase the moral relationship formed through it. Employers owe wages after employment ends, business partners settle accounts, and spouses retain obligations after divorce. Lawfulness is the floor; iḥsān is the higher standard that turns a painful conclusion into a just one. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺. It is not lawful”**) Divorce before touching matters, which means no blame does not mean no ethics returns divorce before touching to a marriage may end before consummation.

**DIVORCE BEFORE TOUCHING**

***“to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers”*** closes with divorce before touching. A community can help by providing mediation, legal advice, financial support, and protection from stigma. The woman’s future should not be destroyed by an early divorce. The case is like two families who prepare a wedding and then call it off a week before, and one of them returns every plate it borrowed. The plates go back clean, the guests go home, and the two families still nod to each other across the market for the next twenty years. A marriage may end before consummation reaches a reader today who tells himself that a marriage which never happened leaves nothing behind it and nobody owed. The verse gives him a compensation, a measure and a duty, and a marriage may end before consummation asks what he wants to be known as in a street that watched the engagement. Because the closing sentence names the good-doers, the mutʿah gift makes a marriage may end before consummation show that the manner of a parting is the part of the story that is remembered. The half of the dowry in the case of a named sum is set out in the next verse. And the duty of kindness between those who part is guarded in the same stretch. (4:20 — **“If you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given the former ˹even˺ a”**) The mutʿah gift makes a marriage may end before consummation practical; no blame does not mean no ethics therefore matters.

## Verse 2:237

> And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE HALF-DOWRY RULE**

***“And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on”*** establishes the half-dowry rule. This verse gives the financial rule when a marriage ends before consummation but after a specific mahr has been agreed. The woman is entitled to half of the specified dowry. The rule recognizes the contract and the emotional reality of the marriage while also accounting for the fact that consummation did not occur. The dowry is the woman’s right, not a purchase price and not a gift that the husband can reclaim at will. Once specified, it belongs to her according to the contract. If the husband has already paid the full amount, the legal details concerning return of half are handled through fairness and consent; he may choose to leave the whole amount with her. If it was deferred, the due portion must be settled. The woman may waive her right voluntarily, and the husband may choose to pay more than the required half or release any claim to a return. The verse does not permit pressure. A family, guardian, or husband must not frighten or shame a woman into surrendering her dowry. A waiver obtained through coercion is not the graciousness praised by the verse. Two early readings address the one holding the marriage contract. A widespread interpretation identifies him as the husband, who can complete the gift by paying the full amount. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”**) Because the half-dowry rule frames voluntary waiver, voluntary waiver returns attention to the half-dowry rule.

**VOLUNTARY WAIVER**

***“a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it”*** deepens voluntary waiver. Some jurists discussed the role of a guardian in particular circumstances. These details require qualified legal advice; the ethical principle is that the woman’s financial right is protected and any generosity is voluntary. To waive it is closer to taqwā encourages the more generous course. The woman may leave the half without resentment, and the husband may pay the full amount without using the law’s minimum to impoverish her. Generosity is not the same as surrender under pressure. It is an act chosen for Allah after one’s right and safety have been recognized. The verse thus prevents legal entitlement from becoming the whole measure of conduct. A person may be within the minimum rule yet act harshly. Taqwā asks what is fair, compassionate, and likely to reduce harm. It also recognizes that the poorer spouse may need the full amount and should not be expected to perform generosity for public approval. Do not forget graciousness between yourselves—wa-lā tansaw al-faḍl baynakum—is a beautiful principle for separation. The couple may remember the good that existed, refrain from exposing secrets, return belongings, speak fairly about one another, and protect any children from the conflict. Even when love has ended, basic honour can remain. Graciousness does not require denying abuse or concealing a danger from those who need protection. It means that truth is spoken without revenge and rights are pursued without unnecessary humiliation. (2:236 — **“There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the”**) Since generosity is closer to taqwā follows the half-dowry rule, voluntary waiver links purpose to generosity is closer to taqwā.

**GENEROSITY IS CLOSER TO TAQWĀ**

***“or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do”*** clarifies generosity is closer to taqwā. A person can make a lawful claim and still show faḍl, excellence and generosity. The verse belongs with a series that prevents economic abuse. A husband may not divorce a wife before consummation and use the unsettled dowry to punish her. A wife may not falsely claim payment or seize property beyond her right. Both parties should document what was paid, what remains due, and what each voluntarily waives. Modern contracts may include a prompt and deferred dowry, gifts, and shared property. The parties should seek legal and religious advice at the beginning rather than waiting for anger. Clear records are a protection, not a sign of mistrust. Allah sees whether the waiver was voluntary, whether the husband hid assets, whether the family pressured the woman, and whether the couple preserved each other’s dignity. Human witnesses may hear the formal agreement, but Allah knows the private threat or manipulation behind it. This closing reminder also comforts the person whose generosity was not appreciated. Allah sees the full gift even when people speak as though the giver did nothing. It restrains the person who boasts about waiving a right or humiliates the other for receiving it. A Prophetic teaching measures the best people by their character, while his conduct displayed kindness even in disagreement. A Muslim community should make it possible for marriages to end without turning divorce into social death. (4:4 — **“Give women ˹you wed˺ their due dowries graciously. But if they waive some of it willingly,”**) Graciousness beyond the minimum matters, which means generosity is closer to taqwā returns graciousness beyond the minimum to the half-dowry rule.

**GRACIOUSNESS BEYOND THE MINIMUM**

***“not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”*** closes with graciousness beyond the minimum. Mediation, fair financial settlement, counselling, and protection from gossip are part of the Qur’anic ideal. The case is like two men who dissolve a partnership in a shop and split the stock down the middle; one of them leaves the coffee machine as a gift. The machine was never in the books, the coffee is drunk by the man who stayed, and the street remembers the morning it was carried in. The half-dowry rule confronts anyone treating voluntary waiver as remote; under the half-dowry rule, such a person has counted his rights to the last coin and intends to keep the last word as well. The verse gives him a half, a waiver and a sentence about nearness to God, and the half-dowry rule uses voluntary waiver to ask which choice he would like to be known for. Because the closing words name the eye that misses nothing, voluntary waiver makes the half-dowry rule show that the money and the kindness are written on the same line. The half of the dowry and the two waivers are matched by the rule of the gift before the dowry is named. And the two ways of honour in a separation are set out earlier. (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or”**) Voluntary waiver makes the half-dowry rule practical; generosity is closer to taqwā therefore matters. Today, written marriage contracts should state the dowry clearly so generosity remains voluntary and financial pressure cannot masquerade as waiver.

## Verse 2:238

> Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah

**GUARDING THE PRAYERS**

***“Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle”*** establishes guarding the prayers. After a long passage on marriage, divorce, and family rights, the Qur’an returns the heart to its central covenant: prayer. Guard the prayers—ḥāfiẓū ʿalā al-ṣalawāt—means preserving their times, conditions, purification, direction, movements, recitation, and inward attention. Prayer is not an occasional refuge from life’s problems; it is the regular structure that keeps life oriented toward Allah. The plural prayers refers to the five obligatory prayers established by the Sunnah. Guarding them includes planning work, travel, school, and family responsibilities around prayer rather than treating prayer as whatever remains after every other demand. A person who misses through genuine sleep or forgetfulness prays when he remembers, while deliberate neglect requires repentance and practical change. Allah gives special emphasis to the middle prayer—al-ṣalāt al-wusṭā. The strongest transmitted interpretation identifies it as ʿAṣr, although other early readings considered the middle description differently. The special emphasis teaches that a prayer placed in the middle of work and daylight can be neglected precisely because worldly activity is intense. The Prophet ﷺ warned that whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer is as though his deeds have been nullified, in the authentic reports of Muslim alongside al-Bukhārī. (29:45 — **“Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer. Indeed,”**) Because guarding the prayers frames the middle prayer, the middle prayer returns attention to guarding the prayers.

**THE MIDDLE PRAYER**

***“prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah”*** deepens the middle prayer. The warning highlights its importance; it does not invite believers to neglect the other prayers. Every ṣalāh is obligatory and precious. Stand before Allah devoutly—qūmū lillāhi qānitīn—describes humble obedience, quiet attentiveness, and sincere submission. The body stands, but the heart recognizes that it is in the presence of its Lord. Qunūt can mean obedience, humility, prolonged devotion, and silence where the prayer requires it. Prayer is not a performance for people nearby. A person may stand in a beautiful row while his mind is chasing reputation, profit, or resentment. The believer continually returns his attention to the recitation, the meanings of the words, and the reality of standing before Allah. The placement of the verse shows that divine guidance about family does not replace worship, and worship does not excuse family injustice. Prayer should make people more truthful in divorce, more patient in conflict, and more careful with the rights of children and spouses. If a person prays while continuing deliberate abuse without repentance, he has not allowed prayer to perform its moral work. The Prophet ﷺ was deeply devoted in prayer and also the most merciful in his household. (4:103 — **“When the prayers are over, remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down.”**) Since standing before allah follows guarding the prayers, the middle prayer links purpose to standing before allah.

**STANDING BEFORE ALLAH**

He did not use worship to avoid practical responsibilities. His example joins private devotion with public fairness. The next verse gives concessions during danger, showing that prayer is not abandoned even in crisis. Its form may change according to safety, illness, and ability, but the obligation remains. This teaches that prayer anchors the believer in ordinary life and in emergency. Guarding prayer can require practical preparation: learning the times, keeping wudūʾ, identifying a clean place, arranging work breaks, and asking for reasonable accommodation. Parents teach children gradually, and communities should make mosques safe and accessible for women, elderly people, disabled people, and travellers. The prayer has outward conditions and an inward spirit. Correct timing and movement matter, while khushūʿ—humble attentiveness—deepens its effect. A person should not abandon the outward form because concentration is difficult; he patiently trains the heart. Recitation with understanding, slowing down, remembering death, and reducing distractions can help. The Qur’an says prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing. This is a promise and a test. The servant keeps returning to prayer even when he has fallen, then works to let the prayer reshape his conduct. Think of guarding the prayers through a family that argues for a year about the plan of the house and never pours the foundation. Prayer and family law matters, which means standing before allah returns prayer and family law to guarding the prayers.

**PRAYER AND FAMILY LAW**

The bricks are stacked in the yard, the drawings are on the wall, and the first rain of the winter finds the plot bare. Guarding the prayers reaches a reader today whose days are packed with claims about the rights of a house and no room for the five prayers. Guarding the prayers gives that person a command that stands at the head of the whole stretch, and guarding the prayers asks which of his duties he would keep if he could keep only one. Because the sentence is placed among the laws of the family, the middle prayer makes guarding the prayers show that the household is held up by the prayer before it is held up by the contract. The prayer is named as the thing that holds a person back from the wrong, and another passage of the Book says it plainly. The remembrance is named as the purpose in the chapter of the prophets. The middle prayer makes guarding the prayers practical; standing before allah therefore matters.

## Verse 2:239

> If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know

**PRAYER IN DANGER**

***“If you are in danger, pray on foot or while”*** establishes prayer in danger. The previous verse commanded guarding the prayers, and this verse explains that danger changes the form but does not erase the obligation. If a person is under attack, fleeing a threat, travelling through immediate danger, or unable to stand safely, he prays while walking or riding according to his ability. This is part of ṣalāt al-khawf, the prayer of fear, and part of the wider principle that Allah does not burden a soul beyond capacity. The concession protects both life and worship. A person does not stand exposed to danger merely to preserve an ordinary posture, and he does not abandon prayer because circumstances are difficult. He turns toward the qiblah where possible, performs the movements he can, and signals or adapts when necessary according to reliable legal guidance. The Qur’an gives a detailed form of the prayer of fear in 4:102, and the Prophet ﷺ performed it in more than one way depending on the battlefield. The variations teach flexibility within revelation. The essential purpose is to remember Allah while protecting the community and maintaining vigilance. These rules should not be turned into a performance by untrained individuals in dangerous settings. A person follows the established prayer of fear for his circumstances and consults qualified scholars where possible. (4:102 — **“When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer,”**) Because prayer in danger frames the prophet’s practice, the prophet’s practice returns attention to prayer in danger.

**THE PROPHET’S PRACTICE**

***“riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺”*** deepens the prophet’s practice. The principle is clear even when the details vary. Walking and riding represent movement under pressure. The worshipper may be unable to face the qiblah, bow, or prostrate normally. Allah accepts the prayer according to ability. A person in a vehicle, aircraft, boat, emergency shelter, or medical transport applies the relevant concessions without abandoning the prayer. The concession is not for ordinary laziness. When security returns, the normal form returns as well. Islam distinguishes genuine incapacity from convenience while refusing to make genuine incapacity a cause of guilt. When you are secure, remember Allah as He has taught you. Security brings the obligation to restore the ordinary prayer, not merely to continue the emergency form. The phrase reminds believers that they did not invent the prayer in fear; Allah taught it through revelation and the Messenger’s practice. The instruction also includes gratitude after danger. A person who escapes an accident, conflict, illness, or fear remembers Allah for protection. Security should increase obedience, not make the servant forget the Lord who carried him through danger. The verse does not oppose security planning. A person may assign guards, seek shelter, travel with companions, delay movement, or use communication tools while praying. The Prophet ﷺ took military precautions and arranged the prayer of fear with attention to real threats. (2:238 — **“Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah”**) Since walking or riding follows prayer in danger, the prophet’s practice links purpose to walking or riding.

**WALKING OR RIDING**

***“remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know”*** clarifies walking or riding. Tawakkul includes using means while relying upon Allah. In personal danger, protecting life is important. A victim of violence should seek safety, call for help, and pray in the way possible. No one should be shamed for using a concession during a medical or security emergency. Allah says He taught believers what they did not know. The forms of worship are not products of cultural invention. The community learns through the Qur’an, the Sunnah, and the transmission of qualified scholarship. This should produce gratitude and humility rather than argument over personal preference. The verse also establishes that knowledge has a practical purpose. The details of prayer are learned so that the servant can worship in health, travel, fear, and illness. A Muslim should learn the essentials before an emergency, just as he prepares emergency supplies before a crisis. Prayer in danger tells the frightened heart that Allah remains near even when ordinary order has collapsed. The worshipper may not be able to pray beautifully or at length, but the smallest sincere act of remembrance matters. Allah sees the fear, the effort, and the intention. Once security returns, the believer continues to remember Allah and to repair any missed or incomplete obligations according to qualified guidance. The crisis may become a source of greater reliance and gratitude. (4:101 — **“When you travel through the land,”**) When secure, remember allah as taught matters, which means walking or riding returns when secure, remember allah as taught to prayer in danger.

**WHEN SECURE, REMEMBER ALLAH AS TAUGHT**

Picture prayer under threat in a traveller who keeps his father’s letter in a pocket on the road and reads it again at every stop, and who at last arrives home and finds the writer waiting at the door. The letter was never the point of the journey, and the journey was never the point of the letter. Prayer in danger reaches a reader today who leaves the prayer when his day becomes hard and tells himself that God understands his pressure. The verse gives him a shortened form for the danger and a full order for the safety, and prayer in danger asks which of the two he is living in. Because the closing words speak of what he was taught, the prophet’s practice makes prayer in danger show that the prayer is the receipt for a gift he did not pay for. The remembrance of God in every posture is commanded in another chapter. And the same remembrance is joined to the prayer in the chapter of the prophets. The prophet’s practice makes prayer in danger practical; walking or riding therefore matters.

## Verse 2:240

> Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**SECURITY FOR WIDOWS**

***“Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s”*** establishes security for widows. This āyah addresses the financial and residential security of widows after a husband’s death. It instructs that a bequest should provide maintenance for one year and that the widow should not be expelled from the marital home during that period. The command recognizes that bereavement can combine emotional loss with sudden economic vulnerability. A widow should not be left without shelter while relatives divide the estate. The instruction is a protection, not a reason to control the widow. She may remain in the home if she chooses and if it is safe, but the verse also says that if she leaves, there is no blame upon her for making lawful choices. Relatives must not imprison her, seize her property, or treat her as a burden attached to the estate. The previous verse establishes the widow’s waiting period as four months and ten days, while this verse mentions maintenance and residence for one year. Jurists carefully discussed the relationship between the two passages. The later legal framework, including 2:234 and the inheritance verses in Sūrah al-Nisāʾ, establishes the widow’s waiting period and her fixed inheritance share. Many legal readings treat the earlier one-year residence instruction as superseded or narrowed by later revelation, while others preserve aspects of residence and maintenance through a different legal route. The enduring principle is certain even where the historical legal sequence is discussed: a widow’s inheritance, housing, and support must be protected, and no relative may expel or impoverish her unlawfully. (2:234 — **“As for those of you who die and leave widows behind,”**) Because security for widows frames relationship to the four-month waiting period, relationship to the four-month waiting period returns attention to security for widows.

**RELATIONSHIP TO THE FOUR-MONTH WAITING PERIOD**

***“maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not”*** deepens relationship to the four-month waiting period. Current application should follow qualified Islamic legal advice and the law of the country, especially where property and children are involved. Maintenance is not the same as inheritance. A widow may receive her prescribed share of the estate under 4:12, and she may also have rights to deferred dowry, debts owed to her, housing, and support. The estate must be administered transparently. Relatives cannot say, You have inherited, so we owe you nothing, while taking control of assets or refusing the rights established by law. Where the deceased left young children, the widow may need additional support as their mother and caregiver. The community, relatives, charitable funds, and lawful public systems should help. A widow should not be forced to sell her home or marry a relative in order to survive. Without expelling them condemns a common form of injustice. A husband’s family may attempt to remove the widow immediately, change locks, seize documents, or force her to leave with nothing. Such conduct violates the dignity and security the verse protects. If the home is unsafe or legally belongs to another person under valid law, the solution is secure alternative housing and fair settlement—not abandonment. The prohibition also has a moral dimension. The widow should not be expelled from the family’s care because the husband has died. She remains a human being with honour and rights, not a person whose value ended with the marriage. (4:12 — **“You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless.”**) Since maintenance and inheritance follows security for widows, relationship to the four-month waiting period links purpose to maintenance and inheritance.

**MAINTENANCE AND INHERITANCE**

***“accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise”*** clarifies maintenance and inheritance. Their lawful departure places no blame on the family for decisions they reasonably make afterward. The widow may leave the residence after the relevant waiting period or when the legal framework permits, remarry, work, travel for need, manage wealth, and make other lawful decisions. Relatives may advise but may not dictate her future. The phrase fī anfusihinna bi-l-maʿrūf includes dignified adornment, lawful social activity, and remarriage after the waiting period. It does not mean that a widow must remain permanently in mourning or that the husband’s family owns her choices. Allah is ʿAzīz and Ḥakīm. His might protects the rights of people whom human power may ignore, and His wisdom appears in the gradual development of family law. The community may debate the historical relation between verses, but it may not use technical disagreement as an excuse to exploit widows. The divine law also recognizes different family structures, property arrangements, and circumstances. The executor must seek guidance rather than applying a rigid formula without considering safety, inheritance, debts, children, and the widow’s consent. The verse’s instruction begins with those who die and leave wives, but the wider community must help fulfil its purpose. Relatives should provide food, shelter, companionship, legal support, and protection from harassment. Charitable institutions should establish transparent widow and orphan support. Leaders must enforce property rights and protect women from coercion. (4:7 — **“For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave,”**) No expulsion matters, which means maintenance and inheritance returns no expulsion to security for widows.

**NO EXPULSION**

The Prophet ﷺ praised the person who strives to support widows and the poor, comparing that effort to great worship in reports preserved by Muslim and al-Bukhārī. Caring for a widow is not charity that creates superiority; it is a duty and honour before Allah. Think of security for widows through a farmer who knows the winter is coming and plants his last field anyway, so that the people who eat from his land will have bread after he has gone. The field is his for one more season, and the harvest is theirs for as long as they can remember his name. Security for widows reaches a reader today who writes a will in his last week and forgets the woman who nursed him through his illness. The verse gives her a year, a house and the command that she not be pushed out, and it asks the testator what he thinks he is leaving behind. Because the close names the Almighty and the All-Wise, security for widows teaches that a bequest is a matter of power and of wisdom before it is a matter of paper. Relationship to the four-month waiting period makes security for widows practical; maintenance and inheritance therefore matters.

## Verse 2:241

> Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺

**A GENERAL RIGHT OF KIND TREATMENT**

***“Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced”*** establishes a general right of kind treatment. After detailing dowries, waiting periods, reconciliation, and widowhood, the Qur’an gives a broad ethical command concerning divorced women: they are entitled to a suitable provision—matāʿ bi-l-maʿrūf. The verse reminds the community that divorce does not erase the woman’s dignity or leave her responsible for all the financial and emotional costs of a marriage’s end. The provision can include a compensatory gift, maintenance owed during the relevant waiting period, housing, clothing, and practical support according to the circumstances and the specific legal category of the divorce. The detailed obligations differ depending on whether the marriage was consummated, whether a dowry was specified, whether the divorce is revocable, and whether there are children. A qualified scholar and legal adviser should examine the case rather than applying one amount to every woman. Maʿrūf means what is fair, recognized as good, and consistent with revelation and sound custom. A wealthy man should not offer a token gift while keeping wealth for himself, and a poor man is not required to give what would destroy his ability to survive or support dependants. Fairness considers the woman’s needs, the husband’s means, the length of the marriage, and the rights already established by contract and law. The command is not a payment for the woman’s silence. (2:236 — **“There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is”**) Because a general right of kind treatment frames maʿrūf and ability, maʿrūf and ability returns attention to a general right of kind treatment.

**MAʿRŪF AND ABILITY**

***“women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺”*** deepens maʿrūf and ability. It does not allow a husband to purchase permission to insult, abuse, or conceal wrongdoing. It is an expression of responsibility as the relationship ends. If the couple have children, support for the children remains a separate obligation and must not be counted as a favour to the mother. A marriage may end, but the former spouses remain human beings with rights. The husband must not expose private matters, manipulate children, withhold documents, or use financial dependence to continue control. The wife must also avoid false claims and unlawful seizure, but the presence of conflict never removes the moral requirement of justice. The Prophet ﷺ said that the best people are those best in character to their families, as Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī records. That character is tested not only while affection is strong but when disappointment and resentment appear. A dignified provision can prevent poverty, reduce hostility, and help a woman rebuild her life without being treated as discarded property. The verse calls the provision a duty upon the muttaqūn. Taqwā makes a person fulfil rights even when a court cannot compel him and when relatives will praise him for doing less. It also prevents the recipient from turning a lawful claim into revenge or public humiliation. Both parties remember that Allah sees the settlement and knows whether it was voluntary, fair, and sufficient. (2:237 — **“And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry,”**) Since divorce does not cancel humanity follows a general right of kind treatment, maʿrūf and ability links purpose to divorce does not cancel humanity.

**DIVORCE DOES NOT CANCEL HUMANITY**

The mindful person settles accounts transparently, pays what is due promptly, and does not force the other spouse to beg. He may give more than the minimum because he remembers the years of shared life and the favour that once existed. Generosity is especially valuable when the marriage ends without a clear legal remedy for every loss. This command echoes 2:236, where a woman divorced before consummation and without a fixed dowry is given a suitable gift, and 2:237, where generosity is called closer to taqwā. It also completes the warning in 2:231 against retaining a woman to harm her. The Qur’an’s family law repeatedly joins legal precision with ethical excellence. The later verses of Sūrah al-Ṭalāq explain maintenance and housing according to ability. These passages should be read together. A Muslim cannot cite one verse to minimize a right while ignoring the wider Qur’anic requirement of kindness. Sometimes a former husband cannot provide enough, or he has died, disappeared, or become abusive. The community, relatives, zakāh institutions, and lawful public systems should help divorced women and children. The Qur’anic ethic is not satisfied by telling a vulnerable woman to be patient while those with means refuse support. Social support should preserve dignity. It can include housing, legal assistance, education, childcare, counselling, and protection from harassment. A duty upon the mindful matters, which means divorce does not cancel humanity returns a duty upon the mindful to a general right of kind treatment.

**A DUTY UPON THE MINDFUL**

The aim is to restore independence rather than create a new form of dependence. Think of a general right of kind treatment through a household that moves out of a rented flat and scrubs the floors before the keys go back, though no clause in the lease asks for it. The next family walks into a clean house, and the landlord tells the story for years. A general right of kind treatment confronts anyone treating maʿrūf and ability as remote; under a general right of kind treatment, such a person has paid every sum the law demanded and left his former wife to arrange her own life in silence. The verse gives her a provision and puts the duty on the mindful, and it asks him which list he wants his name to be on. Because the sentence joins the money to the fear of God, maʿrūf and ability makes a general right of kind treatment show that the last payment of a marriage is made to the Lord rather than to the woman. The verse is the ending of the whole stretch about marriage, and the next verse names the purpose of such endings:. The duty of kindness between people who part is guarded earlier in the same passage. Maʿrūf and ability makes a general right of kind treatment practical; divorce does not cancel humanity therefore matters. Today, fair provision after divorce includes material help, dignified speech, and procedures that do not turn separation into social punishment.

## Verse 2:242

> This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand

**CLARITY IN FAMILY LAW**

***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear”*** establishes clarity in family law. This verse concludes the connected passage on divorce, waiting periods, dowry, maintenance, breastfeeding, widowhood, and fairness. Allah says that He makes His revelations clear—yubayyinu Allāhu lakum āyātihi—because family rights are too important to be left to anger, custom, or the power of the strongest person. Clear guidance protects people when emotions make judgement difficult. The Qur’an’s detail is itself a mercy. It addresses situations that families may prefer to avoid discussing: separation before consummation, a widow’s waiting period, breastfeeding, financial support, reconciliation, and the finality of divorce. By bringing these matters into revelation, Allah gives vulnerable people language and rights that private customs might deny them. The purpose is so that you may understand—taʿqilūn. Understanding is more than memorizing legal phrases. It means recognizing the wisdom, limits, purposes, and moral consequences of the rulings. A person who knows the waiting period but uses it to harass his former wife has not understood. A person who knows the maintenance rule but refuses to support children has missed the command’s purpose. The Qur’anic ʿaql connects evidence with action. It asks how a rule protects dignity, prevents harm, and directs people toward taqwā. It also requires humility: complex cases should be referred to qualified scholars and legal authorities rather than settled by personal confidence. (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”**) Because clarity in family law frames understanding requires reflection, understanding requires reflection returns attention to clarity in family law. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing statement as an explanation of divine commands and prohibitions given so that people may understand what obedience requires.

**UNDERSTANDING REQUIRES REFLECTION**

***“to you, so perhaps you will understand”*** deepens understanding requires reflection. Allah’s revelations are clear in their principles, but applying them can require knowledge. Menstrual cycles may be irregular, a divorce may be uttered in anger, assets may be disputed, and parents may disagree about a child’s care. Clear revelation does not remove the need for careful interpretation, evidence, consultation, and due process. The believer distinguishes a clear command from a difficult application. He does not claim that every question has a one-line answer, and he does not use complexity to avoid an obvious duty. The legal schools developed detailed methods precisely because they respected the text’s clarity and the diversity of circumstances. The preceding laws contain boundaries, but they also contain concessions and opportunities for generosity. Divorce is limited, yet reconciliation is possible. Dowry is protected, yet voluntary waiver is praised. Breastfeeding has a suggested period, yet parents may wean through consultation. Widowhood has a defined waiting period, yet the woman retains agency afterward. Understanding means seeing these provisions together. A person should not select the harshest interpretation when Allah has provided ease, nor the easiest interpretation when it destroys another’s rights. Justice and mercy are not opposing values in the Qur’an. Human customs can be useful when consistent with revelation, but they can also make oppression appear normal. A family may treat a widow as property, force a divorced woman to surrender her dowry, or prevent remarriage to preserve social status. (4:35 — **“If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers.”**) Since clarity does not mean simplicity in every case follows clarity in family law, understanding requires reflection links purpose to clarity does not mean simplicity in every case.

**CLARITY DOES NOT MEAN SIMPLICITY IN EVERY CASE**

The Qur’an makes its guidance clear so that people can measure custom by justice rather than justice by custom. The same applies to modern practices. Legal paperwork, family courts, and social expectations should be used to protect rights, not to hide wealth or exclude the vulnerable. The person of understanding asks whether an arrangement fulfils Allah’s purpose. The verse makes knowledge a responsibility. A person who understands the rule must apply it honestly and teach it accurately. He should not use selective quotations to win a family dispute. If he discovers that he misunderstood, he corrects himself and repairs the harm. Teaching and learning the Qur’an mark the best people in a Prophetic instruction, and his conduct showed that teaching includes practical mercy. Knowledge is a trust, especially when it affects marriage, children, property, and personal safety. Think of clarity in family law through a father who explains to his sons why a field is left unsown for a season, and who finds in the spring that one of them has understood and the others have only obeyed. The field produces for the one who listened, and the father's words were never only about the field. Clarity in family law confronts anyone treating understanding requires reflection as remote; under clarity in family law, such a person has learned the rules of the household as a list of permissions and refusals. Law and mercy together matters, which means clarity does not mean simplicity in every case returns law and mercy together to clarity in family law.

**LAW AND MERCY TOGETHER**

Clarity in family law gives him a sentence about clarity and a hope about understanding, and clarity in family law asks what he has understood of the family he lives in. Because the verse speaks of understanding rather than of obeying, clarity in family law teaches that a rule known by heart and not by mind is a wall that keeps nobody warm. Since the hope of the sentence is placed on the reader, the reader sees that the law leaves room for him to arrive at its meaning late. Because the passage that closes here was about women and houses, clarity in family law shows that the Book means the family to be understood and not only administered. The verse closes the stretch before the next one turns to a story of a people who fled their homes. And the same call to understanding is made at the end of the rules of the fast. The reader who keeps the two endings side by side sees a book that explains and then waits to be understood. Understanding requires reflection makes clarity in family law practical; clarity does not mean simplicity in every case therefore matters. Today, family law needs clear teaching, accurate records, and merciful institutions because confusion often injures the person with less power.
