## Verse 2:243

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful

**FLIGHT THAT CANNOT OUTRUN DEATH**

***“Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the”*** establishes flight that cannot outrun death. The verse recalls a large group who left their homes in fear of death. The Qur’an does not identify the town or give every historical detail. Transmitted accounts connect the event to a plague or another deadly danger among Banū Isrāʾīl, but those reports differ in detail. What is certain from the revelation is that thousands fled, Allah caused them to die, and then restored them to life as a sign of His power. The story is not a condemnation of every attempt to escape danger. Islam permits seeking safety, treatment, shelter, and protection. The issue is the heart’s assumption that flight or worldly means can escape Allah’s decree. A person takes means while knowing that life and death remain in Allah’s hand. The command Die and the restoration to life display Allah’s absolute authority. Human beings may plan, build walls, travel, develop medicine, and protect themselves, but none can guarantee life. The verse prepares the reader for the following command to fight in Allah’s cause and to spend for the community: fear of death must not become a reason to abandon every duty. At the same time, the passage does not glorify death or demand reckless exposure. The Prophet ﷺ taught people to avoid plague-stricken areas and not to enter them, while one already inside should not flee, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim preserve in their Ṣaḥīḥ collections. (3:145 — **“No soul can ever die without Allah’s Will at the destined time. Those who desire worldly gain,”**) Because flight that cannot outrun death frames life and death belong to allah, life and death belong to allah returns attention to flight that cannot outrun death.

**LIFE AND DEATH BELONG TO ALLAH**

***“thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them”*** deepens life and death belong to allah. This shows that avoiding contagion and taking precautions are compatible with belief in decree. The restoration of the dead is a sign of the resurrection. The One who returned life to this group can raise all humanity after death. The event is also a direct lesson in Allah’s ability to reverse what people consider final. Death is not a barrier to divine power, and the Hereafter is not an irrational idea. The Qur’an tells such stories not to satisfy curiosity about supernatural spectacle but to establish accountability. If Allah can restore life, then people will return to Him and answer for fear, courage, gratitude, and the use of their life. Fear of death is natural. A believer may feel fear and still act courageously. Courage is not the absence of the survival instinct; it is refusing to let fear cancel an obligation when lawful protection of others requires action. The story warns against collective cowardice that leaves a community defenceless or abandons the vulnerable. The following verses call for spending and speak of the leaders of Banū Isrāʾīl seeking a king to fight. The sequence suggests that life must be used in obedience and service, not merely preserved for its own sake. A long life wasted in fear is not automatically better than a shorter life lived with faith and benefit. (3:154 — **“Then after distress, He sent down serenity in the form of drowsiness overcoming some of you,”**) Since resurrection is possible follows flight that cannot outrun death, life and death belong to allah links purpose to resurrection is possible.

**RESURRECTION IS POSSIBLE**

***“life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful”*** clarifies resurrection is possible. Allah is full of bounty to people. Life itself is a bounty, and restoration is a further sign. Guidance, health, safety, family, knowledge, and opportunities to serve are also gifts. Ingratitude—kufr al-niʿmah—occurs when people receive these gifts but attribute them solely to themselves or use them against Allah’s purposes. Widespread ingratitude warns believers that gratitude cannot be assumed from survival. A person who escapes a disease should not merely return to old negligence. He thanks Allah through obedience, care for others, and responsible use of renewed opportunity. Because the Qur’an leaves the town unnamed, believers should not build doctrine on uncertain details. The story’s lesson remains valid without knowing whether the event involved a particular plague, town, or tribe. This is a Qur’anic discipline: take the guidance that revelation confirms, and avoid turning transmitted possibilities into certainty. The same restraint applies to contemporary disasters. No person should confidently declare that a particular victim was punished or that a catastrophe has one hidden meaning known only to him. Allah knows the wisdom of events. People respond with repentance, practical care, and compassion. Think of flight that cannot outrun death through a village that builds a wall on the side of the river because that is where the last flood came through, and leaves the door on the hill open. (40:68 — **“He is the One Who gives life and causes death. When He decrees a matter,”**) Fear and responsibility matters, which means resurrection is possible returns fear and responsibility to flight that cannot outrun death.

**FEAR AND RESPONSIBILITY**

The water arrives from the hill in the spring, and the wall on the river is the only part of the story the neighbours remember. A community fleeing death reaches a reader today who has spent his years avoiding every risk that might shorten his life. The verse gives him a crowd of thousands who ran and a word that found them all, and it asks him what the running was for. Because the close names the bounty and the ingratitude in one breath, life and death belong to allah makes flight that cannot outrun death show that the life a person guards is the gift he did not buy. The story of the towns that were left empty is told again in the chapter of the cave. And the lesson of a test in battle is drawn from the two armies in another chapter. Life and death belong to allah makes flight that cannot outrun death practical; resurrection is possible therefore matters.

## Verse 2:244

> Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**COURAGE AFTER THE LESSON OF DEATH**

***“Fight in the cause of Allah,”*** establishes courage after the lesson of death. After recalling the people who fled in fear of death, the Qur’an commands the believers to fight in Allah’s cause. The verse is a call to courage when defence and the protection of the community are required. It does not praise violence for its own sake or command individuals to attack people who have not attacked them. Its meaning is governed by the limits already given: fight those who fight, do not transgress, accept cessation, and keep the objective of ending persecution. The story of those who fled death teaches that preserving life is not the only human duty. If fear makes a community abandon every responsibility, the vulnerable may be left to aggressors. Courage means taking a lawful risk to protect others when there is a reasonable duty and capacity to do so. Fī sabīl Allāh refers to striving for a cause approved by Allah. A conflict motivated by revenge, tribal pride, conquest, wealth, or personal ambition cannot become holy merely through religious language. The cause must be just, the authority legitimate, the means proportionate, and the conduct within the revealed limits. The broader meaning of striving includes resisting one’s own desires, seeking knowledge, supporting the oppressed, spending for public welfare, and speaking truth to power. (2:190 — **“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you,”**) Because courage after the lesson of death frames in allah’s cause, in allah’s cause returns attention to courage after the lesson of death. Ibn ʿAbbās joins the command to fight with Allah’s knowledge of spoken words, inward intentions, and the consequences of disobedience.

**IN ALLAH’S CAUSE**

***“and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*** deepens in allah’s cause. Armed fighting is a restricted form that requires conditions and cannot be separated from the Qur’an’s protection of life and its prohibition of transgression. Allah is Samīʿ and ʿAlīm. He hears the leader’s call, the soldier’s fear, the victim’s cry, and the peace proposal that a powerful person tries to conceal. He knows whether the fighter seeks Allah’s pleasure or fame, whether a commander is protecting civilians or using a cause for ambition, and whether a person is refusing duty out of wisdom or cowardice. This ending prevents both hypocrisy and despair. A person may appear brave to people while being corrupt before Allah, and a frightened person may possess great sincerity. Divine judgement reaches the hidden intention and the actual conduct. Fighting is not an individual’s private decision. It requires a legitimate community or state authority, consultation, evidence, and a clear objective. The chaos of self-appointed groups is itself destructive. Individuals who declare others unbelievers and attack civilians violate the command rather than applying it. The community must also provide discipline and accountability. Orders that violate Allah’s limits cannot be obeyed, and commanders must investigate abuses. Those who kill non-combatants, torture prisoners, betray safe conduct, or destroy without necessity are transgressors even if they claim a righteous cause. (2:243 — **“Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of”**) Since hearing the call to courage follows courage after the lesson of death, in allah’s cause links purpose to hearing the call to courage.

**HEARING THE CALL TO COURAGE**

The verse does not demand that every person fight physically. Capacity, skill, health, family responsibilities, and the nature of the threat matter. A person may support a just defence through medical care, food, shelter, communication, diplomacy, or financial assistance. The obligation is applied according to ability and lawful authority. Nor does fear justify abandoning people who depend upon one’s protection. A person may feel afraid and still take the next responsible step. Prayer, consultation, training, and solidarity help turn fear into disciplined courage. The aim is to restore safety, freedom from persecution, and the ability to worship Allah. When that aim is achieved, fighting must stop. The Prophet ﷺ accepted treaties and safe conduct and commanded mercy to non-combatants. Victory over an enemy does not give permission to humiliate or destroy his family. The believer remembers that all parties will return to Allah. Fighting may be necessary, but it is never outside moral accountability. The one who begins a war for ego and the one who restrains himself for Allah are not equal, even if both claim courage. Think of courage after the lesson of death through a man who repairs the roof of the mosque in his own street and tells everyone he meets that nobody else lifted a hand. The roof keeps the rain out for twenty years, and the story of the repairs is told in the market with his name attached to it. Authority and discipline matters, which means hearing the call to courage returns authority and discipline to courage after the lesson of death.

**AUTHORITY AND DISCIPLINE**

Courage after the lesson of death addresses a present-day giver: he gives his money to a cause and expects the world to record the gift. The verse gives him a hearing and a knowledge that precede his own account of himself, and it asks him who the fight was for. Because the sentence names the One who hears before the One who knows, in allah’s cause makes courage after the lesson of death show that the words of a man on the road are counted with his deeds. Since the fighting is named as a duty rather than a choice, the field shows a person that his words are tested beside his conduct. Here the Book joins a heavy duty to the names of God, and the same pair closes the command of the prayer elsewhere in the chapter. The lesson of the field is drawn out again where the Book speaks of the two armies. In allah’s cause makes courage after the lesson of death practical; hearing the call to courage therefore matters.

## Verse 2:245

> Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**THE METAPHOR OF A LOAN**

***“Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will”*** establishes the metaphor of a loan. Allah is free of all need, yet He calls charitable spending a good loan—qarḍ ḥasan. The metaphor honours the giver by promising that what is offered for Allah’s sake will be returned with multiplication. A loan normally expects repayment, but Allah does not need the servant’s wealth. The expression teaches that charity is secure with Him and that no sincere gift is lost. A qarḍ ḥasan is given from lawful wealth, with sincere intention, without humiliating the recipient, and without demanding an unfair return. It can include financial support, food, education, medical care, shelter, and resources for a just public cause. The goodness lies in the source, intention, method, and benefit. Allah multiplies the reward many times, as explained in 2:261: a seed produces seven ears, each with a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills. Multiplication may appear as blessing in the giver’s wealth, forgiveness, protection, guidance, benefit to descendants, or reward in the Hereafter. The servant does not dictate the form of repayment; he trusts Allah’s wisdom. The promise is not a guarantee that every donation produces immediate worldly profit. A person may give and remain poor, but his charity can still be accepted and multiplied beyond worldly measurement. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) Because the metaphor of a loan frames multiplication without calculation, multiplication without calculation returns attention to the metaphor of a loan. Ibn ʿAbbās understands the good loan as sincere charity that seeks Allah alone, with increase belonging to the One who gives and withholds provision.

**MULTIPLICATION WITHOUT CALCULATION**

***“multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases”*** deepens multiplication without calculation. The verse protects generosity from the market’s narrow calculation. Allah withholds and gives abundantly—yaqbiḍu wa-yabsuṭu—reminds people that provision is in His hand. Wealth may expand or contract as a test. The person who gives does not lose control of his future because Allah can replace what he spends. The person who withholds should not assume that hoarding guarantees safety. This does not deny human economic responsibility. A person budgets, supports dependants, repays debts, and invests lawfully. The verse teaches that planning should not become an excuse for miserliness or the belief that wealth is independent of Allah. The immediate context includes preparation for a just struggle and support for the community. Spending may therefore include equipment, food, medical care, refuge, and assistance to families affected by conflict. It also includes the broad charitable purposes named throughout the Qur’an. The cause must be lawful; donations to terrorism, aggression, corruption, or the abuse of civilians are not a qarḍ ḥasan. Institutions receiving funds must be transparent. A charity cannot invoke Allah’s promise to hide fraud, excessive salaries, or political manipulation. Trustees are responsible for directing money to its stated purpose. Wealth can become a rival to Allah when a person loves it more than truth and refuses every claim upon it. (9:103 — **“Take from their wealth ˹O Prophet˺ charity to purify and bless them,”**) Since provision narrowed and enlarged follows the metaphor of a loan, multiplication without calculation links purpose to provision narrowed and enlarged.

**PROVISION NARROWED AND ENLARGED**

***“and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned”*** clarifies provision narrowed and enlarged. Spending breaks the illusion of absolute ownership. The giver says through action that money is a trust, not a master. This is why charity is called purification in 9:103. The recipient also has dignity. A gift should not be accompanied by reminders, insults, public photography without consent, or conditions that create dependence. The Qur’an warns that injury can cancel the reward of charity. The best giver seeks Allah’s acceptance, not the recipient’s humiliation or the audience’s applause. To Him you will be returned gives the metaphor its final seriousness. The wealth left behind will not accompany a person, but its use will. Every coin spent, withheld, earned, or taken unjustly returns to the account before Allah. The wise investor sends a portion ahead through charity and righteous support. The return also relativizes temporary scarcity. A person may feel that generosity makes him vulnerable, but Allah controls the final balance. The believer gives within ability, asks Allah for blessing, and avoids both waste and fear-driven hoarding. Think of the metaphor of a loan through a merchant who leaves his goods in the hands of a partner while he travels, and who spends the journey worrying about the stock. The goods are sold at a price he never asked for, and the worry was the only part of the trip that was his. (57:11 — **“Who is it that will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply ˹many times over˺ for them,”**) Spending in allah’s cause matters, which means provision narrowed and enlarged returns spending in allah’s cause to the metaphor of a loan.

**SPENDING IN ALLAH’S CAUSE**

The metaphor of a loan reaches a reader today who counts every gift he has made and wonders when the return will appear in his account. The verse gives him a loan, a promise and a return, and it asks him where he thinks the increase is kept. Because the hands that decrease and increase are named before the gathering at the end, multiplication without calculation makes the metaphor of a loan show that the wealth he holds is already on its way somewhere. Since the question is addressed to a person rather than to a crowd, the reader sees that the invitation stands open in every generation. The same invitation is made with the same words in the chapter of the mutual disregard. And the figure of the multiplication is drawn out in the parable of the grain. Multiplication without calculation makes the metaphor of a loan practical; provision narrowed and enlarged therefore matters.

## Verse 2:246

> Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**LEADERSHIP REQUESTED AFTER DISPLACEMENT**

***“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a”*** establishes leadership requested after displacement. This story follows the account of a people who feared death and the command to spend and strive. The chiefs of Banū Isrāʾīl asked a prophet to appoint a king so they could fight in Allah’s cause. Their request sounded courageous, but the prophet tested the sincerity behind their words: would they still fight when the command brought real danger, sacrifice, and discipline. The question is not cynicism. It is prophetic knowledge of human weakness. People often ask for a grand opportunity while imagining that it will cost little. A person may demand change, justice, or victory in the abstract, then retreat when truth requires money, time, risk, or the loss of status. They cited their expulsion from their homes and separation from their children as reasons to fight. Their grief was real, and defending the oppressed can be a righteous duty. The Qur’an does not shame those who want to return home or protect families. It asks whether their stated motive will remain firm when the path becomes difficult. The story also shows that fighting is not an individual adventure. The community seeks a king and accepts organized leadership. A just defence requires coordination, discipline, resources, and an authority capable of making decisions and protecting civilians. Private factions that act without accountability create the very disorder the community is trying to end. (2:243 — **“Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of”**) Because leadership requested after displacement frames displacement and the desire for justice, displacement and the desire for justice returns attention to leadership requested after displacement.

**DISPLACEMENT AND THE DESIRE FOR JUSTICE**

***“king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied,”*** deepens displacement and the desire for justice. When fighting was prescribed, most turned away. Their problem was not lack of information; the command had become clear. Their speech had outrun their courage. This is a recurring Qur’anic lesson: claims are tested by action. A person may speak about sacrifice, but Allah knows who remains faithful when comfort is threatened. The verse does not imply that every person who refuses combat is a wrongdoer. Legitimate exemptions, inability, illness, family obligations, and the absence of lawful authority matter. The criticism concerns those who demanded the command and then abandoned it out of hypocrisy, cowardice, or attachment to worldly safety. The request for a king shows that leadership is necessary for collective action, but it also raises the question of whom the community should follow. A leader must possess the knowledge, character, ability, and trustworthiness required by the task. Popularity, wealth, lineage, and loud promises are not enough. The community’s obedience is also bounded. It obeys a leader in what is right and refuses a command that violates Allah’s limits. The prophet in the story does not flatter the people; he exposes the gap between their words and their likely conduct. Good leadership tells the truth before asking for sacrifice. Only a few remained steadfast. The Qur’an often shows that numbers do not determine truth. A small group with sincerity can withstand a larger group whose commitment is shallow. (4:75 — **“And what is it with you?”**) Since the failure of words without commitment follows leadership requested after displacement, displacement and the desire for justice links purpose to the failure of words without commitment.

**THE FAILURE OF WORDS WITHOUT COMMITMENT**

***““How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our”*** clarifies the failure of words without commitment. This does not glorify isolation or contempt for the majority. It encourages believers not to abandon a righteous duty merely because support is limited. The few must still act wisely. Sincerity without planning is not enough. They need consultation, preparation, lawful authority, and care for those who depend upon them. Allah’s help is sought through both faith and responsible means. The closing statement returns judgement to Allah. He knows which people turned away because of legitimate inability and which chose betrayal after demanding the command. Human observers see only part of the situation. This warning also prevents leaders from labelling every reluctant person a hypocrite without understanding his circumstances. Allah’s knowledge covers the heart, the promise, the fear, the capacity, and the deed. The believer asks Allah for honesty before making a public commitment and for courage after the commitment has been made. Think of leadership requested after displacement through a village that signs a paper to rebuild the canal together in the dry season. And then finds that the water is low in every house and the tools are locked in the sheds when the work begins. The canal is cleared by four men in the end, and the water reaches the fields of the whole village the next spring. A community seeking leadership reaches a reader today who promises in the assembly what he does not intend to carry into the street. (8:72 — **“Those who believed, emigrated, and strived with their wealth and lives in the cause of Allah,”**) Leadership and obedience matters, which means the failure of words without commitment returns leadership and obedience to leadership requested after displacement.

**LEADERSHIP AND OBEDIENCE**

***“children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”*** closes with leadership and obedience. The verse gives him a crowd in the thousands, a prophet who asked twice and a field where the promise ended, and leadership requested after displacement asks which of the two days of a promise he lives in. Because the close speaks of a knowledge that misses neither the words nor the running, displacement and the desire for justice makes leadership requested after displacement show that the pledge of a person is already in a book he cannot edit. Since the few who stood are named without their names, the reader sees that the Book remembers the deed before the man. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the unnamed prophet as Samuel in a transmitted reading, while another early report identifies the king given to them as Saul. Because the request names the fight and not the spoil, the request shows how defeated people speak and want their place back. The test with the river and the few who stayed appears in the river test that follows. And the lesson of the two armies that met is drawn in another chapter. (4:59 — **“O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”**) Displacement and the desire for justice makes leadership requested after displacement practical; the failure of words without commitment therefore matters.

## Verse 2:247

> Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”

**LEADERSHIP IS A TRUST FROM ALLAH**

***“Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he”*** establishes leadership is a trust from allah. The prophet announces that Allah appointed Ṭālūt, known in the biblical tradition as Saul, as king. The people objected because he did not belong to the lineage they expected and did not possess abundant wealth. Their objection exposes a common assumption: that leadership belongs to the richest family, the most prestigious tribe, or the person who claims the highest status. The verse does not provide a simple political formula for every historical society. It teaches that authority is a trust and that the qualifications for it must be judged by justice, knowledge, ability, and suitability—not merely by wealth or inherited prestige. In this story, the prophet’s declaration establishes Ṭālūt’s appointment, and the people are tested in whether they will accept a qualified leader rather than their preferred candidate. Allah increased Ṭālūt in knowledge and physical strength—basṭatan fī al-ʿilm wa-l-jism. Knowledge includes strategic judgement, understanding the mission, leadership wisdom, and the ability to distinguish truth from deception. Physical strength includes health, endurance, courage, and the ability to carry the responsibilities of command. The verse is not praising appearance for its own sake. A beautiful or wealthy person is not automatically qualified. Nor does physical disability disqualify a person from leadership when the relevant role does not require particular physical abilities. The criterion is capacity for the actual trust, combined with knowledge and moral integrity. (4:58 — **“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people,”**) Because leadership is a trust from allah frames knowledge and physical capacity, knowledge and physical capacity returns attention to leadership is a trust from allah.

**KNOWLEDGE AND PHYSICAL CAPACITY**

***“be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has”*** deepens knowledge and physical capacity. The people asked how Ṭālūt could rule when he had not been given abundant wealth. The response corrects the belief that money proves wisdom or entitlement. Wealth can support administration, but it can also corrupt judgement, attract flatterers, and make a leader dependent upon the interests of the rich. A leader should be provided lawful resources to fulfil the office, but personal abundance is not the same as public competence. The poor should not be excluded from responsibility merely because they lack inherited wealth, and the wealthy should not assume that their property gives them a right to rule. Allah has chosen him over you refers to the particular divine appointment in this narrative. It does not give every ruler permission to claim that his power is directly chosen by Allah and therefore beyond criticism. Human leaders remain accountable, and the Qur’an commands justice, consultation, and fulfilment of trusts. A community must examine qualifications and hold its leaders accountable. The story teaches the people to overcome selfish criteria, not to surrender all discernment. In other contexts, Muslims select leaders through consultation and lawful public processes, while every authority is bound by Allah’s moral limits. The people had asked for a king to organize the defence of their homes, but they resisted the prophet’s choice because of status and wealth. The test reveals that they wanted victory on their own terms. (42:38 — **“who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation,”**) Since wealth is not the main qualification follows leadership is a trust from allah, knowledge and physical capacity links purpose to wealth is not the main qualification.

**WEALTH IS NOT THE MAIN QUALIFICATION**

***“not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed”*** clarifies wealth is not the main qualification. True obedience accepts a qualified leader even when he is not socially impressive, provided the appointment is lawful and the leader acts within justice. The following verse gives a sign confirming Ṭālūt’s kingship, and the later verses test whether the people will obey his command at the river. Leadership is therefore established through evidence and then tested through practice. Allah is Wāsiʿ, All-Encompassing, and ʿAlīm, All-Knowing. His gifts are not limited by the narrow criteria people use. He knows which person can bear a trust, what a community needs, and what hidden consequences follow a choice. His vastness also means that leadership is not a scarce honour that must be monopolized by one family. A believer should ask Allah to appoint people of knowledge, strength, justice, and mercy, while avoiding envy when responsibility is given to someone else. Leadership is a burden before it is an honour. Knowledge and strength require character. Without honesty, knowledge becomes manipulation; without mercy, strength becomes oppression. The Prophet ﷺ taught that authority is a trust and that a person who seeks it out of ambition may be left to himself. A leader should be chosen for service, not for the ability to collect praise. Citizens and followers also have duties: obeying lawful commands, offering sincere counsel, refusing corruption, and not treating the leader as infallible. The story’s lesson concerns both the qualities of leadership and the heart’s response to it. (2:246 — **“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”**) Choosing a king beyond wealth matters, which means wealth is not the main qualification returns choosing a king beyond wealth to leadership is a trust from allah.

**CHOOSING A KING BEYOND WEALTH**

***“him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.””*** closes with choosing a king beyond wealth. Think of leadership is a trust from allah through a village that needs a new keeper for the communal well and chooses the man who carries the heaviest buckets, though he owns no land and speaks in a slow voice. The well is kept for thirty years, and the village remembers the year they argued about the man before they remembered the water. Leadership is a trust from allah confronts anyone treating knowledge and physical capacity as remote; under leadership is a trust from allah, such a person has been passed over for a post in his own town because his family is small and his purse is light. The verse gives him a king taken from the trades, a kingdom that is given rather than earned, and two reasons from God rather than from men, and it asks him which ledger he reads when he measures a person. Because the close names the Bountiful and the Knowing, knowledge and physical capacity makes leadership is a trust from allah show that the worth of the man is hidden in the hand that made him. The coming of the ark is promised as the sign of the appointment in the verse that follows. And the same freedom in the giving of a kingdom is seen in the story of the two armies. (28:26 — **“One of the two daughters suggested, “O my dear father! Hire him.”**) Knowledge and physical capacity makes leadership is a trust from allah practical; wealth is not the main qualification therefore matters. Today, leadership should be weighed through knowledge, capacity, character, and public trust rather than wealth, family name, or spectacle.

---

## Verse 2:248

> Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”

**A SIGN FOR A DOUBTING COMMUNITY**

***“Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the”*** establishes a sign for a doubting community. The people had objected to Ṭālūt’s appointment because he lacked wealth and expected lineage. Their prophet then gave a sign: the tābūt, the Ark or chest associated with the Children of Israel, would return to them. The sign confirmed that the appointment was from Allah rather than a personal claim by Ṭālūt. The Qur’an does not require believers to accept every leader who claims divine support. In this specific story, a prophet announced a sign from Allah, and the sign was part of the revealed test. Later communities must judge leadership through sound evidence, justice, consultation, and lawful process. No modern political object can simply be identified with the Ark without proof. The Ark carried relics from the family of Mūsā and Hārūn. Transmitted reports describe the contents as including remnants of tablets, the staff of Mūsā, and other sacred items, but the Qur’an does not specify every object. The believer affirms what Allah stated and does not turn uncertain historical reports into creed. The relics reminded Banū Isrāʾīl of revelation, prophetic guidance, and Allah’s past favour. Their value was not magical power independent of Allah. Sacred objects can serve as reminders when Allah gives them a role, but worship and ultimate reliance belong to Allah alone. (48:4 — **“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they”**) Because a sign for a doubting community frames the ark and the sacred relics, the ark and the sacred relics returns attention to a sign for a doubting community.

**THE ARK AND THE SACRED RELICS**

***“Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the”*** deepens the ark and the sacred relics. The Companions loved and preserved things connected with the Prophet ﷺ, and authentic hadith in separate reports preserved by al-Bukhārī and Muslim record their respect for his hair, water, and clothing. Such reports concern the exceptional blessing of the Prophet’s tangible relics and cannot be used to justify superstition, trafficking in alleged relics, or attributing independent power to objects. The Ark carried sakīnah, tranquillity and settled reassurance from Allah. Sakīnah is not merely a pleasant emotion. It is a divine gift that steadies the heart when fear, disagreement, and uncertainty are intense. The community needed more than a political symbol; it needed inner certainty that the defence ahead was under Allah’s care. Allah sends tranquillity to believers in other situations, especially when hearts are tested. It may appear as patience, clarity, unity, and courage rather than the removal of every danger. Ṭālūt’s army would still face a river and a formidable enemy, but sakīnah would help the sincere obey. The Ark was carried by angels. This is part of the unseen that Allah disclosed. The angels act by Allah’s command and do not possess independent power. Their presence turns the return of the Ark into a sign from the Lord, not a political recovery achieved only through human skill. (2:246 — **“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”**) Since sakīnah from the lord follows a sign for a doubting community, the ark and the sacred relics links purpose to sakīnah from the lord.

**SAKĪNAH FROM THE LORD**

***“family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the”*** clarifies sakīnah from the lord. Muslims affirm the existence and work of angels without imagining their nature beyond revelation. The lesson is that Allah can support a community through means it does not expect. Human beings should use ordinary means while remaining open to the unseen wisdom of Allah. The verse ends, if you are believers. A sign benefits the person who is willing to believe and obey. The same event can be dismissed by a person whose heart is committed to pride. The Israelites had asked for evidence, but the real test was whether they would submit after evidence arrived. Believers should not demand miracles as a condition for every command. Allah has given the Qur’an, the prophetic model, creation, conscience, and historical signs. When a clear proof is established, the servant acts instead of continually moving the standard of evidence. The Ark connects present leadership with prophetic history. A community can receive a new leader without abandoning its past; it remembers the revelation and relics that shaped it. But memory must produce obedience, not nostalgia. The people needed to follow Ṭālūt in the present, not merely admire the history of Mūsā and Hārūn. Muslims likewise honour the Prophet ﷺ and the early generations by following their faith and character rather than turning names, objects, or historical sites into substitutes for obedience. (8:11 — **“˹Remember˺ when He caused drowsiness to overcome you, giving you serenity.”**) Angels and the unseen matters, which means sakīnah from the lord returns angels and the unseen to a sign for a doubting community.

**ANGELS AND THE UNSEEN**

***“angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.””*** closes with angels and the unseen. Think of a sign for a doubting community through a family that loses its father's ring in a flood and finds it years later in the silt of the garden. The ring is the same ring, the ground is the same ground, and the year it was found is remembered as the year the family began to speak to one another again. A sign for a doubting community confronts anyone treating the ark and the sacred relics as remote; under a sign for a doubting community, such a person has lost a good thing and decided that God has finished with him and his house. The verse gives him a chest returned to a people who had given it up, and a sign for a doubting community asks what he would do if the lost thing came back carried by hands he could not see. Because the close names the belief of the watcher, the ark and the sacred relics makes a sign for a doubting community show that the mercy often arrives before the faith that reads it. The test by the river is set out in the verse after this one. And the answer of the few who trusted is kept in their prayer at the field. (16:49 — **“And to Allah ˹alone˺ bows down ˹in submission˺ whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on”**) The ark and the sacred relics makes a sign for a doubting community practical; sakīnah from the lord therefore matters. Today, claims about sacred relics and supernatural political signs require evidence, while reassurance remains a gift sought from Allah alone.

---

## Verse 2:249

> When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”

**THE RIVER AS A TEST**

***“When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and”*** establishes the river as a test. Ṭālūt’s army was tested by a river before facing Jālūt, known in the biblical tradition as Goliath. The command was simple: do not drink from the river except a permitted handful. The test was not about the water’s nutrition alone. It measured discipline, trust, and the ability to obey a clear instruction when thirst and fatigue made disobedience attractive. A community preparing for a difficult responsibility needs more than numbers. It needs people who can restrain immediate appetite for a higher purpose. The river revealed that many who had promised to fight were not ready to govern their desires. Whoever drinks from it is not of me means that the disobedient person is not counted among those who follow Ṭālūt in this test and mission. It does not automatically mean that every drinker became an unbeliever or left Islam. Qur’anic and prophetic language can describe a person as not belonging to a group in obedience, excellence, or method without declaring him outside the faith. The exception of the handful shows that the command was not irrational deprivation. A small amount was allowed to meet need. The test required restraint, not self-harm. This is a general principle: obedience is measured within the limits Allah gives, and lawful concessions should not be treated as weakness. (2:153 — **“O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient”**) Because the river as a test frames not of me, not of me returns attention to the river as a test. An account from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the army’s thirst and the river as a test that separated those able to continue from those ruled by immediate appetite.

**NOT OF ME**

***“whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he”*** deepens not of me. Most of the army drank, leaving only a few who obeyed. Numbers can create confidence, but they cannot replace sincerity. A large group may be vulnerable to panic, peer pressure, and immediate desire, while a small group may possess discipline and certainty. The few who remained should not become arrogant. Their success was by Allah’s permission, and they still had to face fear. The story praises faithful perseverance, not contempt for people who struggled. In a community, those who are stronger should teach and support the weak rather than celebrate their failure. Even after obeying and crossing the river, the believers said they lacked strength against Jālūt and his army. Obedience does not remove natural fear. A person may do the right thing and still feel inadequate before a large challenge. Faith does not require pretending to be invulnerable. Their honest admission allows the people of certainty to answer with perspective. They do not deny the size of the enemy; they place it beneath Allah’s power. A small group can overcome a large group by Allah’s permission, but this is not a promise that every small force wins or a licence to ignore strategy. It is a call to trust while taking responsible means. Those certain that they will meet Allah possess yaqīn. (2:246 — **“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”**) Since the majority fails the test follows the river as a test, not of me links purpose to the majority fails the test.

**THE MAJORITY FAILS THE TEST**

***“and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain”*** clarifies the majority fails the test. Belief in the final meeting changes the scale of fear. The enemy may threaten the body, but Allah controls the final destiny. The person who remembers resurrection is less likely to betray truth for temporary safety, though he remains responsible for preserving life and avoiding reckless risk. Certainty also produces accountability. Victory does not make a person righteous if he fought for pride, and defeat does not make a sincere person a failure. Allah judges intention, conduct, and patience. The statement Allah is with the patient echoes 2:153. Divine companionship is support, guidance, and reward. It does not mean the patient never thirsts, fears, or loses companions. It means that endurance under obedience is seen and strengthened. Ṣabr here includes restraint before the battle, courage after fear, and continuing to obey when the crowd has withdrawn. It also includes not insulting the majority or allowing victory to produce cruelty. Ṭālūt’s leadership required a test that exposed capacity. A commander must know the difference between a real need and uncontrolled indulgence. The people also needed to trust a lawful command rather than debate every instruction while the enemy approached. In modern life, disciplined communities use training, clear procedures, nutrition, rest, and consultation. The river story is not a command to create arbitrary hardships for followers. (3:139 — **“Do not falter or grieve, for you will have the upper hand, if you are ˹true˺ believers”**) Fear after crossing matters, which means the majority fails the test returns fear after crossing to the river as a test.

**FEAR AFTER CROSSING**

***“they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.””*** closes with fear after crossing. Leaders who impose needless deprivation or test people for vanity are not imitating Ṭālūt’s wisdom. Think of the river as a test through a caravan that sets out on a hard road where the rule is one cup of water at each well, and half the travellers drink from the skins they were told to carry unopened. The wells are still ahead of them, the road is still long, and the ones who arrive are the ones who trusted the instruction more than the thirst. The river as a test confronts anyone treating not of me as remote; under the river as a test, such a person has counted the numbers in his own quarrel and decided that nothing can be done. The verse gives him a river, a crowd that drank and a few who crossed, and it asks him which company he would have been standing in that morning. Because the close names the steadfast as the ones with God, not of me makes the river as a test show that the strength of a person is measured before the battle and not after it. The prayer of the two companies before the battle is kept in the verse that follows, and the two armies are described again in another chapter. (8:45 — **“O believers! When you face an enemy, stand firm and remember Allah often so you may triumph”**) Not of me makes the river as a test practical; the majority fails the test therefore matters.

## Verse 2:250

> When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**THE SUPPLICATION OF A SMALL ARMY**

***“When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they”*** establishes the supplication of a small army. After the river test reduced the army and fear arose at the sight of Jālūt’s force, the believers turned to Allah. Their prayer contains three requests: an abundance of patience, firmness of feet, and help against the hostile force. They do not claim that their own courage is sufficient. They ask for the inner and outer means of steadfastness. Pour upon us patience—afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabran—is an image of patience filling and covering them. They know that they need more than a brief burst of courage. Fear, fatigue, grief, and uncertainty can return repeatedly. The servant asks Allah to make patience abundant enough for the full trial. Make our feet firm refers literally to standing in battle and metaphorically to remaining firm in faith, discipline, and moral conduct. A person may have physical courage but lose his principles under pressure. The believers ask for both kinds of stability. Firmness does not mean refusing to retreat when retreat is strategically necessary or remaining in a position that guarantees pointless destruction. It means not abandoning the lawful objective through panic, betrayal, or uncontrolled flight. (90:17 — **“and—above all—to be one of those who have faith and urge each other to perseverance and urge”**) Because the supplication of a small army frames firm feet, firm feet returns attention to the supplication of a small army. An account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās takes the prayer as a request for patience, firmness in the field, and victory over Goliath’s forces.

**FIRM FEET**

***“prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our”*** deepens firm feet. Sound strategy can include movement, regrouping, negotiation, or withdrawal when these serve protection and justice. Help us against the disbelieving people does not turn the enemy into a dehumanized category. The prayer concerns the hostile army that is actively confronting them. The Qur’an commands justice even toward opponents and forbids transgression. Victory is requested so that aggression may end and the community may worship safely, not so that hatred can be satisfied. The believers understand that causes matter but are not independent. Training, numbers, leadership, weapons, and planning are means; Allah gives them effect. Reliance upon Him does not excuse neglecting preparation, and preparation does not make Allah unnecessary. The order of the scene is instructive. The believers do not pray as a substitute for action; they pray before and during responsible action. Supplication aligns the heart with Allah, purifies intention, and protects against arrogance. A person who asks Allah for help should also ask whether his cause, means, and conduct are just. The Prophet ﷺ made supplication in battle, consulted his Companions, arranged the ranks, and took practical precautions. His example rejects both magical thinking and materialist self-reliance. (2:249 — **“When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river.”**) Since help belongs to allah follows the supplication of a small army, firm feet links purpose to help belongs to allah.

**HELP BELONGS TO ALLAH**

***“steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.””*** clarifies help belongs to allah. The prayer is in the plural. A community under pressure needs shared patience. Individuals support one another by speaking truthfully, sharing resources, caring for the wounded, and avoiding rumours that spread panic. Leaders should not demand patience while hiding information or wasting lives through vanity. The strongest person may need support, and the apparently weak person may give the word that steadies the group. The Qur’an praises believers who encourage one another to patience and mercy. The prayer applies beyond armed conflict. A student facing examinations, a family enduring illness, a community resisting corruption, and a person leaving addiction can ask Allah for patience, firm feet, and help against the forces that pull him away from obedience. The enemy may include fear, desire, injustice, or Satan’s whispering, though the believer must not turn ordinary people into symbolic enemies without reason. The supplication also teaches the correct order of priorities: seek patience before asking for victory. Without patience, success can be corrupted by pride; with patience, even a difficult result can become a means of reward. Think of the supplication of a small army through a farmer who asks the sky for rain in the morning and spends the afternoon digging the channel through which it will run. (3:123 — **“Indeed, Allah made you victorious at Badr when you were ˹vastly˺ outnumbered. So be mindful of Allah,”**) Prayer before action matters, which means help belongs to allah returns prayer before action to the supplication of a small army.

**PRAYER BEFORE ACTION**

The rain comes, the channel carries it to the roots, and the field that is watered is the one with the trench. The supplication of a small army reaches a reader today who stands before a hard task and asks only for the result. The verse gives him three requests in the order of a battle, the heart and the feet before the crown, and the supplication of a small army uses firm feet to ask which choice he has been praying for. Because the men who prayed were the ones who had kept their hands from the river, the supplication of a small army teaches that a prayer of this kind is made by a person who has already obeyed. The next verse preserves the prayer’s answer. And the men are remembered with the steadfast in the same story. Firm feet makes the supplication of a small army practical; help belongs to allah therefore matters.

## Verse 2:251

> So they defeated them by Allah’s Will, and David killed Goliath. And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all

**VICTORY BY ALLAH’S PERMISSION**

***“So they defeated them by Allah’s Will, and David killed Goliath. And”*** establishes victory by allah’s permission. The small believing group defeated the larger force by Allah’s permission. This phrase does not deny human effort. The believers obeyed, endured, planned, and fought under Ṭālūt’s leadership. It means that causes do not operate independently of Allah, and success is not proof that the victorious are entitled to pride or that every victorious cause was just. The same principle protects believers after defeat. A sincere community may lose worldly battles without losing Allah’s favour. The measure is obedience, justice, and patience, not numbers or immediate results. Victory can be a test of gratitude and defeat a test of perseverance. David—Dāwūd—killed Jālūt, the champion of the opposing army. The Qur’an mentions the decisive event without glorifying physical strength alone. David was part of a community under lawful leadership and a just cause. His victory illustrates how Allah can bring relief through a person whose apparent resources are small. The Qur’an later describes David as a prophet, worshipper, judge, and leader. His story therefore continues beyond battlefield success. A person who defeats an enemy but cannot control his own ego has not reached the wisdom Allah gave David. Allah gave David mulk, authority or kingship, and ḥikmah, wisdom. Authority without wisdom becomes oppression, while wisdom without the ability to protect people may be unable to restrain aggression. David’s example joins competence with moral judgement. (38:26 — **“˹We instructed him:˺ “O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land,”**) A report on victory by allah’s permission comes through Ibn ʿAbbās, who identified David as the one who killed Goliath before receiving kingship, wisdom, prophethood, and knowledge of armour-making.

**DAVID AND GOLIATH**

***“Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed.”*** deepens david and goliath. He is later commanded to judge between people with truth and not follow desire. This is an important leadership principle. A ruler, judge, or community leader needs knowledge of revelation, understanding of circumstances, courage, consultation, and self-restraint. The possession of power is not a sign of personal holiness. It becomes a trust measured by justice. Allah taught David what He willed, including judgement, revelation, and skills useful for public welfare. The wording preserves humility: knowledge is granted according to Allah’s will, and no human being possesses all knowledge. A leader should continue learning and consult people with expertise rather than assuming that authority has made him infallible. The Prophet ﷺ praised useful skills and lawful work. The Qur’an later describes David making armour, and authentic hadith say that he ate from the work of his own hands. A righteous leader can combine worship, craftsmanship, administration, and service. If Allah did not repel some people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted. This is a general statement about Allah placing checks upon tyranny. He may protect the vulnerable through a just ruler, a courageous witness, a community organization, a court, or people who resist oppression. Without any restraint, powerful groups could consume the weak without consequence. The verse does not make all conflict beneficial. Human beings must seek peaceful solutions when possible, defend the innocent, and avoid transgression. (2:246 — **“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”**)

**KINGSHIP AND WISDOM**

***“Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another,”*** clarifies kingship and wisdom. The repelling can include law, mediation, public accountability, and nonviolent resistance as well as lawful defence. The principle is the preservation of justice, not a celebration of violence. Allah’s bounty is to all worlds—al-ʿālamīn. His gifts include life, guidance, opportunities for reform, and the means by which oppression is checked. A victorious community should recognize that its power is a gift and use it to establish justice, protect minorities, feed the poor, and end revenge. David’s later story contains warnings about judgement and desire. Even a prophet with authority must remain humble before Allah. Political success does not suspend accountability. The real victory is not merely killing the enemy champion. It is preserving faith, protecting people, and developing a just society afterward. A community that wins a battle and then loots, enslaves, or oppresses has converted victory into corruption. The believer asks Allah for victory over the ego as well as protection from external aggression. The Prophet ﷺ taught that true strength lies in controlling anger. This inner victory is essential for anyone given power over others. Think of victory by allah’s permission through a town that raises a small guard on the bridge because the river beyond it is full of rival traders, and that sleeps behind the guard for a hundred years. The bridge is guarded by men, and the peace it keeps is the mercy of a Lord who checks one people with another. (38:17 — **“Be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say. And remember Our servant, David, the man of strength.”**)

**TAUGHT WHAT ALLAH WILLED**

***“corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all”*** closes with taught what allah willed. Victory by allah’s permission confronts david and goliath in a reader who believes that his own strength is the only wall between his house and the world. The verse gives him a small company, a sling that ended a giant, a crown given to a shepherd and a mercy that holds the nations apart. And it asks him who is keeping the world from falling while he sleeps. Because the close names the grace that reaches all, showing through victory by allah’s permission that the quiet street he lives in is one of the gifts he never paid for. The story of the two armies is closed with a sentence about the signs, where the Book calls the whole narrative a proof of the message. And the same law of the repelling of peoples is stated in the chapter of the pilgrimage. Because victory by allah’s permission opens into david and goliath, kingship and wisdom joins victory by allah’s permission to david and goliath. Since kingship and wisdom develops victory by allah’s permission, david and goliath carries the transition. Taught what allah willed matters, which means kingship and wisdom answers david and goliath. David and goliath gives practical form to victory by allah’s permission; taught what allah willed sets its horizon. Today, victory by allah’s permission shapes david and goliath in present decisions. (34:10 — **“Indeed, We granted David a ˹great˺ privilege from Us, ˹commanding:˺ “O mountains! Echo his hymns!”**)

## Verse 2:252

> These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers

**HISTORY AS REVELATION**

***“These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O”*** establishes history as revelation. After recounting the story of the Children of Israel, Ṭālūt, David, and Jālūt, Allah declares that these are His revelations recited in truth. The account is not folklore assembled for entertainment or a political myth invented by the Prophet ﷺ. It is revelation that corrects, selects, and interprets history for moral guidance. The Qur’an often tells earlier stories without providing every chronological detail. Its purpose is not to satisfy every historical curiosity but to show Allah’s power, the consequences of fear and arrogance, and the qualities required of a community. The omission of unnecessary detail preserves the lesson from being buried under trivia. Truth here belongs to both the revelation’s source and its faithful message. Allah knows what happened in the past, and He reveals what humanity needs to know. The story teaches that leadership is a trust, numbers do not guarantee victory, patience is essential, and Allah can restrain corruption through people who obey Him. Truth also means that the stories are presented without tribal propaganda. Banū Isrāʾīl are neither praised as a race nor condemned as a race. The Qur’an acknowledges their prophets and righteous individuals while exposing disobedience. A community’s honour depends on faith and conduct, not ancestry. Think of history as revelation through a man who reads the letters his grandfather wrote from a war he never saw, and who finds his own name in the last line of the third page. (2:246 — **“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”**) A reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās takes these revelations as the Qur’an’s truthful account of earlier nations, carried to the Messenger through Gabriel.

**IN TRUTH**

***“Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers”*** deepens in truth. The battles are old, the ink is brown, and the letter is addressed to him. History as revelation confronts in truth in a reader who reads the old stories as curiosities and turns the page. The verse gives him a whole narrative called a revelation and a messenger called one of the messengers, and the rule carried by 2 252 asks what he has done with what he has read. Because the sentence ends on the truth of the recitation, the rule carried by 2 252 teaches that a story in this Book is a message with an address on it. Since the whole passage was recited to a messenger rather than written for a library, the reader sees that the lesson of the story is meant for the one who hears it. The ranks of the messengers are opened in the following āyah; the rule carried by 2 252 also the greatest of the revelations of that chapter is named a little later. Because history as revelation opens into in truth, the rule carried by 2 252 joins history as revelation to in truth. Since the rule carried by 2 252 develops history as revelation, in truth carries the transition. The lasting horizon of 2 252 matters, which means the rule carried by 2 252 answers in truth. In truth gives practical form to history as revelation; the lasting horizon of 2 252 sets its horizon. (3:44 — **“This is news of the unseen that We reveal to you ˹O Prophet˺.”**)

**THE RULE CARRIED BY 2 252**

Today, history as revelation shapes in truth in present decisions. History as revelation stays bound to the rule carried by 2 252 because in truth supplies the human setting of history as revelation. The lasting horizon of 2 252 carries history as revelation into conduct shaped by the rule carried by 2 252. This declaration also authenticates the Messenger who conveys the account. He did not witness the ancient battle, consult its surviving soldiers, or inherit its details from his own people. Receiving a truthful account of it is therefore part of the sign of revelation. Yet the proof is not offered as bare information: it asks the hearer to recognize the same Lord who guided the earlier community and now guides this one. Historical truth creates present responsibility. If Allah’s recitation exposes cowardice, pride, patience, and faithful courage in an earlier people, the later reader must examine those qualities in himself. The story remains living guidance precisely because its truth comes from the One who knows every generation.

## Verse 2:253

> We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills

**ALL MESSENGERS ARE HONOURED**

***“We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank.”*** establishes all messengers are honoured. The verse says that Allah favoured some messengers over others while Muslims are required to believe in all of them. Preference in rank does not permit insulting or rejecting any prophet. Allah gave each messenger a distinct mission, sign, community, and degree of honour, and He alone knows the full wisdom of those distinctions. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught that no Muslim should demean one prophet to elevate another. He described the prophets as brothers in one faith, and he described himself as nearest to Jesus son of Mary across earthly life and the final return, according to reports collected by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Honour is therefore joined to continuity, not rivalry. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke refers especially to Mūsā, who is called Kalīm Allāh, the one to whom Allah spoke. The manner of divine speech is affirmed as befits Allah’s majesty, without imagining a human voice, organ, or physical limitation. The verse is a sign of the different honours Allah granted His messengers. This distinction never denies that every prophet received revelation. All received revelation through the means Allah chose. It means that Allah gave some a distinctive mode or degree of communication. Believers affirm the report and leave the modality to Allah. Some messengers were raised in degrees—rafaʿa baʿḍahum darajāt. The highest rank belongs to those Allah identified as especially favoured, including the messengers of firm resolve, and the final messenger Muhammad ﷺ holds the comprehensive mission to humanity. (3:49 — **“and ˹make him˺ a messenger to the Children of Israel ˹to proclaim,”**)

**ALLAH SPOKE TO SOME**

***“To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had”*** deepens allah spoke to some. The exact ranking is known fully to Allah, and human beings should not turn it into a competition that leads to disrespect. Rank before Allah is accompanied by responsibility. A higher degree means a greater burden of conveyance, patience, and leadership. The believer should not seek honour merely for status; he asks for the ability to fulfil the trust given to him. Allah gave ʿĪsā clear signs, including his birth without a father, speaking in infancy, healing by Allah’s permission, and other miracles described in 3:49 and 5:110. These signs prove his prophethood; they do not make him divine. The repeated phrase by Allah’s permission protects tawḥīd and places the miracle within the power of the Creator. He was supported by the Rūḥ al-Qudus, commonly understood as the angel Jibrīl, the Holy Spirit. The Qur’an also describes revelation as a spirit that gives life to hearts. The verse’s immediate meaning concerns divine support for Jesus in his mission, while the broader lesson is that messengers are strengthened by means beyond ordinary human resources. After clear proofs came, later communities still fought and differed. The problem was not that revelation had failed to clarify everything; human beings brought desire, envy, power, and group loyalty into their response. Some believed and some disbelieved. Clear evidence does not force a person who is determined to protect his interest. The verse distinguishes the existence of disagreement from the moral cause of disagreement. (5:110 — **“And ˹on Judgment Day˺ Allah will say, “O Jesus, son of Mary!”**)

**DEGREES OF RANK**

***“willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while”*** clarifies degrees of rank. Honest scholarly difference is not the same as rejecting a clear proof out of hostility. The Qur’an elsewhere praises those who differ while seeking the truth and condemns those whose division is driven by transgression. Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another affirms Allah’s power. He could have compelled all people into one outward pattern, but He allowed a world in which moral choice, obedience, rebellion, and testing occur. His allowing an action does not mean that He loves the action or excuses the person who commits it. The final phrase, Allah does what He wills, does not cancel responsibility. The Qur’an repeatedly commands people to believe, choose justice, and avoid oppression. Divine decree encompasses human choices, while human beings are accountable for what they knowingly choose and do. The verse does not teach that believers should unite by pretending every belief is identical. The messengers share tawḥīd, and Muslims affirm the distinct revelations and laws Allah gave. Unity means returning to truth and justice, not suppressing clear differences or turning them into hatred. A Muslim can honour Jesus, Moses, and their followers while remaining firm that worship belongs to Allah alone and that Muhammad ﷺ is the final messenger. Conviction and respect coexist. Think of all messengers are honoured through a teacher who spends a year explaining one chapter to a class and finds in the examination that half of them heard the words and half of them heard the lesson. (2:252 — **“These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth.”**)

**JESUS AND THE HOLY SPIRIT**

***“others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills”*** closes with jesus and the holy spirit. The bell rings, the papers go home, and the year of teaching is the same year for the whole room. All messengers are honoured confronts allah spoke to some in a reader who has become bitter because his family did not accept what he knows to be true. The verse gives him generations who fought by a choice rather than by a knowledge, and it asks him whether the quarrel of other people is his to settle. Because the close puts the matter in the will of the Lord, degrees of rank teaches that a man is asked for the plain word and not for the outcome of it. The next āyah turns belief toward spending, while another sūrah recalls the clear proofs granted to Jesus. Because all messengers are honoured opens into allah spoke to some, degrees of rank joins all messengers are honoured to allah spoke to some. Since degrees of rank develops all messengers are honoured, allah spoke to some carries the transition. Jesus and the holy spirit matters, which means degrees of rank answers allah spoke to some. Allah spoke to some gives practical form to all messengers are honoured; jesus and the holy spirit sets its horizon. Today, all messengers are honoured shapes allah spoke to some in present decisions. (3:45 — **“˹Remember˺ when the angels proclaimed, “O Mary! Allah gives you good news of a Word from Him,”**)
