## Verse 2:254

> O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers

**SPEND BEFORE THE FINAL DAY**

***“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before”*** establishes spend before the final day. The believers are told to spend from Allah’s provision before the Day of Resurrection arrives. Wealth is a trust and an opportunity whose usefulness ends at death, while the reward of how it was used remains. The command includes zakāh, support for dependants, voluntary charity, relief, and every lawful expenditure that fulfils Allah’s rights and the rights of people. From what We have provided corrects the illusion of absolute ownership. A person earns through work, but his life, ability, resources, opportunities, and the natural world that sustains him are all gifts from Allah. Spending becomes gratitude when it is lawful, sincere, and directed toward benefit. On that Day there will be no bayʿ, no trade or bargaining by which a person can purchase escape. A person cannot offer wealth after death to erase a life of refusal. The Qur’an repeatedly warns that ransom will not be accepted once the final judgement has arrived. This does not mean that all worldly transactions are bad. Lawful trade is permitted, and honest business can be worship. The warning concerns treating the Hereafter as a market that can be negotiated after the opportunity for deeds has ended. The wise person makes the investment now. There will be no khullah, intimate friendship or alliance that can save a person independently of Allah. Family, political connections, popularity, and proximity to a respected leader cannot replace faith and righteous action. (3:91 — **“Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of”**)

**NO BARGAINING**

***“the arrival of a Day when there will be no”*** deepens no bargaining. This does not deny the emotional value of friendship in the world or the benefit of righteous companionship. It denies the belief that a created relationship can override Allah’s judgement. The Prophet ﷺ warned his closest relatives to save themselves through faith and deeds, showing that lineage cannot substitute for obedience, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim record. A believer loves family and friends by encouraging them toward good, not by promising a rescue he does not control. The verse does not deny every form of intercession. Other Qur’anic passages establish that intercession occurs only by Allah’s permission and for those with whom He is pleased. No prophet, angel, saint, or ancestor intercedes independently or can be invoked as a power alongside Allah. The correct response is to seek Allah’s mercy directly, follow His Messenger ﷺ, and hope in the intercession He grants. This protects tawḥīd from both denying revealed intercession and turning created beings into objects of worship. The command to spend is urgent because wealth can disappear through death, illness, economic change, or sudden disaster. More importantly, the chance to earn reward ends when the soul departs. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a person’s wealth is truly what he sends ahead through charity, while the remainder belongs to heirs, as al-Bukhārī records. This urgency must be balanced with responsibility. The believer supports family, pays debts, and avoids waste. He does not give in a way that makes dependants beg, but he does not let fear turn provision into an idol. (57:15 — **“So Today no ransom will be accepted from you ˹hypocrites˺, nor from the disbelievers.”**)

**NO FRIENDSHIP AS A SUBSTITUTE FOR FAITH**

***“bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers”*** clarifies no friendship as a substitute for faith. The disbelievers are the wrongdoers identifies the theological injustice of rejecting Allah’s ownership and the practical injustice of withholding rights while relying on wealth and connections. The statement concerns those who persist in disbelief, not a licence to treat all non-Muslims unjustly. Muslims must still act with kindness and justice toward peaceful people of other faiths. A believer should also fear forms of wrongdoing within his own life. One may affirm Islam but wrong people through hoarding, fraud, unpaid wages, or refusal to support dependants. The verse’s moral warning reaches anyone who treats Allah’s provision as a private entitlement without accountability. Spending purifies attachment. The person who gives does not become poorer in the ultimate account. He learns reliance, compassion, and gratitude. Charity should be protected from showing off, reminders, and injury to the recipient. The Prophet ﷺ described hidden charity among the deeds receiving special protection on the Day of Resurrection, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim record. Quiet giving is not the only valid form, but privacy often protects sincerity. Think of spend before the final day through a traveller who plans to buy the tickets for the whole family at the border because the queue at home is long. The gates close in the evening, the queue at the border is longer, and the money in his pocket buys nothing after the last bell. Spend before the final day confronts no bargaining in a reader who intends to settle his accounts with his Lord when he has a little more capital. (20:109 — **“On that Day no intercession will be of any benefit,”**)

**INTERCESSION BELONGS TO ALLAH**

The verse gives him a day with no bargaining and no intercession, and it asks him when he thinks the open market will close. Because the sentence about the wrongdoers follows the command so closely, showing through spend before the final day that the belief in the heart reaches the hand in the end. The earlier command of the fighting stands a little above this verse, and the greatest verse of the chapter follows it. The reader of the three together sees a chapter that moves from the field to the purse and from the purse to the seat of the Lord. Because spend before the final day opens into no bargaining, no friendship as a substitute for faith joins spend before the final day to no bargaining. Since no friendship as a substitute for faith develops spend before the final day, no bargaining carries the transition. Intercession belongs to allah matters, which means no friendship as a substitute for faith answers no bargaining. No bargaining gives practical form to spend before the final day; intercession belongs to allah sets its horizon. Today, spend before the final day shapes no bargaining in present decisions.

## Verse 2:255

> Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest

**THE SUPREME VERSE**

***“Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is”*** establishes the supreme verse. This āyah is known as Āyat al-Kursī, the Verse of the Footstool. It gathers the foundations of tawḥīd, Allah’s perfect life, sustaining authority, knowledge, ownership, permission, power, and transcendence. The verse moves from the declaration of divine oneness to the negation of every weakness and then to the affirmation of Allah’s complete dominion. The Prophet ﷺ told Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that it is the greatest verse in the Book of Allah, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. Its greatness is not a magical property detached from understanding. It is great because it gives the heart a complete vision of who Allah is and why no created rival deserves worship. Allah is al-Ḥayy, the Ever-Living. His life is perfect, beginningless and everlasting, and unlike created life it is not dependent upon food, rest, time, or bodily processes. He is al-Qayyūm, the One who sustains Himself and sustains everything else. Every creature depends upon Him at every moment, while He depends upon no one. This pair of names gives the believer security. Human protectors tire, forget, die, or become unable to help. Allah never loses awareness or power. The servant can turn to Him in the night, in fear, poverty, illness, and confusion, knowing that the Sustainer is always living and never absent. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. Human beings require rest because their bodies and minds are limited. Allah is not overcome by weakness, inattention, or fatigue. He does not need sleep in order to recover, and no moment of creation falls outside His care. The statement is also a spiritual comfort. When every human helper is unavailable, Allah remains aware. He hears the hidden prayer, sees the injustice that no court noticed, and preserves the universe without strain. (20:109 — **“On that Day no intercession will be of any benefit,”**)

**ALLAH IS AL-ḤAYY AND AL-QAYYŪM**

***“in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is”*** deepens allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm. The believer sleeps after taking lawful means because he trusts the Guardian who never sleeps. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. The phrase encompasses people, angels, animals, matter, wealth, power, and every visible and unseen realm. Human beings possess property only by delegated permission. This is why wealth must be earned lawfully, spent responsibly, and returned through charity and inheritance. Ownership also means that no created ruler has absolute authority. Governments, families, employers, and scholars exercise limited trusts. They cannot command disobedience to Allah or claim ownership of people’s souls. Tawḥīd liberates the servant from treating any human power as ultimate. Who can intercede with Him except by His permission. Intercession—shafāʿah—belongs to Allah. He may honour prophets, angels, and righteous servants by allowing them to intercede, but no created being can force Allah, negotiate as an equal, or independently remove punishment. This guards the believer from both denying revealed intercession and worshipping intermediaries. The verse’s question is rhetorical: no one can intercede without permission. Believers seek Allah directly through prayer, repentance, and obedience. They also hope for the Prophet’s intercession because Allah grants it, without invoking the Prophet ﷺ as an independent divine power. Allah knows what is before and behind them—what is present, future, past, visible, hidden, and connected to their circumstances. Created beings know only what Allah teaches them. They cannot encompass His knowledge except what He wills. The verse establishes Allah’s omniscience without requiring people to imagine how His knowledge relates to time. This is a source of accountability and comfort. The hidden intention behind a charity, the pain of a widow, and the secret injustice of a powerful person are all known. (34:23 — **“No intercession will be of any benefit with Him, except by those granted permission by Him.”**)

**NO DROWSINESS AND NO SLEEP**

***“ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His”*** clarifies no drowsiness and no sleep. A person cannot hide a deed from Allah, and a sincere act cannot be lost because humans failed to notice it. Allah says His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth. The Kursī is an unseen created reality associated with Allah’s dominion. Classical reports and exegetes discuss it as a footstool distinct from the ʿArsh, the Throne. The Qur’an does not require us to imagine its form or measure it through human comparison. Affirming the verse means affirming what Allah said without likening Him to creation. The vastness of the Kursī points to the greatness of the created heavens and earth and, by implication, the immeasurable greatness of their Creator. Allah is not contained by the Kursī or by any created space. Preserving them does not tire Him. The universe is maintained without effort, weakness, or recovery. Human administrators become exhausted by a single household or institution; Allah sustains all worlds simultaneously. This refutes any idea that creation places a burden upon Him or that He needs assistants to complete His power. The statement also gives believers confidence in divine care. The laws of nature, the order of life, and the final resurrection are not difficult for Allah. What appears impossible to humans is within His effortless power. Al-ʿAliyy is the Most High, exalted above creation and every imperfection. Al-ʿAẓīm is the Most Great, possessing perfect majesty. These names complete the verse by directing worship upward in meaning: the heart honours Allah above every rival, fear, desire, and authority. Reciting Āyat al-Kursī should therefore produce humility and reliance. It is not a charm recited while a person continues to worship wealth, fame, or superstition. Its protection is realized through faith, remembrance, and obedience. (53:26 — **“˹Imagine˺ how many ˹noble˺ angels are in the heavens!”**)

**COMPLETE OWNERSHIP**

***“Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest”*** closes with complete ownership. Think of the supreme verse through a caravan that crosses a country where the guards of the road change every few miles, and one night the travellers learn that the whole route lies inside the lands of a single lord. The tents are pitched in the open, the horses are untied, and nobody in the caravan sleeps badly after the letter is read. The supreme verse confronts allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm in a reader who cannot sleep because he has measured his troubles against his own strength. The verse gives him a Lord who does not doze, a throne that covers the sky and the ground. And a knowledge that is opened by permission, and it asks him whose keeping he is relying on when he shuts his eyes. Because the close names the Most High and the Greatest, showing through the supreme verse that the night watch is kept by the One who never kept it in a hurry. The warning about the intercession is repeated with its day in the preceding āyah; the supreme verse also the call of a messenger who was sent to the whole world comes in another chapter. Because the supreme verse opens into allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm, no drowsiness and no sleep joins the supreme verse to allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm. Since no drowsiness and no sleep develops the supreme verse, allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm carries the transition. Complete ownership matters, which means no drowsiness and no sleep answers allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm. Allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm gives practical form to the supreme verse; complete ownership sets its horizon. Today, the supreme verse shapes allah is al-ḥayy and al-qayyūm in present decisions. (6:59 — **“With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him.”**)

## Verse 2:256

> Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**FAITH CANNOT BE FORCED**

***“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out”*** establishes faith cannot be forced. There is no compulsion in religion—lā ikrāha fī al-dīn—is a foundational Qur’anic principle. Faith is recognition, conviction, and willing submission of the heart. A person may be forced to repeat words or perform an outward action, but coercion cannot create sincere īmān. Therefore Muslims invite through truth, wisdom, character, and clear evidence rather than through forced conversion. This freedom from compulsion leaves Islam’s truth claims intact and does not make every belief equally valid. The next phrase says that the right course has become distinct from error. Islam declares guidance and misguidance to be real, while refusing to make coercion the method by which people are made to accept guidance. The Arabic rushd means right direction, maturity, and sound judgement, while ghayy means error and deviation. Revelation clarifies the difference, and people are responsible for how they respond. Freedom here is moral freedom under Allah’s knowledge, not freedom from consequences. A person may choose disbelief, but he cannot demand that Allah treat every choice as equally true in the Hereafter. The Prophet ﷺ conveyed the message, answered questions, made treaties, and lived among communities of different faiths. He did not force the People of the Book to convert. The Qur’an commands Muslims to debate in the best manner and to protect one who seeks safety. The believer must reject ṭāghūt, every false object or authority that is obeyed or worshipped in opposition to Allah. (29:46 — **“Do not argue with the People of the Book unless gracefully,”**)

**CLARITY AND FREEDOM**

***“clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah”*** deepens clarity and freedom. It includes idols, Satan, tyrannical rulers, corrupt ideologies, and any created power that claims the right to define ultimate truth independently of Allah. Rejecting ṭāghūt does not require attacking people. It means refusing worship, unjust obedience, and false claims of divinity. A person can respect a lawful government, cooperate with neighbours, and honour parents without giving them obedience in sin. The firm believer retains conscience and refuses to make any human being an absolute authority. Whoever rejects false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the firmest handhold—al-ʿurwah al-wuthqā. The image suggests a secure rope or handle that does not break. The condition has two parts: negation and affirmation. One leaves false worship and turns to Allah. Merely rejecting one idol without accepting truth leaves the heart empty; merely claiming belief while serving rivals leaves the testimony incomplete. The handhold is firm because Allah is firm, not because human faith never fluctuates. Believers may experience weakness, grief, or questions, but they return to the Qur’an, Sunnah, prayer, and repentance. Allah strengthens those who seek Him. No compulsion in religion does not forbid a Muslim community from having moral and legal norms. Every society regulates conduct to protect life, property, family, and public safety. The principle forbids forcing a person’s heart or converting religion into a tool of humiliation. Non-Muslims living under a lawful covenant retain their rights, and Muslims may not abuse them because they do not share the faith. (9:6 — **“And if anyone from the polytheists asks for your protection ˹O Prophet˺,”**)

**REJECTING THE ṬĀGHŪT**

***“has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*** clarifies rejecting the ṭāghūt. Likewise, a family cannot force a daughter or son to pretend to believe. Parents may teach, advise, and set reasonable household rules, but they cannot manufacture conviction through violence. The Prophet ﷺ said that consent matters in marriage, and the same moral seriousness applies to religious commitment. The Muslim’s duty is balāgh, clear conveyance. He explains tawḥīd, answers sincere questions, and embodies mercy. Guidance itself belongs to Allah. Coercive preaching often produces hypocrisy, resentment, or outward conformity without the heart’s submission. This principle is also relevant to intra-Muslim disagreement. A person may advise about prayer, creed, or ethics, but he should not force public declarations or accuse people’s hearts without evidence. Accountability and social protection can exist without pretending that compulsion creates faith. Allah hears the invitation, the threat, the forced statement, and the private confession of faith. He knows who genuinely believes, who speaks under coercion, who manipulates the principle to avoid accountability, and who is prevented from expressing truth. This is why final judgement cannot be delegated to ordinary people. The verse gives confidence to the believer and protection to the vulnerable. Truth is clear, but human beings must respond with justice and wisdom. Think of faith cannot be forced through a father who buys his son a shop in the market and finds in the spring that the boy has left it locked to work with the boats at the harbour. The shop stands open in the records of the town, and the work at the boats is the only trade that ever paid the household. (28:56 — **“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺,”**)

**THE FIRMEST HANDHOLD**

Faith cannot be forced confronts clarity and freedom in one present-day reader; rejecting the ṭāghūt meets, under the demand of faith cannot be forced, someone raised to treat communal religion as family honour rather than a matter of the heart. The verse gives him a command against compulsion, a plain road and a handhold that holds, and rejecting the ṭāghūt asks what he would be protecting if he forced a mind into a shape it did not choose. Because the close of faith cannot be forced identifies whoever hears and knows, showing through faith cannot be forced that the faith of a person is a trust between him and his Lord. The spending of the community is commanded just before this verse. And the Lord who keeps the heavens and the earth is named in the verse before it. Because faith cannot be forced opens into clarity and freedom, rejecting the ṭāghūt joins faith cannot be forced to clarity and freedom. Since rejecting the ṭāghūt develops faith cannot be forced, clarity and freedom carries the transition. The firmest handhold matters, which means rejecting the ṭāghūt answers clarity and freedom. Clarity and freedom gives practical form to faith cannot be forced; the firmest handhold sets its horizon. Today, faith cannot be forced shapes clarity and freedom in present decisions.

## Verse 2:257

> Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**ALLAH AS THE GUARDIAN OF BELIEVERS**

***“Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness”*** establishes allah as the guardian of believers. Allah is walī, Guardian, Protector, and intimate supporter of those who believe. His guardianship includes guidance, care, protection from spiritual confusion, forgiveness, and help in obeying Him. It does not mean that believers will experience no physical pain or worldly loss. The prophets and righteous people were tested, but Allah guarded their faith and gave their trials meaning. The believer’s first allegiance is to Allah. Family, friends, teachers, governments, and institutions can provide support, but none is an independent guardian. The heart trusts created means while relying ultimately upon Allah. This frees the servant from despair when a human helper fails and from worshipful dependence upon people. The plural darknesses—ẓulumāt—suggests many forms of confusion and harm: shirk, ignorance, hypocrisy, injustice, sinful desire, fear, and despair. The light—nūr—is singular because truth and guidance have one source. Allah brings believers through revelation, the Messenger’s example, sound understanding, repentance, and righteous companionship. The movement is often gradual. A new believer may leave major sin but still need healing from old habits. A person may know a ruling but need time to develop trust and discipline. Allah’s guardianship includes opening the next step and giving strength to continue. The servant responds by learning and obeying rather than demanding instant perfection. Those who disbelieve take ṭawāghīt, false guardians and authorities. (10:62 — **“There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve”**)

**FROM DARKNESSES TO LIGHT**

***“and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods”*** deepens from darknesses to light. These can be idols, Satan, tyrannical leaders, ideologies, desires, or social systems that claim ultimate obedience. They promise security, identity, wealth, or power, but their protection ends in deeper darkness. Created powers cannot grant forgiveness, control the unseen, or save a person from Allah’s judgement. Nothing here makes every relationship with a non-Muslim harmful or permits unjust treatment. A person may receive lawful worldly assistance from people of any faith and remain obligated to show justice and kindness. The issue is ultimate spiritual guardianship and allegiance, not ordinary cooperation. Allah’s light clarifies the purpose of life and frees people from slavery to created things. A person who knows that Allah alone controls benefit and harm is less vulnerable to political intimidation, commercial manipulation, and social pressure. He can respect authority without worshipping it and seek wealth without becoming its servant. The light also reveals injustice. Guidance does not remain private comfort; it requires truthful testimony, fair contracts, care for the weak, and resistance to oppression. A person cannot claim to have left darkness while benefiting from corruption and refusing to see its victims. The final warning describes the end of those who die upon disbelief and remain aligned with false guardians. It is a warning to the living, not a licence to declare the final fate of named individuals. (6:122 — **“and a light with which they can walk among people,”**)

**FALSE GUARDIANS**

***“who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who”*** clarifies false guardians. Allah knows what guidance reached each person and what he did with it. The believer fears that his own attachments may become rivals. He asks Allah to keep him firm and does not assume that a religious identity alone guarantees safety. Guardianship is connected to faith, obedience, and sincere return. A sacred hadith says that whoever shows enmity to one of Allah’s friends, Allah declares war against him, and that the servant draws near through obligations and voluntary deeds until Allah loves him, according to a report al-Bukhārī collected in his Ṣaḥīḥ. The awliyāʾ of Allah are not defined by claims, costumes, or miracles. They are people of faith and taqwā. This protects the community from false spiritual authorities. A person who claims special guardianship while demanding worship, money, or unquestioning obedience is leading people toward darkness, not light. Think of allah as the guardian of believers through a man who is shown two roads out of a valley at dusk; one climbs towards a village with lamps in it, and the other falls away into a plain with no light at all. The roads were cut by other feet long before he came, and the only thing that belongs to him is the choice of the one he takes. Allah as the guardian of believers confronts from darknesses to light in a reader who thinks of his faith as a private opinion that costs him nothing either way. (5:16 — **“through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace,”**)

**LIGHT AND FREEDOM**

***“will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”*** closes with light and freedom. The verse gives him a Guardian, a road out of darkness and a warning about a dwelling without an end, and it asks him who is leading him by the hand he never looks at. Because the sentence says the believers are brought out rather than that they climbed out, showing through allah as the guardian of believers that the strength to leave a dark place was never his own. The same two roads are named in the chapter of the cattle, where the Book speaks of those who were in darkness and were brought into light by their Lord. And the close of the chapter calls the believers to ask for mercy on the day of the return. Because allah as the guardian of believers opens into from darknesses to light, false guardians joins allah as the guardian of believers to from darknesses to light. Since false guardians develops allah as the guardian of believers, from darknesses to light carries the transition. Light and freedom matters, which means false guardians answers from darknesses to light. From darknesses to light gives practical form to allah as the guardian of believers; light and freedom sets its horizon. Today, allah as the guardian of believers shapes from darknesses to light in present decisions. (14:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Ra. ˹This is˺ a Book which We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ so that you may”**)

## Verse 2:258

> Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? ˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death.” He argued, “I too have the power to give life and cause death.” Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west.” And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

**POWER CAN PRODUCE ARROGANCE**

***“Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship?”*** establishes power can produce arrogance. The verse presents a ruler who argued with Ibrāhīm about Allah because Allah had given him kingship. The Qur’an does not name the ruler; an early report identifies him as Nimrod, but the moral lesson does not depend upon the name. Authority gave him the illusion that he could define reality and challenge the Creator. Power can make a person forget that it is borrowed. A ruler, employer, scholar, or wealthy individual may begin to think that because people obey him, the universe must obey him too. The verse exposes this confusion: human authority is limited, while Allah gives life, causes death, and controls every created power. Ibrāhīm begins with a clear proof: My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death. The ruler replies that he can give life and death. One early explanation states that he released one condemned person and killed another, pretending that this was equivalent to creation and death. His answer was a rhetorical trick, not a genuine response to Ibrāhīm’s argument. A ruler can decide whether a person lives under a legal sentence, but he cannot create a living being from nothing, control the soul, or reverse death by his own power. Human medicine can preserve life and postpone death through means, but it does not make the physician the Creator. The distinction between cause and ultimate source is central to tawḥīd. Ibrāhīm then gives a proof the ruler cannot redefine: Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west. (6:102 — **“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. ˹He is˺ the”**)

**GIVING LIFE AND CAUSING DEATH**

***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death.” He argued, “I”*** deepens giving life and causing death. The challenge moves from a manipulated social example to a universal order beyond the king’s control. The sun’s regular movement is a sign of a Creator whose authority cannot be imitated by political theatre. The ruler is confounded—fa-buhita alladhī kafara. He has no coherent answer. Silence after a clear proof is not the same as humble acceptance; a person may be intellectually defeated yet remain morally stubborn. The Qur’an records the collapse of the argument, while Allah knows whether the heart later repented. Ibrāhīm’s exchange demonstrates that reasoned debate can be useful when it clarifies truth. He begins with a principle, exposes the false analogy, and presents a proof the opponent cannot manipulate. He does not insult the ruler’s body, family, or ethnicity. His confidence comes from evidence and trust in Allah. The Qur’an also warns against fruitless argument. A debate is beneficial when participants seek truth, understand the evidence, and accept correction. It becomes harmful when the aim is humiliation, performance, or protecting power. Muslims should not imitate the ruler’s arrogance while criticizing it. The closing statement says that Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people—al-qawm al-ẓālimīn. This does not mean that Allah prevents every wrongdoer from ever receiving information or repentance. It means that the person who persists in injustice and arrogance is deprived of the special guidance that leads to humble acceptance. His wrongdoing becomes a barrier he chooses and reinforces. The Qur’an summons everyone to guidance, and a living wrongdoer can still repent. (3:189 — **“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.”**)

**THE DECISIVE COSMIC SIGN**

***“too have the power to give life and cause death.” Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the”*** clarifies the decisive cosmic sign. A ruler can turn from oppression, a scholar from pride, and a wealthy person from exploitation. But guidance requires abandoning the posture that treats power as proof of truth. Authority should be measured by justice and humility. A government that provides security does not own its citizens’ souls. A leader cannot declare himself the source of life, law, or prosperity. He is a servant who will answer for blood, property, and speech. Ibrāhīm’s example also encourages truthful counsel to power. The adviser uses evidence, avoids flattery, and does not assume that a ruler’s confidence makes his argument true. Where direct confrontation creates danger, wisdom may require a different method, but truth must not be sold for safety or favour. The sun’s rising from the east reminds people that the world follows an ordered pattern. Regularity does not make creation divine; it makes the Creator’s wisdom visible. The ruler can neither command the sun nor guarantee tomorrow’s sunrise. Every created power is contingent and dependent. The believer uses this awareness in daily life. He respects worldly causes but does not fear them as independent gods. He seeks lawful help while keeping the heart attached to Allah. Imagine two men disputing the height of a courtyard wall, and one of them asks the other to hold back the tide with his hand. The tide comes in every evening, the wall is measured in the morning, and the man who spoke of the sea never spoke of the wall again. (67:1 — **“Blessed is the One in Whose Hands rests all authority. And He is Most Capable of everything”**)

**DEBATE AND ITS LIMITS**

***“east. So make it rise from the west.” And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”*** closes with debate and its limits. Power can produce arrogance confronts giving life and causing death in one present-day reader; the decisive cosmic sign meets, under the demand of power can produce arrogance, a tradesman whose new authority has persuaded him that rank settles every argument. The verse gives him a king with a throne and a friend of God with a sunrise; the decisive cosmic sign asks, through power can produce arrogance, which of the two would stand if the sky were asked to move. Because the close names the wrongdoers as the ones left without guidance, showing through power can produce arrogance that the greatest loss of a powerful man is the hearing he no longer has. The argument from the rising of the sun is kept beside another proof presented in Sūrah al-Anʿām. And the same mercy that keeps a believer's road lit is asked for at the close of this chapter. Because power can produce arrogance opens into giving life and causing death, the decisive cosmic sign joins power can produce arrogance to giving life and causing death. Since the decisive cosmic sign develops power can produce arrogance, giving life and causing death carries the transition. Debate and its limits matters, which means the decisive cosmic sign answers giving life and causing death. Giving life and causing death gives practical form to power can produce arrogance; debate and its limits sets its horizon. Today, power can produce arrogance shapes giving life and causing death in present decisions. (16:78 — **“And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing,”**)

## Verse 2:259

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink—they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”

**A RUINED TOWN AND A QUESTION**

***“Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die”*** establishes a ruined town and a question. The verse describes a person who passed a devastated town and wondered how Allah could restore it after its death. The Qur’an does not name the town or the person. Classical exegetes transmitted an identification with ʿUzayr and a particular Israelite town, but the revelation itself leaves the identity open. The lasting lesson is Allah’s power to restore life and the movement from uncertainty to certainty. The question need not have been arrogant denial. It can be a request to understand how resurrection occurs. Ibrāhīm similarly asked Allah to show him how He gives life to the dead, and Allah did not condemn him for wanting his heart reassured. The moral difference lies between sincere inquiry and stubborn rejection after truth is clear. Allah caused the person to die for a hundred years and then raised him. The event makes time itself part of the sign. A century passes, yet the person’s experience is like a day or part of a day. Human awareness of time is limited and subjective, while Allah controls life, death, memory, and perception. The miracle is not presented as a scientific model of every resurrection. It is a particular sign Allah gave to one person. It demonstrates that the One who created life can suspend and restore it, and that the long interval between death and resurrection is no obstacle to divine power. The food and drink remained unchanged while the person and his donkey underwent death and restoration. The contrast shows that Allah can preserve one thing, transform another, and reverse a third according to His will. Creation is not an independent system that limits its Creator. The verse does not invite superstition about preserving food or treating a miracle as an ordinary technique. It calls the reader to recognize divine power and to trust revelation about matters beyond ordinary experience. Scientific investigation can study food decay, but it cannot make this unique sign a routine human process. The donkey’s remains became a visible sign of bodily resurrection. Allah showed the bones being raised and clothed with flesh. The image directly answers the objection that bones, once scattered and decayed, cannot become living bodies again. If Allah created the body initially, He can reassemble it after death. (2:260 — **“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.”**) A report on a ruined town and a question comes through Ibn ʿAbbās, who identified the traveller as ʿUzayr and the ruined settlement as a town whose dead inhabitants Allah restored after the hundred-year sign.

**DEATH FOR A HUNDRED YEARS**

***“for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained”*** deepens death for a hundred years. The Qur’an answers the same objection in Sūrah Yāsīn: Who will give life to bones while they are disintegrated. Say, He will give them life who produced them the first time. The ability to originate life is evidence of the ability to restore it. The person’s experience is made a sign—āyah—for humanity. A miracle benefits people when it leads to knowledge and gratitude, not when it becomes a story detached from its Lord. The event teaches that apparent finality is not final for Allah: ruins can be rebuilt, bones can be clothed, and a person can be returned from death. The verse also challenges civilizational despair. A destroyed town may be physically gone for a period, but communities can be rebuilt through justice, knowledge, work, and Allah’s permission. Hope must not become passivity; people restore what they can while trusting Allah with what exceeds their control. When it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that Allah is capable of everything.’ His knowledge is not only intellectual. It is certainty formed through a sign and directed toward worship. He does not claim that he now understands every mystery. He recognizes the central truth: Allah’s power is unlimited and His resurrection promise is credible. A believer can similarly say, I do not know how, without saying, It cannot be. Human inability to imagine a process does not limit Allah. Humility allows the mind to investigate while accepting the limits of created knowledge. The story is connected to the Day when every person is raised. Resurrection is not merely a demonstration of power; it is the foundation of accountability. If people return to Allah, then hidden injustice, forgotten charity, and unpunished crimes all have a final reckoning. This should affect present conduct. The person who believes he will be raised does not treat property, time, or another person’s life as disposable. He prepares for the return through faith, repentance, and good works. Think of a ruined town and a question through a farmer who finds a dry field in the month of the drought and tells himself that nothing will grow there again. He sleeps through the season, wakes in the spring of the following year, and finds a green line along the ditch where the seed had fallen from his own sack. (36:78 — **“And they argue with Us—forgetting they were created—saying, “Who will give life to decayed bones?””**)

**FOOD AND DRINK PRESERVED**

***“here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink—they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And”*** clarifies food and drink preserved. The ditch was watered by no one, the season was the same season, and the seed had been lying there since the day he gave up. A ruined town and a question confronts death for a hundred years in a reader who stands in front of a thing that has been broken for years and asks how it could ever be put right. The verse gives him a city in ruins, a man who slept a century and a donkey that was gathered from its bones. And it asks him what part of his own life he thinks is beyond the hand that kept the food fresh. Because the close names a power over everything, showing through a ruined town and a question that the ruin he sees is a picture of the hour before the rebuilding and not of the end. The raising of the dead is argued from the same power in the scene of the birds. And the same hand is named over the earth and the heavens in the verse about the possession of all things. Because a ruined town and a question opens into death for a hundred years, food and drink preserved joins a ruined town and a question to death for a hundred years. Since food and drink preserved develops a ruined town and a question, death for a hundred years carries the transition. The donkey and the bones matters, which means food and drink preserved answers death for a hundred years. Death for a hundred years gives practical form to a ruined town and a question; the donkey and the bones sets its horizon. Today, a ruined town and a question shapes death for a hundred years in present decisions. A ruined town and a question stays bound to food and drink preserved because death for a hundred years supplies the human setting of a ruined town and a question. The donkey and the bones carries a ruined town and a question into conduct shaped by food and drink preserved. (2:258 — **“Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because”**)

**THE DONKEY AND THE BONES**

***“look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.””*** closes with the donkey and the bones. The reconstructed bones make the proof visible in stages: preservation of the food, decay of the animal, assembly of the frame, and clothing with flesh all answer different aspects of the traveller’s question. The sequence does not suggest that resurrection is difficult for Allah; it teaches a human observer through signs he can follow. Its conclusion therefore belongs to knowledge as worship. Once the sign is clear, the proper response is not fascination with the mechanism but confession of Allah’s unrestricted power and readiness for the resurrection it proves. (22:5 — **“O humanity! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection,”**)

## Verse 2:260

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**IBRĀHĪM’S REQUEST FOR REASSURANCE**

***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you”*** establishes ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance. Ibrāhīm asks Allah to show him how He gives life to the dead. Allah asks, Do you not believe. Ibrāhīm immediately affirms his faith: Yes, but so that my heart may be reassured. His request is not disbelief or denial. It is a desire for ṭumaʾnīnah, a deeper settled certainty in the heart. This distinction is important. A believer may ask how a matter occurs without doubting that Allah can do it. Faith has degrees of certainty, and the heart can seek greater tranquillity through reflection and signs. The Prophet ﷺ taught that sincere questions are not blameworthy when they seek understanding rather than escape from obedience. Ibrāhīm’s answer shows that intellectual conviction and emotional reassurance can coexist. A person may know that Allah is powerful yet feel shaken by grief, death, or an unanswered question. Asking Allah for clarity can strengthen the heart. What is blameworthy is refusing to accept truth until every unseen reality becomes physically visible. The Qur’an presents Ibrāhīm as a model of both certainty and inquiry. He questioned his people, observed the signs of the heavens, and rejected false gods. His questions were steps toward tawḥīd, not excuses to remain inactive. Allah commands Ibrāhīm to take four birds, become familiar with them, place portions of them on different hills, and call them. The Qur’an’s details establish that the creatures were separated and that their return occurred by Allah’s command. Classical exegetes discuss the precise manner in which Ibrāhīm handled the birds and the meaning of the instruction to become accustomed to them. (2:258 — **“Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because”**) A transmitted reading from Ibn ʿAbbās understands Abraham’s request as a desire for settled reassurance about how scattered bones are gathered, not doubt in Allah’s power.

**BELIEF AND THE NEED FOR REASSURANCE**

***“not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four”*** deepens belief and the need for reassurance. The lesson does not depend upon reconstructing every physical detail. The event is a miracle, not a recipe for human resurrection. It demonstrates that distance, separation, decay, and scattered remains do not prevent Allah from restoring life. Modern science may examine biological processes, but no experiment can reproduce the divine sign described here. The birds come swiftly when called. The one who created and scattered them knows each part and can bring them together. The speed of their return displays command over matter, identity, and life. The miracle answers the recurring human objection that a body cannot be restored after its components are dispersed. It also gives a personal sign to Ibrāhīm. He does not merely hear an abstract argument; he witnesses an event that settles his heart. Allah knows the particular form of reassurance each servant needs, though ordinary believers do not demand miracles on their own terms. The final names are al-ʿAzīz and al-Ḥakīm. Allah’s might makes resurrection possible, and His wisdom determines how signs are given and what they teach. Power without wisdom would be an incoherent concept, but Allah’s acts are both possible and purposeful. The sign is not given to satisfy entertainment or curiosity. It teaches resurrection, strengthens a prophet for his mission, and refutes the idea that death is beyond Allah’s control. A miracle should deepen worship rather than become a spectacle. The verse gives permission to seek reassurance in a respectful way. A grieving person may ask Allah to strengthen his heart, study evidence, speak with a knowledgeable teacher, and observe signs of mercy and creation. (3:190 — **“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the day and”**)

**THE FOUR BIRDS**

***“birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then”*** clarifies the four birds. He should not be ashamed of the need for comfort. At the same time, he should distinguish a request for reassurance from a demand that Allah obey a private test. The heart settles through Qur’an, prayer, remembrance, truthful companionship, and reflection. The believer says, I know Allah is capable, even while asking for greater yaqīn. The preceding verses have described Allah’s power over life and death, the resurrection of a person after a hundred years, and Ibrāhīm’s own request for reassurance. Together they establish that resurrection is certain and that faith rests upon Allah’s power, not on human imagination. The chapter will move from these signs into further guidance about charity, contracts, and social life, showing that belief in resurrection must shape conduct. A person who expects to be raised treats every life as sacred, every trust as accountable, and every charitable act as an investment with Allah. Certainty about the Hereafter is not withdrawal from the world; it is a reason to act justly within it. Think of ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance through a child who is told by his father that the seed in the ground will come up as wheat, and who digs a hole every week to check. The father gives him a pot, a seed and a windowsill, and the boy waters his own plant until the day it can be seen from the door. Ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance confronts belief and the need for reassurance in one present-day reader; the four birds meets, under the demand of ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance, someone who has been told about the raising of the dead all his life and finds that the words have not reached his heart. (41:53 — **“We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to”**)

**THEY WILL COME TO YOU SWIFTLY**

***“call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.””*** closes with they will come to you swiftly. The verse gives him a friend of God asking for a sight, four birds in his own two hands and a call that brought them back, and the four birds asks what he wants his own certainty to be built on. Because the close names divine might joined to wisdom, showing through ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance that the Lord who raised the birds is the Lord who arranges the seasons of a single heart. The scene of the man who was made a sign for a town stands just before this one. And the chapter’s final passage affirms this same power over the dead. Because ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance opens into belief and the need for reassurance, the four birds joins ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance to belief and the need for reassurance. Since the four birds develops ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance, belief and the need for reassurance carries the transition. They will come to you swiftly matters, which means the four birds answers belief and the need for reassurance. Belief and the need for reassurance gives practical form to ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance; they will come to you swiftly sets its horizon. Today, ibrāhīm’s request for reassurance shapes belief and the need for reassurance in present decisions. (22:5 — **“O humanity! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection,”**)

## Verse 2:261

> The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing

**A SEED THAT MULTIPLIES**

***“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause”*** establishes a seed that multiplies. The Qur’an compares spending in Allah’s cause to a single grain that produces seven ears, with a hundred grains in each ear. The image begins with something small and hidden, then shows growth far beyond the original. Charity may seem to reduce a person’s immediate wealth, but Allah can place blessing in what remains and multiply the reward in ways no human calculation can contain. The metaphor does not promise that every donation produces visible financial profit. It promises divine multiplication of reward, and that reward may include forgiveness, contentment, protection, benefit to descendants, social repair, and everlasting recompense. Allah’s accounting is wider than the balance sheet. Allah’s cause—sabīl Allāh—includes every lawful effort that serves worship, justice, mercy, and human welfare. It includes zakāh, support for relatives and orphans, feeding the hungry, education, healthcare, refuge, debt relief, and legitimate defence of the oppressed. The cause must itself be lawful; giving money to aggression, terrorism, fraud, or corruption is not a righteous expenditure. The giver should verify the organization, the purpose, and the likely benefit. Sincerity does not excuse negligence. A charity with poor records should not be trusted merely for pious branding. The closing words—yuḍāʿifu liman yashāʾ—show that multiplication is according to Allah’s wisdom. The amount is not the only measure. A small gift from a poor person may be greater than a large gift from wealth, especially when the sacrifice and sincerity are greater. (2:245 — **“Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over?”**) Ibn ʿAbbās reads the seven ears and hundred grains as multiplication from one gift to seven hundred, with further increase belonging to Allah’s wisdom.

**SPENDING FOR ALLAH’S CAUSE**

***“of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven”*** deepens spending for allah’s cause. A private donation may outweigh a public one made to gain reputation. The Qur’an’s parable also protects the giver from pride. The seed grows by Allah’s permission. The servant plants and waters, but Allah creates the increase. He thanks Allah for enabling the charity and asks Him to accept it. The reward is connected to the ethics of giving. Wealth should be lawful, the intention directed to Allah, and the recipient treated with dignity. Reminding people of a gift, insulting them, seeking control, or giving contaminated or worthless property can destroy the spiritual benefit, as the following verses explain. A gift should meet a real need. Food should be edible, clothing suitable, and financial support delivered in a way that preserves privacy. A person does not give away what his dependants urgently require and then call the resulting neglect charity. A single act of giving can produce many effects. Food restores strength, education opens opportunity, medical care preserves life, and debt relief frees a family from fear. Those helped may then help others. Like a seed, charity can grow through relationships and institutions beyond what the original giver sees. This is why Islam joins personal generosity to public systems such as zakāh. Individual gifts express mercy, while organized distribution can address structural need. Both should be transparent and accountable. Allah is Wāsiʿ, All-Encompassing in generosity, knowledge, and ability. (2:215 — **“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say,”**)

**ALLAH MULTIPLIES AS HE WILLS**

***“ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward”*** clarifies allah multiplies as he wills. His resources do not run out when servants give. He is ʿAlīm, knowing the giver’s intention, the recipient’s need, and every consequence of the gift. People may overlook quiet charity, but Allah does not. The two names also teach balance. The giver does not demand that Allah multiply according to his schedule, and he does not despair when the worldly result is invisible. The seed may be growing in a realm he cannot yet see. Think of a seed that multiplies through a man who plants a single row of maize at the edge of his plot because the rest of the field is rented to another. The row becomes a hedge, the hedge feeds his family for a month, and the neighbour who rented the field asks him for seed the following year. A seed that multiplies confronts spending for allah’s cause in a reader who counts what he puts into a cause as money that has left his hand for good. The verse gives him a seed, seven ears and a hundred grains in each, and it asks him whether he has ever seen a farmer refuse to sow because the ground would swallow the seed. Because the close names the Bountiful and the Knowing, the reader is taught that no gift is lost and no intention is missed. The same picture of the seed that becomes many is used in Sūrah al-Anʿām. (59:9 — **“As for those who had settled in the city and ˹embraced˺ the faith before ˹the arrival of˺”**)

**THE CONDITIONS OF A GOOD GIFT**

***“even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”*** closes with the conditions of a good gift. And the giving that follows this verse is described with its wrong way in the next one. Because a seed that multiplies opens into spending for allah’s cause, allah multiplies as he wills joins a seed that multiplies to spending for allah’s cause. Since allah multiplies as he wills develops a seed that multiplies, spending for allah’s cause carries the transition. The conditions of a good gift matters, which means allah multiplies as he wills answers spending for allah’s cause. Spending for allah’s cause gives practical form to a seed that multiplies; the conditions of a good gift sets its horizon. Today, a seed that multiplies shapes spending for allah’s cause in present decisions. A seed that multiplies stays bound to allah multiplies as he wills because spending for allah’s cause supplies the human setting of a seed that multiplies. The conditions of a good gift carries a seed that multiplies into conduct shaped by allah multiplies as he wills. (9:103 — **“Take from their wealth ˹O Prophet˺ charity to purify and bless them,”**)

## Verse 2:262

> Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**CHARITY MUST REMAIN A GIFT**

***“Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and”*** establishes charity must remain a gift. This verse gives the conditions that preserve the reward of charity. The giver spends for Allah and does not follow the gift with mann, reminding the recipient of what was given, or adhā, words and actions that cause hurt. A donation can be physically helpful yet spiritually corrupted if the giver later turns it into a chain around the recipient’s neck. Did you not remember what I did for you. Without me you would have nothing. Everyone should know that I supported you. Such words can destroy dignity and create dependence. Giving should leave the recipient grateful to Allah rather than permanently humiliated before the donor. The reward is with their Lord. People may forget the gift, reject the giver, or criticize the way it was offered. Allah does not lose the sincere act. The phrase also teaches the giver not to demand repayment from the recipient. He seeks his account with Allah, whose reward is safer and more generous than human gratitude. This does not mean that a charity may be hidden when public reporting is needed or that a donor cannot keep lawful records. Transparency protects trust. The danger is publicity or reminder used to establish superiority and control rather than accountability. The promise of no fear and no grief belongs to the Hereafter and can also bring tranquillity in this life. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**THE REWARD IS WITH ALLAH**

***“do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or”*** deepens the reward is with allah. The giver who trusts Allah is less fearful of poverty and less grieved when worldly recognition does not come. He knows that the real transaction has not been lost. The promise does not guarantee that a generous person will never face anxiety or sadness. Believers can experience both while remaining sincere. It promises that Allah will protect them from the final fear and grief of abandonment when they meet Him. The recipient has dignity before he receives the gift. He is not a project for the donor’s image or a prop in a publicity campaign. A Muslim asks what form of assistance preserves privacy and independence. A cash transfer may be better than a public food distribution; a loan may be appropriate in one case and a grant in another; training may be more beneficial than a one-time payment. The Qur’an’s guidance is adaptable, but the moral rule is firm: do not make a person pay emotionally for receiving help. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the upper hand is better than the lower hand while also protecting the recipient from humiliation. Sincerity—ikhlāṣ—is not a feeling that needs to be announced. A giver can examine whether he would still give if no one knew, whether he is angry when the recipient cannot praise him, and whether he uses charity to gain political or personal influence. (2:215 — **“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say,”**)

**NO FEAR AND NO GRIEF**

***“hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and”*** clarifies no fear and no grief. If the intention becomes mixed, he renews it rather than abandoning all good. Public charity can be good when it encourages others, funds a visible project, or fulfils a public duty. It should be accompanied by humility and accurate reporting, not by boasting or pressure. The verse also covers what happens months or years after a gift. A donor may later use past charity to demand obedience, win a family dispute, or silence criticism. Such conduct reveals that the gift was treated as a purchase. The recipient remains free to make lawful choices and offer advice; charity does not make him the donor’s property. If hurtful words have already been spoken, repentance includes apologizing, stopping the reminders, and restoring the recipient’s dignity. Allah’s mercy remains open. Think of charity must remain a gift through a man who pays the school fees of his brother's children and then tells the story at every wedding in the family for ten years. The children finish their schooling, the story is worn thin by the telling, and the brother's table is the one place where the man is never seated at ease. Charity must remain a gift confronts the reward is with allah in a reader who has helped a relative through a hard year and cannot stop mentioning the help at every gathering. The verse gives him a gift, a silence after it and a reward kept by his Lord; no fear and no grief asks, through charity must remain a gift, which of the two payments he would rather have. (76:8 — **“and give food—despite their desire for it—to the poor, the orphan, and the captive”**)

**RESPECTING THE RECIPIENT**

***“there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”*** closes with respecting the recipient. Because the close removes the fear and the grief from the giver, showing through charity must remain a gift that the remark made after a gift costs him more than the money did. Since the reward is kept by the Lord and not by the receiver, the reader sees that the silence of a giver is part of his deed. The same promise of a reward with the Lord is made to the givers in the following āyah; no fear and no grief also the manner of the giving is described in the parable of the garden. Because charity must remain a gift opens into the reward is with allah, no fear and no grief joins charity must remain a gift to the reward is with allah. Since no fear and no grief develops charity must remain a gift, the reward is with allah carries the transition. Respecting the recipient matters, which means no fear and no grief answers the reward is with allah. The reward is with allah gives practical form to charity must remain a gift; respecting the recipient sets its horizon. Today, charity must remain a gift shapes the reward is with allah in present decisions. (9:60 — **“Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy, for those employed to administer it,”**)

## Verse 2:263

> Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing

**KINDNESS CAN BE BETTER THAN MONEY**

***“Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity”*** establishes kindness can be better than money. A kind word—qawl maʿrūf—and forgiveness are better than charity that is followed by hurt. The verse does not diminish material assistance. A hungry person needs food and a debtor may need money. It teaches that the spiritual and moral manner of giving matters so much that an apparently generous gift can become worse than a respectful refusal if the gift humiliates and injures the recipient. Sometimes a person cannot give financially. A gentle explanation, sincere apology, useful information, prayer, or referral to someone able to help can preserve dignity. The one who asks should not be mocked or treated as a burden. The one who cannot give should say so kindly rather than making promises he cannot keep. Forgiveness—maghfirah—can mean overlooking an offensive request, declining to shame someone who cannot repay, or forgiving a person’s manner while addressing the underlying need. It does not require surrendering a legitimate right or remaining in an unsafe situation. A victim can seek justice and still refuse the desire to humiliate the wrongdoer. The pairing of kindness and forgiveness shows that charity is relational. Wealth can solve an immediate problem, but mercy can protect the person’s heart and future. The recipient should leave with hope rather than a new wound. A person who gives may unconsciously assume superiority. The verse corrects this by reminding him that the recipient is not less valuable before Allah. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) A reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās makes the kind word include prayer and praise for another person, while forgiveness overlooks an offence without using generosity to injure.

**FORGIVENESS AS A GIFT**

***“followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing”*** deepens forgiveness as a gift. The donor is being tested through wealth, while the recipient may be tested through need. The roles can reverse quickly, and both are servants of the same Lord. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah does not look at bodies or wealth but at hearts and deeds. This should shape charitable institutions: no degrading photographs, no public queues designed for spectacle, no insulting language, and no conditions that force people to praise the donor. Allah is Ghaniyy, Self-Sufficient. He does not need the charity, praise, or obedience of His servants. This name removes the donor’s illusion that he has done Allah a favour. Allah commands charity for the benefit of people and the purification of the giver; His dominion is not increased by a donation. Because Allah is free of need, He can reward a small gift enormously. The giver is not competing with Allah or reducing divine wealth. He is using a provision that Allah entrusted to him. Allah is Ḥalīm, Forbearing. He delays punishment for those who give arrogantly, injure recipients, or use His name for reputation. This forbearance is an opportunity to repent, not evidence that hurtful charity is acceptable. A person should correct his intention and conduct before the hidden damage becomes a pattern. The name also teaches the giver to be patient with those he helps. A recipient may be slow to repay, anxious, disorganized, or unable to express gratitude. (17:53 — **“Tell My ˹believing˺ servants to say only what is best.”**)

**CHARITY AND HUMAN DIGNITY**

Patience does not excuse fraud, but it prevents a donor from turning assistance into constant complaint. There are times when giving money would enable addiction, corruption, or dependence. A person can refuse while offering a safer alternative. A parent may pay a bill directly instead of handing over cash; a charity may provide treatment rather than fund destructive conduct. The refusal should still be kind and free of humiliation. The verse’s ideal is not indiscriminate giving. It is beneficial assistance administered with wisdom, honesty, and mercy. A community guided by this āyah makes help accessible without forcing people to expose their poverty. It trains volunteers to speak respectfully, funds professional services, and ensures that those who ask are not punished for their need. It also teaches recipients that accepting help does not remove their agency or right to make lawful decisions. Charity becomes iḥsān when the giver seeks Allah, the recipient is honoured, and the assistance produces genuine benefit. Think of kindness can be better than money through a woman at a well who has no bucket of her own and greets every traveller as he fills his; she carries nothing home, and the whole village remembers the morning with her in it. Kindness can be better than money confronts forgiveness as a gift in a reader who has nothing to give and thinks that he has therefore nothing to offer at all. The verse gives him a kind word, a forgiveness and a place above the coin, and it asks him who told him that a poor man's hands are the only part of him that counts.

**ALLAH IS SELF-SUFFICIENT**

Because the close names the Self-Sufficient, showing through kindness can be better than money that the Lord of the worlds asks for the kind answer of a person because that answer is what the person is. Since the coin never reaches the Lord of the worlds, the reader sees that a gift is measured by the manner it is wrapped in. The kind word is joined to the same patience of the Lord in the verse about the giving that is spoiled. And the good word is asked of the believers in another chapter, where the Book sets the manner of a person beside his faith. Because kindness can be better than money opens into forgiveness as a gift, charity and human dignity joins kindness can be better than money to forgiveness as a gift. Since charity and human dignity develops kindness can be better than money, forgiveness as a gift carries the transition. Allah is self-sufficient matters, which means charity and human dignity answers forgiveness as a gift. Forgiveness as a gift gives practical form to kindness can be better than money; allah is self-sufficient sets its horizon. Today, kindness can be better than money shapes forgiveness as a gift in present decisions.
