## Verse 2:264

> O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain—leaving it just a bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people

**CHARITY CAN BE SPIRITUALLY CANCELLED**

***“O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their”*** establishes charity can be spiritually cancelled. The verse warns believers not to destroy the reward of charity through mann and adhā: reminding recipients of the gift, demanding submission or praise, and hurting them with words. The physical donation may have helped for a moment, but the spiritual reward can be nullified when the giver turns it into a tool of humiliation. This warning is directed to believers because even a person who begins with faith can corrupt an act through later behaviour. Sincerity is not secured merely by making the initial payment. The giver protects the charity after giving by remaining humble, avoiding reminders, and seeking Allah’s acceptance rather than the recipient’s dependence. The verse compares injurious charity with spending to be seen—riyāʾ. The person who gives for reputation may receive worldly praise, photographs, business connections, or political influence, but he has not prepared a lasting account with Allah. The problem is not that people happen to notice a good deed; the problem is making their notice the purpose of the deed. Public charity can be valid and sometimes beneficial when it encourages others, reports a public trust, or funds a visible project. The giver should renew intention and protect recipients from being displayed. If applause comes unexpectedly, he thanks Allah and does not let it become the aim. The image is of a smooth stone covered with a thin layer of dust and soil. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**SHOWING OFF**

***“wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of”*** deepens showing off. Rain falls heavily and washes everything away, leaving the stone bare. The charity and outward appearance are like the dust; the rain of judgement reveals that no rooted reward remains. The person expected a harvest but had not planted in sincere soil. The metaphor also warns against relying on appearance. A large donation can be spiritually empty, while a small private gift can be immense before Allah. The heart is the ground in which the deed grows. If arrogance and showmanship cover it, the outward act may not survive the test of the Hereafter. They have no power over anything they earned. The giver who sought only human praise cannot rely upon that praise before Allah. The social status, photographs, or influence obtained from charity cannot purchase forgiveness. He may have gained worldly advantage, but he has no control over the eternal reward. The phrase does not mean that the recipient received no practical benefit. A meal can feed someone even if the giver’s intention was corrupt. It means the donor has no claim to the spiritual harvest he destroyed through hypocrisy and injury. Charity should not expose a person’s poverty unnecessarily. Donors and organizations must seek consent before using names, images, stories, or personal details. Children and refugees are especially vulnerable to being turned into publicity. The Qur’an’s concern with hurtful words includes the subtle humiliation of making a recipient feel permanently indebted. (2:271 — **“To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you,”**)

**THE SMOOTH STONE**

***“a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain—leaving it just a”*** clarifies the smooth stone. A gift also should not be used to buy political loyalty, silence abuse, or pressure a person into an unlawful relationship. The recipient remains free before Allah and retains his rights. The verse links showing off with not believing in Allah and the Last Day. A person may speak religiously but act as though human approval is the final judgement. Belief in the Hereafter should make Allah’s evaluation more important than a temporary audience. The Prophet ﷺ warned that the first people judged may include a scholar, a fighter, and a charitable person whose deeds were performed for reputation, in the hadith recorded by Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. The hadith is a terrifying reminder that impressive deeds require sincere intention. Riyāʾ can be subtle and can enter after a sincere beginning. A person should not abandon a good deed simply because people notice it; he should correct the intention and continue where the deed is beneficial. If he has injured someone, he apologizes and restores dignity without making the apology another performance. Allah’s guidance is sought through hidden worship, remembrance, honest self-examination, and asking for acceptance. The believer fears hypocrisy without becoming paralysed by obsessive doubt. Think of charity can be spiritually cancelled through a man who paints the front of a house he does not own because the street will see it from the road. The paint holds for one season, the wood underneath goes on rotting, and the owner of the house returns in the spring to a wall of flakes. (107:1 — **“Have you seen the one who denies the ˹final˺ Judgment”**)

**NO POWER OVER WHAT WAS EARNED**

***“bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people”*** closes with no power over what was earned. Charity can be spiritually cancelled confronts showing off in a reader who gives to the mosque in the month of the festival and makes sure that his name is read out with the list. The verse gives him a rock, a thin layer of soil and a heavy rain, and it asks him what remains of his gift when the rain has passed through the street. Because the close names the people who cannot keep their own reward, the smooth stone teaches that a deed needs a reason deeper than the ground it fell on. The parable of the fertile hill is given right after this verse. And the two kinds of giving are drawn together in the closing verses of the passage. Because charity can be spiritually cancelled opens into showing off, the smooth stone joins charity can be spiritually cancelled to showing off. Since the smooth stone develops charity can be spiritually cancelled, showing off carries the transition. No power over what was earned matters, which means the smooth stone answers showing off. Showing off gives practical form to charity can be spiritually cancelled; no power over what was earned sets its horizon. Today, charity can be spiritually cancelled shapes showing off in present decisions. (18:103 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Shall we inform you of who will lose the most deeds”**)

## Verse 2:265

> And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure and believing the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**A ROOTED CHARITY**

***“And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure and believing”*** establishes a rooted charity. After the image of a smooth stone whose dust is washed away, this verse gives the opposite image: a fertile garden on elevated ground. The garden represents a charitable act rooted in sincerity—ibtighāʾ marḍāt Allāh—and in the strengthening or purification of the giver’s soul. Its reward grows because the foundation is sound. A garden on a hill receives rainfall and benefits from good drainage, sunlight, and protection from stagnant water. The image suggests a deed that is well-placed, healthy, and able to produce repeatedly. Sincere charity can benefit the recipient immediately and continue through education, healing, family stability, and the good practices that grow from it. The giver seeks Allah’s pleasure rather than public praise. His intention does not have to be perfectly free from every passing thought; he renews it and resists the desire to be admired. He gives because Allah loves generosity and because people have rights, not because he wants to own the recipient’s loyalty. A private gift often protects sincerity, but public giving can also be good when it encourages others or fulfils a public trust. The test is whether the giver would still want the good done if his name were removed. Allah sees the intention and the conduct more fully than people do. The phrase tathbītan min anfusihim can mean seeking to strengthen the soul, confirm sincerity, or establish the heart in obedience. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) Ibn ʿAbbās connects the elevated garden with spending that sincerely seeks Allah’s pleasure and rises from settled conviction that the gift will be rewarded.

**A GARDEN FED BY SINCERE PURPOSE**

***“the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when”*** deepens a garden fed by sincere purpose. Spending weakens the grip of miserliness and trains the servant to trust Allah. It also turns concern for the poor into a settled character rather than an occasional emotional reaction. A person strengthens himself through regular charity, even if small, and through spending in ways that require patience and responsibility. He learns that his identity is not secured by accumulation. The heart becomes more stable when it is attached to Allah rather than to possessions. Heavy rain produces abundant fruit, while light rain is sufficient. This illustrates that sincere deeds bear fruit according to the conditions Allah knows. A wealthy person may give much, while a poor person gives little but with a greater sacrifice. A large project may produce public benefit, while a small meal quietly given to a hungry neighbour may be immense in Allah’s account. The verse does not make small charity insignificant. If the soil is fertile, even light rain sustains it. A person who cannot donate large amounts can give time, food, expertise, advocacy, or a kind word. What matters is sincere rootedness and beneficial effect. The garden image also teaches planning. A charity must be maintained rather than launched with enthusiasm and abandoned when attention moves elsewhere. Donors should choose sustainable projects, monitor funds, and listen to the people being served. The best assistance helps people become stable rather than keeping them permanently dependent upon unpredictable gifts. (2:272 — **“You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills.”**)

**STRENGTHENING THE SOUL**

***“heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy”*** clarifies strengthening the soul. The giver must still support his family and fulfil debts. Strengthening the soul does not mean destroying the household’s legitimate provision. Allah loves balanced obedience. The verse closes with Allah’s vision—baṣīr—of all that people do. He sees the gift, the intention, the recipient’s condition, the sacrifice involved, and the harm or benefit that follows. A public donation may be praised while a hidden gift is unknown; Allah sees both without confusion. This sight also warns institutions. They may publish attractive reports while misusing funds or harming communities. Allah sees what the auditors and donors do not. Transparency, independent oversight, and truthful reporting are forms of taqwā. If many believers give sincerely, the community becomes like a landscape of gardens: provision circulates, knowledge grows, and people shelter one another. Charity is not merely emergency relief; it can build schools, clinics, housing, safe water systems, and opportunities for dignified work. The projects must remain subordinate to people’s rights. A beautiful building that leaves the poor hungry is not automatically a garden of righteousness. Fruit is measured by benefit and sincerity. The case is like two plots on a hillside, one watered by the channel and the other left to the rain. The channel dries up in a hard year, the rain still comes, and the two fields are green in the same month. (92:17 — **“But the righteous will be spared from it—”**)

**HEAVY RAIN AND LIGHT RAIN**

***“rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”*** closes with heavy rain and light rain. A rooted charity confronts a garden fed by sincere purpose in a reader who gives less than a neighbour and takes that as a verdict on his own deed. The verse gives him a heavy rain and a drizzle over the same ground; strengthening the soul asks, through a rooted charity, which of the two the garden was waiting for. Because the close of a rooted charity identifies whoever sees what people do, showing through a rooted charity that the size of the gift belongs to the purse and the worth of it belongs to the heart. The rock that loses its soil is described just before this verse. And the same pair of reward and fear is promised to the sincere givers. Because a rooted charity opens into a garden fed by sincere purpose, strengthening the soul joins a rooted charity to a garden fed by sincere purpose. Since strengthening the soul develops a rooted charity, a garden fed by sincere purpose carries the transition. Heavy rain and light rain matters, which means strengthening the soul answers a garden fed by sincere purpose. Seeking allah’s pleasure gives practical form to a rooted charity; heavy rain and light rain sets its horizon. Today, a rooted charity shapes a garden fed by sincere purpose in present decisions. (3:92 — **“You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish.”**)

## Verse 2:266

> Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect

**A TERRIFYING PICTURE OF LOST PROVISION**

***“Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and”*** establishes a terrifying picture of lost provision. This verse presents a vivid parable about a person who possesses a flourishing garden and depends upon it in old age while children are weak and unable to support him. A fiery whirlwind destroys it at the moment he needs it most. The image follows the discussion of charity and the loss of reward through showing off, reminders, and injury. A deed may appear valuable for years, then be destroyed by a final act of hypocrisy or harm. The parable is emotionally powerful because the garden represents security, family, livelihood, and accumulated effort. Its destruction is not a minor reduction in comfort. It leaves the elderly person and dependent children exposed. The Qur’an asks whether anyone would wish for such a fate, inviting the heart to recognize the horror of losing the Hereafter’s harvest after believing it was secure. Old age and weak children represent vulnerability. A person may need the fruits of his past work when his physical strength declines and his dependants cannot replace him. In the same way, a believer needs the reward of his deeds when he stands before Allah unable to return and act again. The image also teaches responsibility toward parents and children. Wealth should not be accumulated only for personal prestige while dependants are left insecure. Charity and family support must be balanced. A person who gives publicly to impress people but neglects those under his care has misunderstood both generosity and worship. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) A transmitted account from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the vulnerable owner as elderly with dependants unable to support themselves when the burning wind destroys the garden.

**AGE AND DEPENDANTS**

***“all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old”*** deepens age and dependants. The destructive wind contains fire—iʿṣār fīhi nār—a sudden force that combines movement and burning. It evokes the way a hidden spiritual disease can destroy the reward of an outwardly impressive life. The person may have cultivated charity, prayer, or service, but the fire of showing off, arrogance, and injury can consume the harvest. The image does not mean that every mistake erases every good deed. It warns about deliberate corruption and about the danger of assuming that a deed is safe merely because it was large or long ago. Sincere repentance can repair what was damaged while life remains. The garden contains every kind of fruit, suggesting abundant opportunity. A person may have been given wealth, health, education, time, influence, and access to many forms of good. These are gardens planted by Allah. The question is how they are cultivated and whether the harvest is protected from destructive conduct. A wealthy person can use assets to support family, create employment, fund education, relieve debt, and care for the poor. If he uses them for vanity, corruption, or harm, the apparent garden becomes a source of loss. The fruit is judged by its moral use. The whirlwind is sudden. A person cannot assume that he will have years to correct his intention or repair a wrong. Death, illness, economic collapse, public scandal, and the loss of opportunity can arrive without warning. The wise servant reviews his deeds regularly and does not postpone repentance. (2:180 — **“It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should”**)

**THE FIERY WHIRLWIND**

***“with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This”*** clarifies the fiery whirlwind. This urgency should not produce panic or obsessive fear. It should produce practical habits: hidden charity, honest apologies, clear wills, lawful earnings, and consistent worship. The believer asks Allah to accept deeds and to protect them from corruption. Allah makes the revelation clear so that people may reflect—yatafakkarūn. Reflection connects the image with personal life. What garden has Allah entrusted to me. Who depends upon its fruit. What kind of fire could destroy it. Is my charity nourishing people or feeding my ego. The mind that reflects does not stop at the image. It changes behaviour. It protects the rights of recipients, controls speech, and seeks a sincere ending. The parable also demands communal compassion. Elderly people, orphans, single parents, and children should not be left at the mercy of sudden loss. Zakah, social support, fair inheritance, and responsible institutions can preserve the garden of a family when its provider is gone. The person who helps protect another family’s provision may find that Allah protects his own harvest. Charity is a network of mercy, not only a private transaction. Think of a terrifying picture of lost provision through a man who plants a grove in the year his first child is born and waters it every dry season until his hair is white. The fire comes on the evening after his youngest son's wedding, and the only thing that survives is the line of the ditch he dug with his own hands. (4:2 — **“Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺,”**)

**FRUITS OF THE GARDEN**

***“is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect”*** closes with fruits of the garden. A terrifying picture of lost provision confronts age and dependants in a reader who has built his whole standing on one good deed of his youth and has not looked at it in years. The verse gives him a flourishing garden, an old age and a fire in one night, and the fiery whirlwind asks what he would have left if the wind turned before the morning. Because the close asks him to reflect rather than to weep, showing through a terrifying picture of lost provision that the question is a warning given early enough to be used. Since the garden is described before the fire, the reader sees that the loss was drawn for him in full before he was asked to answer. The contrast of the two gardens is stated in the preceding āyah; a terrifying picture of lost provision also the same call to reflection closes the passage of the spending. Because a terrifying picture of lost provision opens into age and dependants, the fiery whirlwind joins a terrifying picture of lost provision to age and dependants. Since the fiery whirlwind develops a terrifying picture of lost provision, age and dependants carries the transition. Fruits of the garden matters, which means the fiery whirlwind answers age and dependants. Age and dependants gives practical form to a terrifying picture of lost provision; fruits of the garden sets its horizon. Today, a terrifying picture of lost provision shapes age and dependants in present decisions. (18:32 — **“Give them ˹O Prophet˺ an example of two men.”**)

## Verse 2:267

> O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy

**GIVE FROM GOOD PROVISION**

***“O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and”*** establishes give from good provision. Allah commands believers to spend from the good things they have earned and from the produce He brings forth from the earth. The sources include wages, business profits, crops, livestock, minerals, and all lawful provision. Charity should be drawn from ṭayyib, what is lawful, wholesome, and worthy—not from stolen money or goods that the giver would never accept for himself. The command links human work with divine provision. A person earns through effort, but the ability to work, the land, the market, and the resources all come from Allah. Gratitude directs a portion back toward the needy and the public good. The verse asks the giver to imagine receiving the item he is offering. Would he accept damaged food, worn-out clothing, defective equipment, or money acquired through deception. If he would take it only while overlooking its defects, he should not choose it for charity. The question exposes a double standard in which the donor protects his own comfort while treating the poor as undeserving of quality. This does not prohibit giving used clothing, surplus food, or second-hand goods. Such items can be valuable when clean, safe, useful, and offered with dignity. The prohibition concerns deliberately selecting the inferior because the recipient is poor. The recipient’s poverty does not reduce his worth before Allah. A person may lack money while possessing faith, knowledge, skill, courage, and honour. Giving good food and useful goods acknowledges this dignity. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) Ibn ʿAbbās reads the good produce as lawful earnings and crops, while the bad portion is what the giver himself would accept only with reluctance.

**DO NOT GIVE WHAT YOU WOULD REJECT**

***“of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do”*** deepens do not give what you would reject. The donor does not bestow value; he fulfils a responsibility with wealth Allah entrusted to him. Institutions should apply the same principle. Relief distributions should not become a way to dispose of expired products, broken equipment, or goods that would violate safety standards. The poor deserve protection from harm and the right to receive what genuinely benefits them. The phrase what you have earned excludes wealth obtained through theft, fraud, bribery, gambling, or other forbidden means. Unlawful property must be returned to its owner where possible. Donating stolen money does not transform theft into charity. If the owner cannot be found, the person seeks qualified advice about removing the unlawful benefit without claiming spiritual credit. Allah accepts only what is good, the Prophet ﷺ taught in a report collected by Muslim. The hadith links the quality of wealth to the quality of worship. A person should examine contracts, wages, taxes, debts, and business practices, not only the item placed in a donation box. The earth’s produce includes crops and fruits that nourish people. Zakah on agricultural production has its own rulings, while voluntary charity can be given from any harvest. Farmers and businesses should avoid waste, protect soil and water, and pay workers fairly. The verse does not permit exploiting land or labour in the name of charitable output. A person can share from what he grows, cooks, or makes. Goodness is not limited to cash. (6:141 — **“He is the One Who produces gardens—both cultivated and wild—and palm trees, crops of different flavours, olives,”**)

**CHARITY AND HUMAN WORTH**

***“not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would”*** clarifies charity and human worth. A nutritious meal, a repaired appliance, a textbook, or professional service can be a valuable gift. Allah is Ghaniyy, Self-Sufficient. He does not need inferior goods or the donor’s wealth. The command is for the giver’s purification and the recipient’s welfare. A person should not imagine that Allah is enriched by his donation; rather, Allah enriches the servant by allowing him to participate in mercy. Because Allah is self-sufficient, He can accept a small sincere gift and multiply it. The giver must not use charity to claim superiority over Allah’s servants. The poor person is not indebted to the donor in a way that permits control. Allah is Ḥamīd, Praiseworthy in His names, actions, and judgement. He deserves praise whether people give or withhold. The verse’s ending shifts the heart from the recipient’s reaction to Allah’s approval. The donor gives for Allah and trusts Him with the reward. Praising Allah also means praising Him through the use of blessings. Wealth becomes an act of ḥamd when it feeds people, protects children, supports knowledge, and removes harm. Think of give from good provision through a man who is invited to a wedding and takes the fruit from the bottom of the basket at his door, where the flies have been. The hosts put the dish out with the others, and the guests pass it on to the next table without lifting the cloth. Give from good provision confronts do not give what you would reject in a reader who clears a shelf of things his own family will not use and calls the pile a donation. (7:31 — **“O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat and drink,”**)

**LAWFUL WEALTH**

***“only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy”*** closes with lawful wealth. The verse gives him the earning of his hands, the produce of the earth and a closed eye in front of his own gift. And it asks him what the receiver would say if he could see the house the sack came from. Because the close names the Self-Sufficient and the Praiseworthy, showing through give from good provision that the Lord of the worlds accepts a gift for its worth and not for its weight. Subsequent āyāt join excellent giving to promised reward, while the preceding garden parable depicts good ground. Because give from good provision opens into do not give what you would reject, charity and human worth joins give from good provision to do not give what you would reject. Since charity and human worth develops give from good provision, do not give what you would reject carries the transition. Lawful wealth matters, which means charity and human worth answers do not give what you would reject. Do not give what you would reject gives practical form to give from good provision; lawful wealth sets its horizon. Today, give from good provision shapes do not give what you would reject in present decisions. (4:29 — **“O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent.”**)

## Verse 2:268

> The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing

**THE FEAR BEHIND MISERLINESS**

***“The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids”*** establishes the fear behind miserliness. When the Qur’an commands generous spending, Satan responds by threatening poverty—al-shayṭān yaʿidukum al-faqr. He whispers that charity will leave a person without security, that supporting others is foolish, or that one must accumulate indefinitely before giving. Responsible planning is not wrong, but fear that prevents every act of generosity is one of Satan’s recurring strategies. A person may possess enough for his needs yet feel permanently threatened. The more he gathers, the more afraid he becomes of loss. Satan turns a real concern about provision into a refusal to trust Allah, a neglect of dependants, or the hoarding of wealth while others suffer. Satan commands faḥshāʾ, indecency and shameful conduct. Misers may be led to exploit workers, steal inheritance, take bribes, consume interest, or humiliate the poor. The fear of poverty becomes an excuse for actions that destroy dignity and community. Satan also invites people to spend extravagantly on desire while claiming that they cannot afford charity. The Qur’an’s word commands does not remove human choice. Satan suggests and beautifies; the person decides. Seeking refuge in Allah, questioning the whisper, and taking lawful means break the cycle. A believer can budget carefully without obeying the demand to become unjust. Allah promises maghfirah. Charity, repentance, and responsible generosity can be means of forgiveness, not because money purchases Allah’s mercy, but because sincere giving reveals faith and purifies attachment. (34:39 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Surely ˹it is˺ my Lord ˹Who˺ gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He”**)

**COMMANDS TO IMMORALITY**

***“you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you”*** deepens commands to immorality. The believer who has been miserly can return to Allah without waiting until he feels completely generous. Forgiveness also covers mistakes in financial judgement when a servant acts sincerely. A person should consult, learn, and correct errors, but he need not be paralyzed by the fear of never giving perfectly. Allah sees the intention and effort. Allah promises faḍl, bounty and increase. The increase may be material provision, blessing in what remains, good relationships, contentment, protection from calamity, or the multiplied reward of the Hereafter. The promise does not turn charity into a guaranteed investment scheme. A believer gives for Allah, not as a technique for forcing a worldly return. The Prophet ﷺ taught that every morning two angels supplicate for replacement for the one who spends and destruction for the one who withholds, in reports that illuminate the fear behind miserliness, collected for the theme of the fear behind miserliness by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. The hadith encourages trust while reminding people that withholding rights has consequences. Islam balances charity with responsibility. The believer pays debts, supports dependants, prepares for genuine needs, and avoids waste. He then gives according to ability. The Prophet ﷺ advised Saʿd not to leave his heirs dependent upon people, showing that generosity does not mean abandoning family. Satan may use either extreme: fear to prevent charity or vanity to cause irresponsible giving. Wisdom identifies the true need, the lawful amount, and the most beneficial form of support. (14:7 — **“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more.”**)

**ALLAH PROMISES FORGIVENESS**

***“forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”*** clarifies allah promises forgiveness. Allah is Wāsiʿ, vast in provision, mercy, and knowledge. His stores do not shrink when servants give, and His knowledge encompasses the giver’s circumstances and the recipient’s need. He knows whether a person is genuinely unable or hiding behind an exaggerated fear of poverty. This knowledge is a comfort to the poor giver. Allah does not demand what he cannot afford. It is a warning to the wealthy who call miserliness prudence while spending freely on luxuries. The believer counters Satan’s threat with the Qur’anic promises: Whatever you spend of good, He will replace it, and If you are grateful, I will surely increase you. He begins with small consistent gifts, gives privately where possible, and observes how generosity changes the heart. A person facing actual financial distress should seek assistance, renegotiate debts, and protect dependants. Asking for help is not a failure of tawakkul. Communities should ensure that the poor are not shamed for needing support. Think of the fear behind miserliness through a man who keeps his grain behind a locked door because a neighbour once told him that the winter would be long. The winter passes, the grain goes mouldy in the dark, and the neighbour who borrowed from him in the spring is the one who carries his harvest to the market. The fear behind miserliness confronts commands to immorality in someone who repeatedly hears an inward argument about old age whenever he opens his purse. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**ALLAH PROMISES BOUNTY**

The verse gives him a threat and a promise, an enemy who speaks of poverty and a Lord who speaks of forgiveness, and it asks him whose voice he has been calling the voice of reason. Because the close of the fear behind miserliness identifies whoever knows what is in the chest, showing through the fear behind miserliness that the whisper is answered by a promise and not by a debate. Because the closing divine names unite vast bounty with complete knowledge, the reader sees that the argument is settled in two places he cannot see. The same promise of forgiveness and bounty is kept in the verse about the good Loan. And the giving that is spoiled by a word is treated in the verses just above this one. Because the fear behind miserliness opens into commands to immorality, allah promises forgiveness joins the fear behind miserliness to commands to immorality. Since allah promises forgiveness develops the fear behind miserliness, commands to immorality carries the transition. Allah promises bounty matters, which means allah promises forgiveness answers commands to immorality. Commands to immorality gives practical form to the fear behind miserliness; allah promises bounty sets its horizon. Today, the fear behind miserliness shapes commands to immorality in present decisions.

---

## Verse 2:269

> Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason

**THE GIFT OF WISDOM**

***“Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is”*** establishes the gift of wisdom. Ḥikmah is more than information. It includes sound understanding, placing matters in their proper context, making the right decision, and acting at the right time and in the right manner. A person may know many facts yet lack wisdom, while another may possess modest information but use it with exceptional judgement and benefit. In this passage about charity, wisdom includes recognizing who has a right, how much can be given, how to preserve dignity, when public reporting is useful, and how to balance generosity with family responsibility. It also includes knowing when a kind word is better than money and when a material gift is essential. The Qur’anic wisdom links learning to obedience. A person who understands that wealth is a trust gives sincerely, avoids reminders, and protects the poor. A person who knows the harms of miserliness resists Satan’s threat. Knowledge that remains only a source of debate has not yet become the abundant good described here. The Prophet ﷺ taught that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives him understanding of the religion, in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. This understanding includes knowing rulings and recognizing their purposes, limits, and ethical application. It should produce humility and mercy rather than contempt for people who are still learning. Allah gives wisdom to whom He wills, and this gift may appear in scholars, parents, workers, leaders, or people whose formal education is limited. It is not restricted to social status or institutional title. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) The contrast therefore makes wisdom accountable: sound judgement is proved not by eloquence alone but by choices that obey Allah. Because insight is a gift, gratitude requires using it rather than claiming personal superiority.

**KNOWLEDGE JOINED TO ACTION**

***“granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But”*** deepens knowledge joined to action. At the same time, a person does not claim wisdom without learning. He seeks teachers, verifies evidence, and accepts correction. The phrase to whom He wills does not teach arbitrary favoritism. Allah knows who is sincere, who is capable, and how a person will use knowledge. The servant asks for wisdom, takes the means of learning, and thanks Allah for any understanding he receives. Whoever receives wisdom receives khayran kathīran, abundant good. Wisdom benefits the person and those around him. It protects from waste, prevents injustice, reconciles families, guides charitable spending, and helps a community respond to changing circumstances without abandoning principles. Wisdom also protects from extremes. A generous person without wisdom may give irresponsibly or enable harm. A cautious person without wisdom may use planning as an excuse for miserliness. A wise believer joins generosity with discernment and firmness with mercy. People of sound understanding—ūlū al-albāb—are those who reach the core of matters. They reflect on revelation, distinguish appearance from reality, and allow truth to change them. In the charity passage, they see that the value of spending depends on intention, source, recipient, and conduct after giving. They also learn from parables. The seed, garden, stone, fire, and Satan’s threat are not decorative images. They train the mind to see invisible spiritual realities through familiar forms. Reflection becomes successful when it leads to gratitude and action. Family disputes, financial decisions, and religious questions often contain competing rights. (16:125 — **“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice,”**)

**ALLAH GIVES WISDOM AS HE WILLS**

***“none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason”*** clarifies allah gives wisdom as he wills. Wisdom means listening before judging, separating facts from emotion, and seeking reconciliation where possible. It does not mean avoiding firm decisions when a right is clear. A judge may be compassionate without becoming partial; a donor may be generous without surrendering accountability. The Prophet ﷺ combined wisdom with clarity. He spoke according to the listener’s understanding, repeated important matters, and chose the appropriate time. Teachers and leaders should imitate this rather than overwhelming people with information or using knowledge to dominate them. The believer can ask Allah for beneficial knowledge and sound judgement. He reads the Qur’an with reflection, studies the Sunnah, consults experienced people, and examines his own motives. Before giving, he asks whether the gift helps, whether it is lawful, and whether it preserves dignity. Before speaking, he asks whether the words are true and useful. Wisdom also grows through repentance. A person who learns from a financial or relational mistake may gain insight that protects others. Allah can turn a failure into abundant good when the servant responds with humility. Imagine two men who inherit the same shop, one of whom spends his evenings at the account books and the other at the door watching the street. The second learns what the customers want before the first has finished his first column, and the shop of the second is the one that is still open. The gift of wisdom confronts knowledge joined to action in a reader who reads the books of his trade for years and finds that his decisions in his own house have not improved. (17:39 — **“This is part of the wisdom which your Lord has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺.”**)

**ABUNDANT GOOD**

The verse gives him a gift that is asked for rather than bought, a privilege above wealth and a company of people who can hear a reminder. And it asks him how often he has asked for the first of the three. Because the close names the people of reason, showing through the gift of wisdom that the mind which takes a warning is the mind that was given the warning as a gift. The gift of understanding is asked for in the prayer of the end of the chapter. And the wisdom that comes from the Lord is named beside the Book in another passage of the chapter. Because the gift of wisdom opens into knowledge joined to action, allah gives wisdom as he wills joins the gift of wisdom to knowledge joined to action. Since allah gives wisdom as he wills develops the gift of wisdom, knowledge joined to action carries the transition. Abundant good matters, which means allah gives wisdom as he wills answers knowledge joined to action. Knowledge joined to action gives practical form to the gift of wisdom; abundant good sets its horizon. Today, the gift of wisdom shapes knowledge joined to action in present decisions.

## Verse 2:270

> Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers

**NOTHING IS HIDDEN FROM ALLAH**

***“Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely”*** establishes nothing is hidden from allah. This verse gathers charity and vows under Allah’s complete knowledge. He knows the amount spent, the source of the wealth, the recipient’s need, the intention of the giver, and the words and circumstances of every vow. A public donation and a private payment are equally visible to Him, as are promises made in a moment of fear or bargaining. The reminder protects both sincerity and justice. A person who gives quietly but receives no praise should know that Allah has recorded it. A person who displays generosity while concealing fraud should know that appearance cannot deceive Allah. The final account includes the inner motive and the outward deed. The preceding verses have described several qualities of charity: it must be lawful, sincere, beneficial, and free from reminders and injury. This verse confirms that every expenditure falls under divine knowledge. Spending on dependants, relatives, or the needy can be worship when done for Allah, while spending on vanity, oppression, or forbidden causes can become a source of sin. A believer should therefore review both the amount and the purpose. He pays obligatory maintenance and zakāh, settles debts, and gives voluntary charity according to ability. He does not neglect family while seeking public praise, and he does not use family responsibility as an excuse to refuse every claim of the poor. A nadhr is a vow by which a person binds himself to an act of worship or obedience. If the vow concerns a lawful act of devotion, fulfilling it is required according to the rules of fiqh. (76:7 — **“They ˹are those who˺ fulfil ˹their˺ vows and fear a Day of sweeping horror”**) A reading from Ibn ʿAbbās joins accepted spending and fulfilled vows to sincerity for Allah’s sake, whose knowledge includes both gift and intention.

**SPENDING AS WORSHIP**

***“known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers”*** deepens spending as worship. The Qur’an praises those who fulfil their vows. If a vow concerns sin or an impossible act, it must not be fulfilled; the person repents and follows the relevant ruling on expiation. The Prophet ﷺ taught that vows do not bring forward or delay anything Allah has not decreed. A vow should therefore not be used as a bargain: If Allah gives me this, I will worship Him, as though the servant can compel divine action. Worship is owed to Allah before the requested outcome arrives. The Sunnah discourages making vows because people may bind themselves to a burden they cannot sustain, or they may fulfil it resentfully and then imagine they have purchased a favour. A person who wants to give charity should give without waiting to make a dramatic vow. Sincere voluntary action is better than turning worship into an emotional contract. If a vow has been made, the person should record it and learn its ruling. Families should not pressure someone into a vow or use a public promise to extract money. Allah knows whether the vow was deliberate, coerced, conditional, or intended as a sinful act. The wrongdoers—ẓālimūn—will have no helpers. A person who uses charity or vows to oppress people cannot rely on wealth, relatives, officials, or public reputation to save him before Allah. Created helpers may assist in the world, but no one can cancel divine accountability. The warning also applies to those who help wrongdoing: an executor who hides assets, an institution that launders corrupt money, or a group that uses a vow to manipulate the vulnerable. (5:2 — **“O believers! Do not violate Allah’s rituals ˹of pilgrimage˺, the sacred months, the sacrificial animals,”**)

**VOWS AND THEIR LIMITS**

Cooperation in righteousness is commanded; cooperation in sin is forbidden. If a person spent unlawfully or made a vow that harmed someone, repentance includes stopping the wrong, restoring property, fulfilling lawful rights, and seeking qualified guidance about expiation. A public vow that misled people may require a public clarification. Private regret alone is not enough when others were harmed. Allah’s knowledge is also a comfort to the sincere person who made a mistake without intending sin. He corrects the error and hopes in Allah’s mercy rather than remaining trapped by obsessive guilt. The believer gives because Allah deserves worship and because people have rights, not because he wants to control Allah or the recipient. He does not demand an immediate worldly return, though he may ask Allah for good in this life and the Hereafter. The good loan metaphor honours the giver, but Allah remains the Lord, not a debtor compelled by a transaction. Think of nothing is hidden from allah through a man who borrows a sum from a friend and then gives the friend a wide berth for years. The debt stands in the friend's book all along, and the man is never seen in the market without looking over his shoulder. Nothing is hidden from allah confronts spending as worship in someone seeking to forget a promise made to God during a difficult night. The verse gives him a register that holds both the gift and the vow, and it asks him who he thinks is keeping the second column.

**DO NOT MAKE UNNECESSARY VOWS**

Because the close names the wrongdoers as those who have no helpers, showing through nothing is hidden from allah that the friends a person gathers in the world are the ones who stay away when the account is read. Since the helpers are named as absent rather than as unwilling, the reader sees that the loss of a wrongdoer is complete before anyone thinks about refusing him. The gifts that are given openly and in secret are weighed in the following āyah; vows and their limits also the reward of the giving is named in the same passage. Because nothing is hidden from allah opens into spending as worship, vows and their limits joins nothing is hidden from allah to spending as worship. Since vows and their limits develops nothing is hidden from allah, spending as worship carries the transition. Do not make unnecessary vows matters, which means vows and their limits answers spending as worship. Spending as worship gives practical form to nothing is hidden from allah; do not make unnecessary vows sets its horizon. Today, nothing is hidden from allah shapes spending as worship in present decisions.

## Verse 2:271

> To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**PUBLIC AND PRIVATE CHARITY**

***“To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the”*** establishes public and private charity. The verse gives a balanced judgement about the visibility of charity. Public giving is good when it encourages others, reports a public trust, or makes an important project possible. Concealing charity and giving it to the poor is better for the giver’s sincerity and for the recipient’s dignity. The verse does not declare every public donation corrupt or every private donation automatically sincere. The deciding question is purpose and effect. A public campaign may feed thousands and inspire a culture of generosity, while a private gift may be used to control or harm. A hidden gift may protect the heart from showing off, while a public zakāh payment may provide transparency. Allah knows the full circumstance. Hidden charity—tukhfūhā—can protect both sides. The giver is less likely to seek praise, and the recipient is less likely to feel exposed. A quiet transfer, anonymous payment, or discreet delivery can preserve a person’s dignity. The donor should not later reveal the secret to win an argument or demand loyalty. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned the person who gives charity so secretly that the left hand does not know what the right hand has given among those shaded by Allah’s mercy on the Day of Resurrection, in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. The image emphasizes sincerity rather than prescribing secrecy in every case. Public giving can be necessary. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**CONCEALING CHARITY**

***“poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you”*** deepens concealing charity. An institution may need published accounts, donors may need to verify funds, and a visible project may encourage others to contribute. A person who gives publicly should protect the recipient from being made a spectacle and should renew his intention when praise arrives. Leaders should also avoid using charity to build a personality cult. A public donation that makes the poor chant the donor’s name or suppresses criticism is no longer simple generosity. Transparency should serve accountability, not domination. Allah promises that charity can erase some sins. This does not erase debts or rights owed to people without restitution, and it does not make deliberate injustice harmless. Repentance, restoration, and lawful settlement remain necessary. The promise refers to Allah’s forgiveness of shortcomings and the purification produced by sincere giving. The person who gives should not become confident that charity permits him to continue fraud. A gift from stolen wealth does not cleanse theft. The best charity is accompanied by lawful earning, repentance, and a change in conduct. The verse specifically mentions giving to the poor—al-fuqarāʾ. Charity should reach those with genuine need, and the giver should learn how to identify need without humiliating people. Not every poor person asks, and not every person who asks lacks resources. Trustworthy institutions and discreet inquiry can help. A gift should be appropriate. Food, rent, medical treatment, education, debt relief, and tools for work may serve different needs. (2:264 — **“O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words,”**)

**PUBLIC CHARITY WITH SINCERITY**

***“of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do”*** clarifies public charity with sincerity. The giver asks the recipient what would help rather than imposing an unwanted project for the sake of public appearance. Allah is fully aware—khabīr—of the gift, the source, the intention, the recipient’s condition, and the public or private consequences. A charity may be celebrated by people while Allah knows that it was accompanied by manipulation. Another may be unknown in the world while Allah knows every sacrifice. This awareness gives the poor giver comfort and the public donor accountability. No good deed is lost, and no spiritual corruption is hidden. The preference for hidden voluntary charity does not abolish organized zakāh. Zakāh often requires records, collection, and distribution. The administrators should preserve confidentiality as far as possible and report finances honestly. The recipients should not be shamed for receiving an obligatory right. The community can combine anonymous assistance with public education about poverty, fair wages, disability, housing, and debt. Good charity relieves immediate need while seeking to remove the causes of preventable deprivation. Think of public and private charity through a man who leaves a bag of rice at his neighbour's door before the dawn prayer and walks away without knocking. The neighbour never learns who left it, and the man finds that he sleeps better on the nights when nobody says his name. Public and private charity confronts concealing charity in a reader who gives in the open because he wants his neighbours to know that he is not a miser. (76:8 — **“and give food—despite their desire for it—to the poor, the orphan, and the captive”**)

**ERASING SINS**

The verse gives him a permission and a better road in one sentence, and it asks him what his gift would look like if the room were empty. Because the close of public and private charity identifies whoever is aware, showing through public and private charity that the quiet gift is the one with only one witness, and that witness is the reason it was given. The open and the secret gift are joined to the promise of the reward in the verse above. And the manner of the giving is guarded in the passage just before it. Because public and private charity opens into concealing charity, public charity with sincerity joins public and private charity to concealing charity. Since public charity with sincerity develops public and private charity, concealing charity carries the transition. Erasing sins matters, which means public charity with sincerity answers concealing charity. Concealing charity gives practical form to public and private charity; erasing sins sets its horizon. Today, public and private charity shapes concealing charity in present decisions. Public and private charity stays bound to public charity with sincerity because concealing charity supplies the human setting of public and private charity. Erasing sins carries public and private charity into conduct shaped by public charity with sincerity.

## Verse 2:272

> You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged

**CHARITY IS NOT A TOOL OF CONVERSION**

***“You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever”*** establishes charity is not a tool of conversion. The verse tells the Messenger ﷺ that he is not responsible for forcing people onto guidance. His duty is to convey the message; guidance of the heart belongs to Allah. The immediate context includes questions about giving charity to people whose faith or attitude may differ from the Muslims. Believers are encouraged to give for Allah’s sake rather than making material assistance conditional upon a person’s conversion. This does not mean that every charitable decision must ignore safety, accountability, or the recipient’s conduct. A charity may refuse to fund violence, addiction, fraud, or exploitation and may require proper documentation. The principle is that the deserving poor should not be denied help merely because the donor cannot control their faith. Allah guides whom He wills through wisdom, evidence, circumstances, and the person’s response. The Prophet ﷺ loved guidance for his relatives and grieved when people refused it, but he could not place faith in their hearts. A donor likewise cannot purchase belief by giving money or punish disbelief by withholding basic mercy. Charity can express the moral beauty of Islam, but it should not be a deceptive sales tactic. The believer gives because Allah commands compassion and because people have rights. He explains faith with wisdom when appropriate, without using hunger or vulnerability to force a declaration. Whatever good you spend is for your own benefit. The recipient receives practical help, but the spiritual reward returns to the donor through purification, forgiveness, and nearness to Allah. (28:56 — **“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺,”**)

**GUIDANCE BELONGS TO ALLAH**

***“He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as”*** deepens guidance belongs to allah. Allah is not enriched by charity. The giver is the one who needs the good deed. This perspective protects against resentment. A person who gives for Allah does not constantly calculate whether the recipient thanked him or whether the social return was sufficient. He evaluates the benefit responsibly but leaves the reward with Allah. If the gift is misused through no fault of his own, Allah knows the intention and effort. Seeking the Face of Allah—ibtighāʾ wajh Allāh—is a Qur’anic expression for seeking His pleasure and acceptance. It does not mean imagining Allah in a created direction. The believer purifies his intention from reputation, political influence, control over recipients, or the desire to appear compassionate. Mixed motives can enter. The servant renews his intention and continues beneficial charity rather than allowing a passing desire for praise to cancel all good. He also chooses privacy when it protects sincerity and public transparency when it protects people’s rights. Allah promises that whatever good is spent will be repaid in full. The repayment may be forgiveness, blessing, protection, a good name that benefits others, or reward in the Hereafter. It is not necessarily a direct financial return. A person may give money and receive contentment, a protected family, or a reward that remains after death. Without being wronged assures that no sacrifice is undervalued. The poor person who gives a small amount, the caregiver who gives time, and the wealthy person who gives much are all judged by intention, ability, and obedience. (60:8 — **“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor”**)

**SPENDING BENEFITS THE GIVER**

***“long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate”*** clarifies spending benefits the giver. Allah does not deprive a person of the reward he deserves. The verse supports charitable kindness beyond the Muslim community. Qur’an 60:8 commands justice and kindness toward people who take no part in fighting Muslims over religion. A Muslim may feed a hungry neighbour, support disaster relief, fund healthcare, or protect a refugee without treating the help as proof that every belief is the same. Faith remains clear while mercy remains broad. The donor does not assist oppression, but he does not allow sectarian hostility to make him indifferent to human need. The Prophet ﷺ was responsible for conveying guidance, not controlling hearts. This distinction protects religious teachers from burnout and manipulation. They teach clearly, model goodness, and pray for people, but they do not measure the value of the message solely by immediate conversions. Likewise, parents and community leaders advise without claiming ownership of another person’s faith. Allah knows the path by which a person may eventually return. Imagine charity beyond conversion through an anonymous planter tending a tree beside a road he does not own. The tree stands for fifty years, the shade falls on the travellers of three generations, and the planter's name is on nothing but the soil. Charity is not a tool of conversion confronts guidance belongs to allah in a reader who has paid for the schooling of a nephew and has watched the boy drift away from the mosque. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**SEEKING THE FACE OF ALLAH**

***“will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged”*** closes with seeking the face of allah. The verse gives him the word of guidance, the will of the Lord and a payment that comes back in full; spending benefits the giver asks him which of the three he was really working for. Because the close promises that no gift is reduced, spending benefits the giver teaches that a charity is measured by the hand that gives and not by the life it changes. The same return is promised to the spenders in the preceding āyah; charity is not a tool of conversion also the reward that is kept with the Lord is named again in the same passage. Because charity is not a tool of conversion opens into guidance belongs to allah, spending benefits the giver joins charity is not a tool of conversion to guidance belongs to allah. Since spending benefits the giver develops charity is not a tool of conversion, guidance belongs to allah carries the transition. Seeking the face of allah matters, which means spending benefits the giver answers guidance belongs to allah. Guidance belongs to allah gives practical form to charity is not a tool of conversion; seeking the face of allah sets its horizon. Today, charity is not a tool of conversion shapes guidance belongs to allah in present decisions. (10:99 — **“Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed,”**)

## Verse 2:273

> ˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah

**HIDDEN POVERTY**

***“˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move”*** establishes hidden poverty. This verse directs charity toward people whose need is not obvious. They are restricted in Allah’s cause—uḥṣirū fī sabīl Allāh—and cannot travel through the land to earn a livelihood. Early reports connect the first audience to the poor Muhājirūn who devoted themselves to Allah’s cause and lacked the freedom, property, or security to pursue ordinary work. The principle extends to anyone whose devotion, disability, displacement, caregiving, study, or other lawful responsibility restricts earning. The verse does not define all poor people as fighters or require poverty as proof of devotion. It teaches donors to notice people whose circumstances limit income and whose dignity prevents them from public begging. A refugee unable to work, a caregiver, a disabled person, a student of beneficial knowledge, or a family trapped by conflict may all need discreet support, depending on the circumstances. An unaware person may think they are rich because they do not ask. Their clothing, speech, and dignity conceal deprivation. This is a challenge to shallow charity systems that help only the person who can stand in a queue and tell a dramatic story. The Qur’an asks believers to look carefully and respectfully for signs of need. Restraint—taʿaffuf—is not pride or refusal of all assistance. It is the effort to preserve dignity and avoid dependence upon people. The community must not exploit this restraint by assuming that quiet people need nothing. Relatives, neighbours, and responsible institutions should learn to offer help without forcing a person to expose private hardship. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**)

**POVERTY HIDDEN BY RESTRAINT**

***“about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not”*** deepens poverty hidden by restraint. You will recognize them by their signs invites attentive compassion, not spying or humiliation. Signs may include inadequate housing, unpaid medical needs, lack of food, inability to travel to work, worn tools, interrupted education, or a sudden change in circumstances. A donor should verify responsibly but protect privacy. No one should be accused of fraud merely because his need is not visible. Allah knows the truth, and human decisions should be based on reasonable evidence and good manners. A person may receive help and later become able to work; the gift is not a permanent label. They do not ask people persistently—lā yasʾalūna al-nāsa ilḥāfan—does not prohibit asking for help when genuine need exists. It praises those who do not harass, pressure, manipulate, or make begging their preferred livelihood while able to work. The needy person may ask clearly and honestly, and the community must respond without contempt. The Prophet ﷺ explained that the truly poor person is not simply the one who goes around asking, but the one whose need is not recognized and who does not persistently beg, in reports that illuminate hidden poverty, collected for the theme of hidden poverty by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. This hadith trains believers to search for hidden need. The verse places a responsibility on donors to be observant. Zakah administrators should develop discreet assessment, and charities should not rely only on public self-referral. Neighbours can check on elderly people, single parents, refugees, students, and disabled people without turning care into surveillance. (9:60 — **“Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy, for those employed to administer it,”**)

**RECOGNIZING SIGNS WITHOUT INTRUSION**

***“in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They”*** clarifies recognizing signs without intrusion. Support can be financial, medical, educational, legal, or vocational. The best help may remove the restriction itself—transport to work, equipment, childcare, a safe home, or documentation for a displaced person. Charity should seek dignity and independence where possible. The verse ends by assuring the giver that Allah knows every good expenditure. A donor may never know the full benefit of a discreet gift, and a recipient may not be able to express gratitude. Allah knows the hidden sacrifice, the careful search for a deserving person, and the kindness that prevented humiliation. The reminder also warns against giving to display one’s ability to identify hidden poverty. The goal is Allah’s pleasure, not the reputation of being perceptive or generous. Individual charity cannot replace just wages, accessible healthcare, protection from exploitation, and responsible public policy. Immediate help belongs beside the wider Qur’anic demand for economic justice. A society that praises the poor for not asking but refuses to create fair opportunities has misunderstood taqwā. Those who can work should be supported toward dignified work, while those unable to work retain a right to care. The categories must be assessed with mercy and expertise rather than suspicion. Think of hidden poverty through a neighbour who sits on his step every evening reading an old book while the other men of the street come home with their tools. Nobody in the street suspects that his cupboard has been empty for a week, and the family that feeds him once a month is the only one that ever learns his name. (59:7 — **“As for gains granted by Allah to His Messenger from the people of ˹other˺ lands,”**)

**THEY DO NOT BEG PERSISTENTLY**

***“do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah”*** closes with they do not beg persistently. Hidden poverty confronts poverty hidden by restraint in a reader who gives at the door of a man whose car is old and whose clothes are clean. The verse gives him a poor man with no asking hand, a face that can be read and a gift that reaches its owner in the account. And it asks him how many such men he has walked past in his own street. Because the close of hidden poverty identifies whoever knows every charity, showing through hidden poverty that the merit of a gift does not depend on the address it reaches. The people whose poverty is not seen are remembered with the neighbours of the giver in the verse about the open and private gift. And the same company is promised abundance in the chapter of the night, where the Book speaks of the guest who came and was turned away. Because hidden poverty opens into poverty hidden by restraint, recognizing signs without intrusion joins hidden poverty to poverty hidden by restraint. Since recognizing signs without intrusion develops hidden poverty, poverty hidden by restraint carries the transition. They do not beg persistently matters, which means recognizing signs without intrusion answers poverty hidden by restraint. Poverty hidden by restraint gives practical form to hidden poverty; they do not beg persistently sets its horizon. Today, hidden poverty shapes poverty hidden by restraint in present decisions. (4:36 — **“Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him. And be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor,”**)

## Verse 2:274

> Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**GENEROSITY AT EVERY TIME**

***“Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night,”*** establishes generosity at every time. This verse praises those who spend by night and day, secretly and publicly. The fourfold description suggests continuity and variety. Charity is not limited to a yearly campaign or a public emergency. A believer remains ready to help when a need appears, whether people see the gift or not. The wording does not require giving money constantly or neglecting family needs. It praises a settled disposition of generosity. The person gives according to ability, fulfils obligations, and looks for lawful opportunities to benefit others. A small regular gift can be more sincere and sustainable than a large donation made once for reputation. Secret giving often protects sincerity and the recipient’s dignity. Public giving can encourage others, support a visible institution, or demonstrate that a public trust is being fulfilled. The verse includes both, showing that the form is not the only measure. Intention and effect determine whether public visibility serves good or vanity. The donor should avoid turning recipients into publicity. If a project requires names, photographs, or stories, consent and privacy matter. Public accounts should report funds accurately without making the poor bear the cost of the donor’s reputation. Night and day also represent ease and difficulty, private and public life, and times of prosperity and scarcity. A person who gives only when he has excess may never learn sacrifice. A person who gives beyond capacity may harm dependants. The Qur’an’s balance is to give from what is lawful and available while preserving rights. (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a”**) A report on generosity at every time comes through Ibn ʿAbbās, who connected the pattern of giving by night and day, secretly and openly, with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. The comprehensive wording also prevents a false choice between private and public generosity. Each can be sincere or corrupt, so the governing question is which form best serves the recipient while protecting the giver’s intention. Therefore the four settings describe moral completeness rather than four unrelated kinds of charity. Because visibility changes the temptations surrounding a gift, intention and the recipient’s welfare must govern the chosen form.

**SECRET AND PUBLIC GIVING**

***“secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there”*** deepens secret and public giving. A gift at night may be especially hidden from people, while a public gift during the day may mobilize a community. Allah knows the intention in both. The believer asks Him to make generosity a character rather than an occasional performance. Their reward is with their Lord assures the giver that no good is lost. People may reject, forget, or misuse the gift, but Allah records the intention and effort. The phrase also protects the donor from expecting gratitude. He may evaluate a charity’s effectiveness and adjust future giving, but he does not transform aid into a debt of personal loyalty. The reward belongs to Allah’s generosity. The servant does not claim that his charity obligates Allah, nor does he despair when the worldly outcome is unseen. The seed and garden parables earlier in the passage teach that reward can grow beyond human observation. The promise of no fear and no grief is especially meaningful for those who worry that giving will leave them insecure. Allah can place blessing in what remains and reward what was sent ahead. In the Hereafter, the generous servant is protected from the fear of losing the eternal account and the grief of discovering that his wealth was wasted. This promise does not guarantee a life without financial anxiety. Believers can face poverty, illness, or loss. It gives them a deeper security and teaches them to seek lawful help when needed rather than being ashamed of dependence during hardship. (2:215 — **“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say,”**)

**SPENDING BY NIGHT AND DAY**

***“will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”*** clarifies spending by night and day. Continuous generosity supports more than emergency relief. It can fund schools, hospitals, water systems, shelters, food programmes, debt relief, and legal aid. A community that spends night and day develops structures that protect people before a crisis becomes catastrophic. Such institutions require governance. Donors should verify accounts, trustees should disclose conflicts, and recipients should be treated with dignity. Generosity without accountability can unintentionally enable corruption. The preceding verses warn against Satan’s threat of poverty. This verse presents the opposite heart: a person who trusts Allah enough to give at different times and in different forms. He does not worship wealth or measure every relationship by profit. His generosity expresses certainty that provision ultimately belongs to Allah. Muslim records the Prophetic teaching that charity does not diminish wealth in its true account. Al-Bukhārī records his preference for the giving hand over the receiving hand, while the Sunnah protects dependants from destitution. Generosity is strongest when joined to wisdom. Think of generosity at every time through a woman who keeps a bowl of coins by her door and drops one in it on her way out and another on her way back in. The bowl fills slowly through the year, the neighbours who watch her never see the whole sum, and the orphans of the street eat through the winter without knowing where the bread comes from. Generosity at every time confronts secret and public giving in one present-day reader; spending by night and day meets, under the demand of generosity at every time, someone accustomed to hearing that charity belongs only to annual accounts and public presentation. (2:272 — **“the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to”**)

**THEIR REWARD IS WITH ALLAH**

The verse gives him a night and a day, a secret and an open gift; spending by night and day asks him which of the four he has been leaving out of his ledger. Because the final words release faithful givers from grief and fear, showing through generosity at every time that the generosity of a person ends where his regret begins and not where his purse does. The same promise was made to the givers who keep their tongues quiet. And the reward of the quiet giver was named with the knowledge of the Lord. Because generosity at every time opens into secret and public giving, spending by night and day joins generosity at every time to secret and public giving. Since spending by night and day develops generosity at every time, secret and public giving carries the transition. Their reward is with allah matters, which means spending by night and day answers secret and public giving. Secret and public giving gives practical form to generosity at every time; their reward is with allah sets its horizon. Today, generosity at every time shapes secret and public giving in present decisions.
